nodes.name: Tate's theorem
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$ over the ring $\Z$, and suppose that for all subgroups $S$ of $G$ the following two conditions hold: \begin{itemize} \item $H^1(S,M) \cong 0$, \item $H^2(S,M) \cong \Z / |S| \cdot \Z$. \end{itemize} Then there is an isomorphism \[ M^G / N_G M \cong G^{\ab}. \] If $\sigma$ is a 2-cocycle representing a generator of $H^2(G,M)$ then the inverse of the isomorphism is given by \[ \reciprocity^{-1}(g) = \sum_{x \in G} \sigma(x,g). \]
nodes.statement_short: For a finite class formation over Z, Tate cohomology H^0 is the abelianization of G, with an explicit cocycle formula for the inverse.
assumptions: $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$ over the ring $\Z$
$\sigma$ is a 2-cocycle representing a generator of $H^2(G,M)$
conclusions: there is an isomorphism \[ M^G / N_G M \cong G^{\ab}. \]
the inverse of the isomorphism is given by \[ \reciprocity^{-1}(g) = \sum_{x \in G} \sigma(x,g). \]
there is an isomorphism \[ M^G / N_G M \cong G^{\ab}. \]

assumptions: $\sigma$ is a 2-cocycle representing a generator of $H^2(G,M)$
conclusions: the inverse of the isomorphism is given by \[ \reciprocity^{-1}(g) = \sum_{x \in G} \sigma(x,g). \]

nodes.name: Representation of a group over a ring
nodes.statement: By a \emph{representation of $G$ over $R$}, we shall mean an $R$-module $M$ with an action of $G$ by $R$-linear maps.
differentia: with an action of $G$ by $R$-linear maps

nodes.name: Notation for the group action
nodes.statement: We shall use the notation $g \bullet m$ for the action of an element $g \in G$ on an element $m \in M$.

nodes.name: Trivial representation
nodes.statement: We'll call $M$ a \emph{trivial} representation if for all $g \in G$ and all $m \in M$ we have $g \bullet m = m$.
differentia: for all $g \in G$ and all $m \in M$ we have $g \bullet m = m$

nodes.name: Categories Mod(R) and Rep(R,G)
nodes.statement: We'll write $\Mod(R)$ for the category of $R$-modules and $\Rep(R,G)$ for the category of such representations.

nodes.name: Restricted representation
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a subgroup of $G$ and $M$ is a representation of $G$ then $M \downarrow S$ will mean the same $R$-module $M$, but regarded only as a representation of $S$.

nodes.name: Invariant submodule
nodes.statement: We shall write $M^S$ for the $R$-submodule of $S$-invariant vectors in $M$.

nodes.name: Invariants of a normal subgroup are a quotient representation
nodes.statement: If the subgroup $S$ is normal then $M^S$ is a representation of the quotient group $G/S$.
conclusions: $M^S$ is a representation of the quotient group $G/S$

nodes.name: Restriction and inflation functors
nodes.statement: The map $M \mapsto M \downarrow S$ defines a functor $\Res : \Rep(R,G) \to \Rep(R,S)$. If $S$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ then then map $M \mapsto M^S$ defines a functor $\Invar : \Rep(R,G) \to \Rep(R, G/S)$. These functors are called \emph{restriction} and \emph{inflation} respectively. These are defined in Mathlib as \texttt{Rep.res} and \texttt{Rep.quotientToInvariantsFunctor}.
nodes.label: def:inflation restriction functors

nodes.name: Cochain complex of a representation
nodes.statement: Given a representation $M$ of $G$, there is a cochain complex of $R$-modules \[ C^0(G,M) \stackrel{d^0}\to C^1(G,M) \stackrel{d^1}\to C^2(G,M) \stackrel{d^2}\to \cdots \] where each term $C^n(G,M)$ is the space of functions $G^n \to M$ with some appropriately defined linear maps $d^i$ linking them. The zeroth module $C^0(G,M)$ should be interpreted as just $M$. The first few of these linear maps $d^i$ are \begin{align*} (d^0 m)(x) &= x \bullet m - m & m \in M, \\ (d^1 f)(x,y) &= x \bullet f(y) - f(xy) + f(x) & f : G \to M,\\ (d^2 f)(x,y,z) &= x\bullet f(y,z) - f(xy,z) + f(x,yz) - f(x,y), & f : G^2 \to M. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Inhomogeneous cochains C^n(G,M) = functions G^n -> M with the standard coboundaries d^0, d^1, d^2.

nodes.name: Group cohomology
nodes.statement: The cohomology groups of $C^\bullet(G,M)$ are called the cohomology groups of the $G$-module $M$, and are written $H^n(G,M)$.

nodes.name: Zeroth cohomology is the invariants
nodes.statement: For example $H^0(G,M)$ is the kernel of the map $d^0 : M \to (G \to M)$. Since $(d^0m)(g) = g \bullet m - m$, an element $m$ is in this kernel if $m$ is in $M^G$, so we have $H^0(G,M) \cong M^G$.
nodes.label: eg:H0

nodes.name: First cohomology of a trivial representation is Hom
nodes.statement: Suppose $M$ is a trivial representation of $G$. Then the map $d^0$ is zero, so $H^1(G,M)$ is the kernel of the map $(d^1f)(x,y) = f(x) + f(y) - f(xy)$. A function $f: G \to M$ is in this kernel if it is a group homomorphism, so we have $H^1(G,M) \cong \Hom(G,M)$.
nodes.label: eg:H1 trivial iso Hom

nodes.name: Cohomology of the trivial group vanishes
nodes.statement: If $G$ is the trivial group then for all $n>0$, $H^n(G,M)\cong 0$.
nodes.label: lem:Hn unit

nodes.name: Proof of vanishing for the trivial group
nodes.statement: Each of the modules $C^n(G,M)$ may be identified with $M$, and the coboundary maps reduce to alternating sums of the form $d^n(m) = \sum_{i=0}^{n+1} (-1)^i m$. Hence $d^n$ is the identity map for odd $n$, and is the zero map for even $m$. It follows that the image of $d^n$ is equal to the kernel of $d^{n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Cochains all identify with M and the coboundaries alternate between identity and zero, so images equal kernels.

nodes.name: Independence of cohomology from the coefficient ring
nodes.statement: The functions $d^i : (G^i \to M) \to (G^{i+1} \to M)$ do not depend on the ring $R$. Consequently, the additive groups $H^n(G,M)$ do not depend on $R$. More precisely there are forgetful functors $F_1 : \Rep(R,G) \to \Rep(\Z,G)$ and $F_2 : \Mod(R) \to \Mod(\Z)$, and there are isomorphisms of functors \[ H^n \circ F_1 \cong F_2 \circ H^n. \] That said, it is very little extra work to prove the cohomological results discussed here in the generality of $\Rep(R,G)$ rather than $\Rep(\Z,G)$.
nodes.statement_short: The cochain differentials do not depend on R, giving an isomorphism of functors H^n F_1 = F_2 H^n.

nodes.name: Functoriality matters for formalization
nodes.statement: At this point it's worth stressing one particular aspect of this theory. Many of the proofs involve showing that certain diagrams commute. When writing proofs on paper, some mathematicians don't give too much thought to the reasons why a particular diagram commutes but when formalizing theorems we need to be more careful than this. For that reason it is important to define all of our objects in as functorial a way as possible. In the example from the previous remark, saying that there is an isomorphism $H^n(G,F_1(M)) \cong F_2(H^n(G,M))$ is not as good as saying that there is an isomorphism of functors $H^n \circ F_1 \cong F_2 \circ H^n$. The isomorphism of functors implies that for every map $f : A \to B$ in $\Rep(R,G)$ we have a commuting square in $\Mod(\Z)$, in which the vertical arrows are the isomorphisms of the objects \[ \begin{matrix} H^n(G,F_1(A)) & \stackrel{H^1(G,F_1(f))}\to & H^n(G,F_1(B))\\ \downarrow &&\downarrow \\ F_2(H^n(G,M)) & \stackrel{F_2(H^1(G,f))}\to & F_2 H^n(G,B) \end{matrix} . \] This commuting square might be crucial in some other proof. This is also the reason why we work with the categories \texttt{Rep R G} and \texttt{ModuleCat R}, rather than with \texttt{Representation R G M} and \texttt{Module R M} which could be more familiar.
nodes.statement_short: Diagrams must commute for reasons, so objects are defined functorially; this is why Rep R G and ModuleCat R are used.

nodes.name: Restriction map
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a subgroup of $G$, then we write $H^n(S,M)$ for the cohomology groups of the restricted representation $M \downarrow S$. If $f : G^n \to M$ is an element of $C^n(G,M)$, then we may restrict $f$ to a function $S^n \to M$. Restricting functions in this way defines a map of cochain complexes $C^\bullet(G,M) \to C^\bullet(S,M)$, and hence a map of cohomology groups \[ \rest : H^n(G,M) \to H^n(S,M). \] This map is called the \emph{restriction map}, and is a morphism of functors from $H^n(G,-)$ to $H^n(S, -) \circ \Res$.
nodes.label: def:restriction map

nodes.name: Inflation map
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, then we write $H^n(G/S,M^S)$ for the cohomology groups of the representation $M^S$ of $G/S$. If $f : (G/S)^n \to M^S$ is an element of $C^n(G/S,M^S)$, then we may ``inflate'' $f$ to a function $G^n \to M$. This inflation process defines a map of cochain complexes $C^\bullet(G/S,M^S) \to C^\bullet(G,M)$, and hence a map of cohomology groups, called the \emph{inflation map}: \[ \infl : H^n(G/S,M^H) \to H^n(G,M). \] More precisely, the inflation map is a morphism of functors from $H^n (G/S, -)\circ \Invar$ to $H^n(G,-)$.
nodes.label: def:inflation map

nodes.name: Exactness of the cochain functor
nodes.statement: The functor taking $M$ to $C^\bullet (G,M)$ is exact. I.e. if $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ is a short exact sequence in $\Rep(R,G)$. Then the corresponding sequence of cochain complexes is exact: \[ 0 \to C^\bullet(G,A) \to C^\bullet(G,B) \to C^\bullet(G,C) \to 0. \]
assumptions: $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ is a short exact sequence in $\Rep(R,G)$
conclusions: the corresponding sequence of cochain complexes is exact
nodes.label: lem:cochainsFunctor exact

nodes.name: Proof of exactness of the cochain functor
nodes.statement: This is already in Mathlib.

nodes.name: Long exact sequence in group cohomology
nodes.statement: Given a short exact sequence $0 \to A \stackrel{f}\to B \stackrel{g}\to C \to 0$ in $\Rep(R,G)$, the corresponding sequence of cochain complexes is exact: $0 \to C^n(G,A) \to C^n(G,B) \to C^n(G,C) \to 0$. This implies that there exist ``connecting homomorphisms'' $\delta : H^n(G,C) \to H^{n+1}(G,A)$, such that the following is a long exact sequence: \[ 0 \to H^0(G,A) \stackrel{H^0(f)}\to H^0(G,B) \stackrel{H^0(g)}\to H^0(G,C) \stackrel{\delta}\to H^1(G,A) \stackrel{H^1(f)}\to H^1(G,B) \stackrel{H^1(g)} \to H^1(G,C) \stackrel{\delta}\to \cdots. \]
nodes.statement_short: A short exact sequence of representations yields connecting maps and a long exact sequence in cohomology.
nodes.label: def:cohomology long exact sequence

nodes.name: Naturality of restriction and inflation on long exact sequences
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of $G$ and suppose we have a short exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ in $\Rep(R,G)$. Then the sequence the sequence $0 \to A \downarrow S \to B \downarrow S \to C \downarrow S \to 0$ is exact in $\Rep(R,S)$. The following diagram commutes, where the rows are the long exact sequences for $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ and for its restriction to $S$, and the vertical maps are restriction. \[ \begin{array}{ccccccc} H^n(G,A) & \to & H^n(G,B) &\to &H^n(G,C)& \to& H^{n+1}(G,A)\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow \\ H^n(S,A) & \to & H^n(S,B) &\to &H^n(S,C)& \to& H^{n+1}(S,A) \end{array} \] Suppose now that $S$ is a normal subgroup of $G$. Then we have for every map $f : A \to B$ in $\Rep(R,G)$ a commuting square in which the vertical maps are inflation. \[ \begin{array}{ccccccc} H^n(G/S,A^S) & \stackrel{H^n(\Invar(f))}\to & H^n(G/S,B^S)\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow \\ H^n(G,A) & \stackrel{H^n(f)}\to & H^n(G,B) \end{array}. \] If $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ is exact in $\Rep(R,G)$ and its inflation $0 \to A^S \to B^S \to C^S \to 0$ is also exact in $Rep(R,G/S)$, then we have a commutative diagram in which the rows are the corresponding long exact sequences and the vertical maps are inflation: \[ \begin{array}{ccccccc} H^n(G/S,A^S) & \to & H^n(G/S,B^S) &\to &H^n(G/S,C^S)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G/S,A^S)\\ \downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow&&\downarrow \\ H^n(G,A) & \to & H^n(G,B) &\to &H^n(G,C)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G,A) \end{array}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Restriction and inflation commute with the maps, including connecting maps, of the long exact cohomology sequence.
assumptions: we have a short exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ in $\Rep(R,G)$
nodes.label: lem:inflation restriction naturality

nodes.name: Proof of naturality of restriction and inflation
nodes.statement: Most of the commuting squares have already been proved if inflation and restriction are defined as morphisms of functors. The remaining two squares are: \[ \begin{matrix} H^n(G,C)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G,A)\\ \rest\downarrow&&\downarrow\rest \\ H^n(S,C)& \stackrel{\delta} \to& H^{n+1}(S,A) \end{matrix} \qquad\textrm{ and }\qquad \begin{matrix} H^n(G/S,C^S)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G/S,A^S)\\ \infl\downarrow&&\downarrow\infl\\ H^n(G,C)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G,A) \end{matrix} . \] Both of these can be deduced from the following statement in Mathlib: \begin{quote} \texttt{HomologicalComplex.HomologySequence.$\delta$\_naturality} \end{quote}
nodes.statement_short: Most squares commute by functoriality; the two connecting-map squares follow from Mathlib's delta-naturality.

nodes.name: Group homology
nodes.statement: There is also a chain complex of $R$-modules: \[ \cdots \stackrel{d_2}\to C_2(G,M) \stackrel{d_1}\to C_1(G,M) \stackrel{d_0}\to C_0(G,M) \] whose $n$-th term is the space of finitely supported functions $f : G^n \to_0 M$, with appropriately defined boundary maps $d_n$. In the literature $C_n(G,M)$ is often defined as $R[G]^{\otimes n} \otimes_R M$, to which it is canonically isomorphic. In the case $n=0$ this is interpreted as meaning $C_0(G,M) = M$. The homology groups of $C_n(G,M)$ are called the \emph{homology groups of $M$} and are written $H_n(G,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Homology of the chain complex of finitely supported functions G^n -> M.
nodes.label: def:group homology

nodes.name: Zeroth homology is the coinvariants
nodes.statement: We'll sometimes write $\single(g,m)$ for the function with value $m$ at $g$ and value zero elsewhere. The $R$-module $C_1(G,M)$ is spanned by the elements $\single(g,m)$ for $g \in G$ and $m \in M$ (\texttt{Finsupp.single} in Mathlib). For such elements we have \[ d_0(\single(g,m)) = g \bullet m - m. \] We shall write $I_G M$ for the submodule of $M$ spanned by elements of the form $g \bullet m - m$. The quotient $M / I_GM$ is commonly called the \emph{coinvariants} of $M$ and is written $M_G$; this is the largest quotient module on which $G$ acts trivially. It follows that $H_0(G,M) \cong M_G$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduces single(g,m), I_G M and the coinvariants M_G, and shows H_0(G,M) = M_G.
nodes.label: eg:homology 0

nodes.name: Homology of the trivial group
nodes.statement: In the case that $G=1$ is the trivial group then for all $n > 0$ we have $H_n(1,M)$. This follows in a similar way to \ref{lem:Hn unit}
nodes.label: eg:homology unit

nodes.name: First homology of a trivial representation
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a trivial representation of $G$ then $H_1(G,M) \cong G^{\ab} \otimes \Z M$. The isomorphism takes a 1-cycle $\single(x,m)$ to $xG' \otimes m$ for $x \in G$ and $m \in M$. (This result is already in Mathlib).
nodes.statement_short: For trivial M, H_1(G,M) is G^ab tensor M.
nodes.label: lem:homology 1 trivial

nodes.name: Proof of H_1 of a trivial representation
nodes.statement: Since $M$ is trivial, the map $d_0 : C_1(G,M) \to C_0(G,M)$ is zero, so every $1$-chain is a 1-cycle. The map $d_1 : C_1(G,M) \to C_0(G,M)$ is given by \[ d_1 \single((x,y),m) = \single(y,x^{-1} \bullet m) - \single(xy,m) + \single(x,m). \] Therefore $H_1(G,M)$ is the quotient of $G \to_0 M$ by the relations \[ \single(xy,m) = \single(x,m) + \single(y,m), \qquad x,y \in G. \] If we fix an $m \in M$, then these relations imply that the map $G \to H_1(G,M)$ defined by $x \mapsto \single(x,m)$ is a group homomorphism. In particular this map descends to a homomorphism $G^{\ab} \to H_1(G,M)$. If we fix $x \in G$ and allow $m$ to vary, then $\single(x,m)$ is $\Z$-linear in $m$. It is therefore a $\Z$-bilinear map $G^\ab \times M \to H_1(G,M)$. Such a map lifts to a linear map $\Phi : G^{\ab} \otimes_{\Z} M \to H_1(G,M)$ given by \[ xG' \otimes m \mapsto \single(x,m) \] To construct an inverse of $\Phi$, we note that all of the relations are in the kernel of the linear map $(G\to_0 M) \to (G^\ab \otimes_\Z M)$ defined by $\single(x,m) \mapsto xG' \otimes m$. Therefore this map descends to a linear map $\Psi : H_1(G,M) \to (G^\ab \otimes_\Z M)$. It is trivial to check that $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are inverses.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit computation with 1-chains: construct Phi from G^ab tensor M and an inverse Psi from the relations.

nodes.name: G is finite
nodes.statement: Throughout this section, the group $G$ is assumed to be finite.

nodes.name: Norm map
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $M$ a representation of $G$ over a commutative ring $R$. There is a canonical linear map $N_G : M \to M$ called the \emph{norm}, defined by \[ N_G(m) = \sum_{g \in G} g \bullet m. \] We shall also regard the norm as a linear map from $C_0(G,M)$ to $C^0(G,M)$, both of which may be identified with $M$. (We'll see in the next lemma that $N_G$ commutes with the action of $G$, so is a morphism in $\Rep(R,G)$. However, we shall only regard it as a morphism in $\Mod(R)$. The reason is that the chain and cochain modules $C^0(G,M)$ and $C_0(G,M)$ are regarded as $R$-modules rather than representations of $G$.)
nodes.label: def:norm

nodes.name: The norm is G-invariant
nodes.statement: For any $g \in G$ and $m \in M$ we have $g \bullet N_G (m) = N_G (m)$ and $N_G (g \bullet m) = N_G (m)$.
nodes.label: lem:norm comm

nodes.name: Proof of G-invariance of the norm
nodes.statement: These equalities follow by reindexing the sums defining $N_G (m)$: \[ g \bullet \sum_{x \in G} x \bullet m = \sum_{x \in G} g \bullet x \bullet m = \sum_{x \in G} x \bullet m, \] \[ \sum_{x \in G} x \bullet g \bullet m = \sum_{x \in G} x \bullet m. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reindex the sums defining the norm.

nodes.name: d^0 composed with the norm is zero
nodes.statement: The composition $d^0 \circ N_G$ is zero.
nodes.label: lem:norm comp d

nodes.name: Proof that d^0 N_G = 0
nodes.statement: The map $d^0 : M \to (G \to M)$ is given by $(d^0 m)(g) = m - g\bullet m$. Using this formula, we obtain (by Lemma \ref{lem:norm comm}) $d^0 (N_G m) (g) = g \bullet N_G m - N_G m = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the formula for d^0 and G-invariance of the norm.

nodes.name: The norm composed with d_0 is zero
nodes.statement: The composition $N_G \circ d_0$ is zero.
nodes.label: lem:d comp norm

nodes.name: Proof that N_G d_0 = 0
nodes.statement: Since the elements $\single(g,m)$ span $C_1(G,M)$, it's sufficient to check that these are all mapped to $0$. We have by \ref{lem:norm comm} \[ N_G(d_0 (\single(g,m))) = N_G( g \bullet m - m) = N_G( g \bullet m) - N_G(m) = 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Check on the spanning elements single(g,m) using invariance of the norm.

nodes.name: Naturality of the norm
nodes.statement: For every map $f : A \to B$ in $\Rep(R,G)$ we have a commuting square: \[ \begin{array}{rcl} A & \stackrel{f}\to & B \\[2mm] N_G\downarrow && \downarrow N_G \\ A & \stackrel{f}\to & B \end{array} . \] Equivalently, $N_G$ is an endomorphism of the forgetful functor $\Rep(R,G) \to \Mod(R)$.
nodes.label: lem:norm naturality

nodes.name: Proof of naturality of the norm
nodes.statement: For $m \in M$ we have \[ f(N_G (m)) = f\left( \sum_{g \in G} g \bullet m\right) = \sum_{g \in G} g \bullet f(m) = N_G(f(m)). \]
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: f is G-equivariant and linear.

nodes.name: Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: Recall that we have a cochain complex $C^n(G,M)$, indexed by $n \in \N$, whose zeroth term may be identified with $M$. We also have a chain complex $C_n(G,M)$ whose zeroth term may be identified with $M$. By \ref{lem:norm comp d} and \ref{lem:d comp norm}, we may glue these together with the map $N_G : M \to M$ to obtain a cochain complex indexed by $\Z$: \[ \cdots \to C_2(G,M) \to C_1(G,M) \stackrel{d_0}\to C_0(G,M) \stackrel{N_G}\to C^0(G,M) \stackrel{d^0}\to C^1(G,M) \to C^2(G,M) \to \cdots \] We shall write $C^n_{\Tate}(G,M)$ for this cochain complex, and we normalize the indices so that for natural numbers $n$ we have $C^n_{\Tate}(G,M) = C^n(G,M)$. This implies $C^{-n-1}_{\Tate}(G,M) = C_n(G,M)$. It follows from \ref{lem:norm naturality} that $C^\bullet_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is functorial in $M$. For an integer $n$, we shall write $H^n_{\Tate}(G,M)$ for the $n$-th cohomology of the complex $C^n_{\Tate}(G,M)$; this is called the $n$-th Tate cohomology of $M$, and is often written $\hat H^n(G,M)$ or (confusingly) just $H^n(G,M)$ in the literature. We stress that Tate cohomology exists only in the case that $G$ is a finite group.
nodes.statement_short: Glue the cochain and chain complexes along the norm into a Z-indexed complex; its cohomology is Tate cohomology.
nodes.label: def:Tate cohomology

nodes.name: Tate cohomology via cohomology and homology
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $M$ a representation of $G$. \begin{itemize} \item The zeroth Tate cohomology $H^0_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is isomorphic to $M^G / N_G(M)$. In particular if $M$ is a trivial representation of $G$ then $H^0_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong M / |G|M$. \item For $n >0 $ we have (an isomorphism of functors in the variable $M$) \[ H^{n}_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong H^{n}(G,M). \] \item There is an isomorphism \[ H^{-1}_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong \ker (N_G : M \to M ) / I_G M, \] Where $I_GM$ is the submodule of $M$ generated by elements of the form $g \bullet m - m$. In particular if $M$ is a trivial representation of $G$ then $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is isomorphic to the $|G|$-torsion in $M$. \item For $n < -1$ we have (an isomorphism of functors in the variable $M$) \[ H^{n}_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong H_{-1-n} (G,M). \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Tate cohomology equals cohomology for n>0, homology for n<-1, and explicit norm quotients in degrees 0 and -1.
assumptions: $G$ be a finite group and $M$ a representation of $G$
conclusions: The zeroth Tate cohomology $H^0_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is isomorphic to $M^G / N_G(M)$
nodes.label: lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology

nodes.name: Proof of Tate cohomology via cohomology and homology
nodes.statement: This result is clear from the definition for $n > 0$ and $n < -1$. We'll discuss the two remaining cases. The $0$-cocycle submodule is the kernel of the map $d^0 : C^0(G,M) \to C^1(G,M)$. This is the same as $H^0(G,M)$, which is isomorphic to $M^G$. On the other hand $B^0_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is by definition the image of $N_G : M \to M$. Similarly, $H_0(G,M)$ is the quotient of $M$ by $I_GM$, and $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is by definition the quotient of $\ker(N_G : M \to M)$ by the same submodule.
nodes.statement_short: Clear from the definition except in degrees 0 and -1, which are computed directly.

nodes.name: Long exact sequence in Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: Since the functors $C^\bullet(G,-)$ and $C_\bullet(G,-)$ are both exact, it follows that $C^\bullet_{\Tate}(G,-)$ is an exact functor. Hence, given any short exact sequence in $\Rep(R,G)$: \[ 0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0, \] we obtain a short exact sequence of Tate complexes and therefore connecting homomorphisms $\delta : H^n_{\Tate}(G,C) \to H^{n+1}_{\Tate}(G,A)$ such that the following is a long exact sequence (for $n \in \Z$): \[ \cdots \to H^n_{\Tate}(G,A) \to H^n_{\Tate}(G,B) \to H^n_{\Tate}(G,C) \to H^{n+1}_{\Tate}(G,A) \to H^{n+1}_{\Tate}(G,B) \to \cdots \] The exactness statements are in Mathlib in the namespace \texttt{HomologicalComplex.HomologySequence}. The connecting maps $\delta : H^n_{\Tate}(G,C) \to H^{n+1}_{\Tate}(G,A)$ coincide with those for cohomology for $n \ge 1$ and with those for homology for $n \le -3$.
nodes.label: def:Tate long exact sequence

nodes.name: Trivial cohomology, homology and Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a representation of $G$ over a ring $R$. \begin{itemize} \item $M$ is said to have \emph{trivial cohomology} if for every subgroup $S \le G$ and every $n > 0$, $H^n(S,M) \cong 0$. \item $M$ is said to have \emph{trivial homology} if for every subgroup $S \le G$ and every $n > 0$, $H_n(S,M) \cong 0$. \item Suppose the group $G$ is finite. Then $M$ is said to have \emph{trivial Tate cohomology} if for every subgroup $S \le G$ and every $n \in \Z$, $H^n_{\Tate}(S,M) \cong 0$. \end{itemize} (We will later see that for a finite group $G$, the three concepts are equivalent.)
nodes.label: def:trivial cohomology

nodes.name: Coinduction along a homomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi : S \to G$ be a group homomorphism and let $M$ be a representation of $S$. We define a representation $\coind_\phi(M)$ of $G$ as follows. As an $R$-module we have \[ \coind_\phi(M) = \{ f : G \to M| \forall s \in S, x \in G, f(\phi(s)x) = s \bullet f(x)\}. \] This space can be regarded as the $(G \to M)^S$, where the action of $S$ is $(s\bullet f)(x)=s \bullet f(\phi(s^{-1})\bullet x)$. The action of an element $g \in G$ on $f \in \coind_\phi(M)$ is defined by \[ (g \bullet f)(x) = f(xg). \] The map $M \mapsto \coind_\phi(M)$ is a functor from $\Rep(R,S)$ to $\Rep(R,G)$, and is implemented in Mathlib as \texttt{Rep.coindFunctor}.
nodes.statement_short: coind_phi(M): functions f: G -> M with f(phi(s)x) = s.f(x), with G acting by right translation.

nodes.name: Induction along a homomorphism
nodes.statement: There is also a functor $\ind_\phi : \Rep(R,S) \to \Rep(R,G)$ which is defined as a quotient of $G \to_0 M$ rather than a subspace of $G \to M$: \[ \ind_\phi(M) = (G \to_0 M) / \langle s \bullet f - f\rangle, \qquad (s \bullet f) (x) = s \bullet f (x \phi(s)). \] The action of an element $g \in G$ on $G \to_0 M$ is defined by $(g \bullet f)(x) = f(g^{-1} x)$; this action descends to $\ind_\phi(M)$. The functor $\ind_\phi : \Rep(R,S) \to \Rep(R,G)$ is implemented in Mathlib as \texttt{Rep.ind}.
nodes.statement_short: ind_phi(M): finitely supported functions G -> M modulo the S-action relations, with G acting by left translation.

nodes.name: Shapiro's Lemma
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then there are isomorphisms for all $n \ge 0$: \[ H^n(G,\coind_S(M)) \cong H^n(S,M), \qquad H_n(G,\ind_S(M)) \cong H_n(S,M), \qquad \] More precisely these are isomorphisms of functors.
nodes.label: lem:Shapiro

nodes.name: Proof of Shapiro's Lemma
nodes.statement: This is already in Mathlib.

nodes.name: Coinduced and induced representations
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group, $R$ a commutative ring and $A$ an $R$-module. \begin{itemize} \item There is a representation of $G$ over $R$ on the space of all functions $f : G \to A$. The action of an element $g \in G$ on $f$ is defined by \[ (g \bullet f) (x) = f(xg). \] This representation is called the coinduced representation and is denoted $\coind_1(G,A)$. \item There is a representation of $G$ over $R$ on the space of all finitely supported functions $f : G \to_0 A$. The action of an element $g \in G$ on $f$ is defined by \[ (g \bullet f) (x) = f(xg), \qquad i.e.\; g \bullet \single(x,m) = \single(xg^{-1},m). \] This representation is called the induced representation and is denoted $\ind_1(G,A)$. \end{itemize} More precisely, $\coind_1(G,-)$ and $\ind_1(G,-)$ are both functors from $\Mod(R)$ to $\Rep(R,G)$.
nodes.statement_short: coind_1(G,A): all functions G -> A; ind_1(G,A): finitely supported ones; G acts by right translation.
nodes.label: def:induced

nodes.name: Coinduced representations have trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: The representation $\coind_1(G,A)$ has trivial cohomology.
nodes.label: lem:coind₁ trivial cohomology

nodes.name: Proof that coinduced representations have trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of $G$ and let $C$ be a set of representatives for the cosets $cS$ of $S$ in $G$. There is an isomorphism of $S$-representations \[ \coind_1(G,M) \downarrow S \cong \coind_1(S,C \to M). \] This isomorphism takes a function $f : G \to M$ to function $S \to (C \to M)$ defined by $s \mapsto (c \mapsto f(cs))$. The isomorphism, together with \ref{lem:Shapiro} and \ref{lem:Hn unit} implies for $n >0$: \[ H^n(S,\coind_1(G,M)) \cong H^n(S,\coind_1(S,C \to M)) \cong H^n(1,C \to M) \cong 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to S as a coinduced module over coset representatives and apply Shapiro's lemma.

nodes.name: Invariants of a coinduced representation
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Then $\coind_1(G,A)^S$ is isomorphic to $\coind_1(G/S,A)$. In particular $\coind_1(G,A)^S$ is has trivial cohomology as a representation of $G/S$.
conclusions: $\coind_1(G,A)^S$ is has trivial cohomology as a representation of $G/S$
nodes.label: lem:coind₁ invariants

nodes.name: Proof of invariants of a coinduced representation
nodes.statement: Let $f : G \to A$. Then $f$ is in the subspace $\coind_1(G,A)^S$ if $f$ is constant on cosets of $S$, i.e. it descends to a function $G/S \to A$. This gives a linear bijection $\coind_1(G,A)^S \cong \coind_1(G/S,A)$, and it's trivial to check that this map is compatible with the action of $G / S$.
nodes.statement_short: S-invariant functions are those constant on cosets, i.e. functions on G/S.

nodes.name: Induced representations have trivial homology
nodes.statement: The representation $\ind_1(G,A)$ has trivial homology.
nodes.label: lem:ind₁ trivial homology

nodes.name: Proof that induced representations have trivial homology
nodes.statement: The restriction of $\ind_1(G,A)$ to a subgroup $S$ is isomorphic to $\ind_1(S, C \to_0 A)$, where $C$ is a set of coset representatives for the cosets $cS$ of $S$ in $G$. Hence by \ref{lem:Shapiro} we have \[ H_n(S,\ind_1(G,A)) \cong H_n(S,\ind_1(S,C\to_0 A)\cong H_n(1,C \to_0 A). \] The result now follows from \ref{eg:homology unit}.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction is induced; apply Shapiro's lemma and homology of the trivial group.

nodes.name: Induced-to-coinduced morphism
nodes.statement: There is a morphism of representations $\ind_1(G,A) \to \coind_1(G,A)$, which takes a finitely supported function $f : G \to_0 A$ to the function $f$. If the group $G$ is finite then this map is an isomorphism. More precisely, this is an isomorphism of functors $\ind_1(G,-) \cong \coind_1(G,-)$.
nodes.statement_short: The inclusion of finitely supported functions; an isomorphism of functors when G is finite.
nodes.label: def:ind₁ to coind₁

nodes.name: Induced representations have trivial Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: If the group $G$ is finite then $\ind_1(G,A)$ and $\coind_1(G,A)$ have trivial Tate cohomology.
nodes.label: lem:induced trivial Tate

nodes.name: Proof that induced representations have trivial Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: These representations are isomorphic, so it's sufficient to prove that $\ind_1(G,A)$ has trivial Tate cohomology (this is the more convenient case to prove). We already know that $\ind_1(G,A)$ has trivial homology. Also, since it is isomorphic to $\coind_1(G,A)$, it must have trivial cohomology. It only remains to prove that $H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(M))$ and $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(M))$ are zero for all subgroups $S$ of $G$. Recall that $\ind_1(G,M)$ is the space of functions $G \to_0 M$, and the action of $G$ is by right-translation: \[ g \bullet \single(x,m) = \single(xg^{-1},m). \] To prove that $H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A))=0$, we use the isomorphism \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology}: \[ H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A)) \cong \ind_1(G,A)^S / N_S \ind_1(G,A). \] A function $f : G \to_0 M$ is $S$-invariant if $f$ is constant on cosets $gS$ of $S$. If we let $\{g_i\}$ be a set of coset representatives, then we have $f = N_S (\sum_i \single(g_i, f(g_i)))$. Therefore $H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A))=0$. For the $n=-1$ case we use the isomorphism \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology}: \[ H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A)) \cong \ker(N_S : \ind_1(G,A) \to \ind_1(G,A)) / I_S \ind_1(M), \] where $I_G \ind_1(M)$ is generated by elements of the form $s \bullet f - f$ for $s \in S$ and $f : G \to M$. Suppose $f:G \to_0 M$ is in the kernel of $N_S$. This implies that the sum of the values of $f$ over each coset of $S$ is zero. We can then write $f$ in the form \begin{align*} f & = \sum_i \sum_{s \in S} (\single(g_i s^{-1}, f(g_is^{-1})) - \single(g_i,f(g_is^{-1})))\\ & = \sum_i \sum_{s \in S} (s \bullet \single(g_i, f(g_is^{-1})) - \single(g_i,f(g_is^{-1}))). \end{align*} Therefore $f \in I_S \ind_1(M)$. This shows that $H^{-1}(S,\ind_1(M)) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Tate degrees 0 and -1 for ind_1, then write invariant and norm-zero functions explicitly using coset representatives.

nodes.name: Representation coind_1'(M)
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group and $M$ a representation of $G$ over a commutative ring $R$. There is a representation $\coind_1' (M)$ on the $R$-module of functions $G \to M$. The action of an element $g \in G$ on a function $f : G \to M$ is given by \[ (g \bullet f)(x) = g \bullet (f (xg)). \]
nodes.label: def:coind₁'

nodes.name: coind_1'(M) is isomorphic to coind_1(G,M)
nodes.statement: The representations $\coind_1'(M)$ and $\coind_1(G,M)$ of $G$ are isomorphic. More precisely there is an isomorphism of functors $\coind_1' \cong \coind_1(G,-) \circ \Forget$, where $\Forget : \Rep(R,G) \to \Mod(R)$ is the forgetful functor.
conclusions: The representations $\coind_1'(M)$ and $\coind_1(G,M)$ of $G$ are isomorphic.
nodes.label: lem:coind₁' iso coind₁

nodes.name: Proof that coind_1' is isomorphic to coind_1
nodes.statement: The map $f \mapsto (x \mapsto x \bullet f(x))$ is an isomorphism from $\coind_1'(M)$ to $\coind_1(G,M)$.

nodes.name: coind_1'(M) has trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: The representation $\coind_1'(M)$ has trivial cohomology.
nodes.label: cor:coind₁' trivial cohomology

nodes.name: Proof that coind_1'(M) has trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: This follows directly from Lemmas \ref{lem:coind₁' iso coind₁} and \ref{lem:coind₁ trivial cohomology}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the isomorphism with coind_1 having trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Invariants of coind_1'(M) have trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a normal subgroup of $G$. Then $\coind_1'(M)^S$ has trivial cohomology as a representation of $G/S$.
conclusions: $\coind_1'(M)^S$ has trivial cohomology as a representation of $G/S$
nodes.label: cor:coind₁' invariants trivial cohomology

nodes.name: Proof that invariants of coind_1'(M) have trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: We've seen in Lemma \ref{lem:coind₁' iso coind₁} that $\coind_1'(M)$ is isomorphic to $\coind_1(M)$. Applying the functor $\Invar$, we obtain an isomorphism between $\coind_1'(M)^S$ and $\coind_1(M)^S$. The result then follows from Lemma \ref{lem:coind₁ invariants}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply invariants to the isomorphism coind_1' = coind_1 and use the coinduced invariants lemma.

nodes.name: Dimension-shifting representation up(M)
nodes.statement: There is an injective morphism $M \to \coind_1'(M)$ which takes a vector $m \in M$ to the constant function on $G$ with value $m$. We define a representation $\up(M)$ to be the cokernel of this map, so that we have a short exact sequence \[ 0 \to M \to \coind_1'(M) \to \up(M) \to 0. \] This construction is functorial in $M$; in particular for every $f : M_1 \to M_2$ in $\Rep(R,G)$, there is a commutative diagram \[ \begin{matrix} 0 & \to & M_1 & \to & \coind_1'(M_1) & \to& \up(M_1) \to 0 \\ &&\downarrow &&\downarrow&&\downarrow \\ 0 & \to & M_2 & \to & \coind_1'(M_2) & \to& \up(M_2) \to 0 \\ \end{matrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: up(M) is the cokernel of M -> coind_1'(M) (constant functions), functorially in M.
nodes.label: def:up

nodes.name: Dimension shifting with up
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be any subgroup of $G$ and let $n \ge 1$. Then the connecting map from the long exact sequence $H^{n}(S,\up(M)) \to H^{n+1}(S,M)$ is an isomorphism. The corresponding map $H^{0}(S,\up(M)) \to H^{1}(S,M)$ is surjective. The isomorphism $H^{n}(S,\up(-)) \cong H^{n+1}(S,-)$ is an isomorphism of functors. This means that for every morphism $f : M \to N$ of representations, the following square commutes: \[ \begin{matrix} H^{n}(S,\up(M)) & \cong & H^{n+1}(S,M) \\ \downarrow && \downarrow \\ H^{n}(S,\up(N)) & \cong & H^{n+1}(S,N) \end{matrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Connecting maps H^n(S,up M) -> H^{n+1}(S,M) are natural isomorphisms for n>=1 and surjective for n=0.
conclusions: the connecting map from the long exact sequence $H^{n}(S,\up(M)) \to H^{n+1}(S,M)$ is an isomorphism
The corresponding map $H^{0}(S,\up(M)) \to H^{1}(S,M)$ is surjective.
nodes.label: cor:up iso

nodes.name: Proof of dimension shifting with up
nodes.statement: We have already shown in Corollary \ref{cor:coind₁' trivial cohomology} that $\coind_1'(M)$ has trivial cohomology, so $H^{r}(S,\coind_1'(M))=0$ for all $r>0$. This implies that the connecting maps are isomorphisms. The commuting square follows from \texttt{HomologicalComplex.HomologySequence.$\delta$\_naturality} because the short exact sequence $0 \to M \to \coind_1'(M) \to \up(M) \to 0$ is functorial in $M$.
nodes.statement_short: coind_1'(M) has trivial cohomology so connecting maps are isomorphisms; naturality from delta-naturality.

nodes.name: Representation ind_1'(M)
nodes.statement: There is a representation $\ind_1' (M)$ on the $R$-module of finitely supported functions $G \to_0 M$. The action of an element $g \in G$ on a function $f : G \to_0 M$ is given by \[ (g \bullet f)(x) = g \bullet (f (xg)),\qquad \text{i.e. } g \bullet \single(g,m) = \single(xg^{-1}, g\bullet m). \] The map $\ind_1'$ is functorial in $M$.
nodes.label: def:ind'

nodes.name: ind_1'(M) is isomorphic to ind_1(G,M)
nodes.statement: The representations $\ind_1'(M)$ and $\ind_1(G,M)$ are isomorphic; more precisely the functors $\ind_1'$ and $\ind_1(G,-) \circ \Forget$ are isomorphic.
nodes.label: lem:ind₁' iso ind₁

nodes.name: Proof that ind_1' is isomorphic to ind_1
nodes.statement: The data of the isomorphism is contained in the lean file; the isomorphism takes $f : G \to_0 M$ to the finitely supported function \[ x \mapsto x \bullet f(x). \] It remains to check linearity and naturality.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit isomorphism f -> (x -> x.f(x)); check linearity and naturality.

nodes.name: ind_1'(M) has trivial homology
nodes.statement: The representation $\ind_1'(M)$ has trivial homology.
nodes.label: cor:ind₁' trivial homology

nodes.name: Proof that ind_1'(M) has trivial homology
nodes.statement: We've shown that $\ind_1'(M)$ is isomorphic to $\ind_1(M)$, which is already known to have trivial homology by \ref{lem:ind₁ trivial homology}.
nodes.statement_short: Transport trivial homology of ind_1 along the isomorphism.

nodes.name: Dimension-shifting representation down(M)
nodes.statement: For any representation $M$, there is a surjective morphism $\ind_1'(M) \to M$, which takes a finitely supported function $f : G \to_0 M$ to the sum $\sum_{x \in G} f (x)$. We define $\down(M)$ to be the kernel of this map. There is therefore a short exact sequence \[ 0 \to \down(M) \to \ind_1'(M) \to M \to 0. \] Both $\down(M)$ and the short exact sequence are functors of $M$; in particular for every map $f : M \to N$ in $\Rep(R,G)$, we have a commutative diagram: \[ \begin{matrix} 0 & \to & \down(M) &\to &\ind_1'(M)& \to& M & \to & 0 \\ &&\downarrow && \downarrow && \downarrow \\ 0 & \to & \down(N) &\to &\ind_1'(N)& \to& N & \to & 0 \end{matrix} . \]
nodes.statement_short: down(M) is the kernel of the summation map ind_1'(M) -> M, functorially in M.
nodes.label: def:down

nodes.name: ind_1'(M) and coind_1'(M) have trivial Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a representation of a finite group $G$ then the representations $\ind_1'(M)$ and $\coind_1'(M)$ have trivial Tate cohomology.
assumptions: $M$ is a representation of a finite group $G$
conclusions: the representations $\ind_1'(M)$ and $\coind_1'(M)$ have trivial Tate cohomology
nodes.label: lem:induced' trivial Tate

nodes.name: Proof that ind_1' and coind_1' have trivial Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: This follows from \ref{lem:induced trivial Tate} together with the isomorphisms \ref{def:ind₁ to coind₁}, \ref{lem:coind₁' iso coind₁} and \ref{lem:ind₁' iso ind₁}.
nodes.statement_short: Transport along the isomorphisms with ind_1 and coind_1.

nodes.name: Dimension shifting in Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: If the group $G$ is finite then for every subgroup $S$ of $G$ and every $n \in \Z$ we have isomorphisms \[ H^n_{\Tate}(S, \up(M)) \cong H^{n+1}_{\Tate}(S,M), \qquad H^{n+1}_{\Tate}(S, \down(M)) \cong H^{n}_{\Tate}(S,M). \]
nodes.label: cor:Tate up down isos

nodes.name: Proof of Tate dimension shifting
nodes.statement: These are the connecting homomorphisms from the short exact sequences linking $\up(M)$ and $\down(M)$ to $M$. They are isomorphisms because $\coind_1'(M)$ and $\ind_1'(M)$ have trivial Tate cohomology.
nodes.statement_short: Connecting maps of the up/down sequences are isomorphisms since the middle terms are Tate-trivial.

nodes.name: Augmentation module
nodes.statement: As an example we consider the case of the trivial representation $R$. The induced representation is then the group ring $RG$, which is referred to Mathlib as \verb|Rep.leftRegular R G|; this is a free $R$-module with basis $\single(g,1)$ for $g \in G$. For simplicity we shall write $[g]$ for the basis vector $\single(g,1)$. The map $\ind_1'(R) \to R$ takes $\sum_{g\in G} x_g [g]$ to $\sum_{g \in G} x_g$. This map is commonly called the augmentation, and its kernel $\down(R)$ the \emph{augmentation module}. We shall write $\aug(R,G)$ for this kernel. The kernel $\aug(R,G)$ is spanned by the elements $[g]-[1]$ for $g \in G$.
nodes.statement_short: The kernel aug(R,G) of the augmentation RG -> R, spanned by [g]-[1].
nodes.label: def:augmentation module

nodes.name: H^{-1} of the augmentation module is the abelianization
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of a finite group $G$. Then there is an isomorphism of $R$-modules \[ S^{\ab} \otimes_{\Z} R \cong H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G)), \] which takes an element $s \otimes 1$ for $s \in S$ to the coset of $[s]-[1]$ in $H^{-1}(S,\aug(R,G)) \cong \aug(R,G) / I_G \aug(R,G)$. In particular, taking $R = \Z$ we have an isomorphism \[ S^{\ab} \cong H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(\Z,G)). \]
nodes.statement_short: S^ab tensor R is isomorphic to H^{-1}_Tate(S, aug(R,G)) via s -> [s]-[1].
assumptions: $S$ be a subgroup of a finite group $G$
nodes.label: lem:Tate -1 aug

nodes.name: Proof of H^{-1} of the augmentation module
nodes.statement: Recall that by \ref{lem:homology 1 trivial}, \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology} we already have an isomorphism $S^\ab \otimes R \cong H_1(S,R) \cong H^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R)$ which takes $s \otimes 1$ to (the coset of) $\single(s,1)$. Furthermore by \ref{cor:Tate up down isos} there is an isomorphism $H^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R) \cong H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(G,R))$. It remains to check that the image of $s \otimes 1$ in $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(G,R))$ is $[s]-[1]$. In the following diagram the rows are short exact sequences and the vertical maps are the differentials in the Tate complex. \[ \begin{matrix} 0 \to C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G)) & \to & C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,RG) & \to &C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R) \to 0\\ \downarrow & &\downarrow & &\downarrow \\ 0 \to C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G)) & \to & C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,RG) & \to &C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,R) \to 0 \end{matrix} \] By \ref{lem:homology 1 trivial}, the image of $s \otimes 1$ in $H^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R)$ is represented by the element $\single(s,1)$ in $C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R)$. To calculate the image in $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G))$, we take a pre-image of $\single(s,1)$ in $C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,RG)$; map that preimage into $C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,RG)$, and then take its preimage in $C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G))$. An obvious pre-image of $\single(s,1)$ in $C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,RG)$ is $\single(s,[1])$. The image of this in $C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,RG) \cong RG$ is $[s]-[1]$. Therefore the image of $s \otimes 1$ in $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G))$ is $[s]-[1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose H_1 = S^ab tensor R with dimension shifting and track the element s tensor 1 through the connecting map.

nodes.name: Inflation-restriction exact sequence
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a normal subgroup of a group $G$ and let $n$ be a positive integer. Assume that for all natural numbers $0 <i < n$ we have $H^{i}(S,M) \cong 0$. Then the following sequence is exact: \[ 0 \to H^{n}(G/S, M^S) \to H^{n}(G,M) \to H^{n}(S,M), \] where the first map is inflation and the second is restriction.
nodes.statement_short: If H^i(S,M)=0 for 0<i<n then 0 -> H^n(G/S,M^S) -> H^n(G,M) -> H^n(S,M) is exact.
assumptions: $S$ be a normal subgroup of a group $G$
for all natural numbers $0 <i < n$ we have $H^{i}(S,M) \cong 0$
nodes.label: thm:inflation restriction sequence

nodes.name: Proof of the inflation-restriction sequence
nodes.statement: This is already in Mathlib for $n=1$. Assume the result is true for some $n\ge 1$; we will prove it for $n+1$ by dimension-shifting. Let $M$ be a representation such that $H^i(S,M)\cong 0$ for all $0 < i < n+1$. This implies $H^i(S,\up(M)) \cong 0$ for all $0 < i < n$. Hence by the inductive hypothesis the following sequence is exact: \[ 0 \to H^n( G/S, \up(M)^S) \to H^n(G, \up(M)) \to H^n(S,\up(M)). \] Recall that we have a short exact sequence of representations of $G$: \[ 0 \to M \to \coind_1'(M) \to \up(M) \to 0. \] Since $0 < 1 < n+1$, our condition on $M$ implies $H^1(S,M) \cong 0$, so by taking $S$-invariants we obtain a short exact sequence of $G/S$-modules: \[ 0 \to M^S \to \coind_1'(M)^S \to \up(M)^S \to 0. \] By \ref{cor:coind₁' invariants trivial cohomology}, $\coind_1'(M)^S$ has trivial cohomology, so we have an isomorphism \[ H^n(G/S, \up(M)^S) \to H^{n+1}(G/S, M^S). \] We now have a diagram where the horizontal maps are inflation and restriction maps and the vertical maps are dimension-shifting isomorphisms. \[ \begin{matrix} 0 &\to& H^{n}(G/S, \up(M)^S) &\to &H^{n}(G,\up(M)) & \to & H^n(S,\up(M)) \\ & & \downarrow & & \downarrow & & \downarrow \\ 0 &\to& H^{n+1}(G/S, M^S) &\to &H^{n+1}(G,M) & \to & H^{n+1}(S,M). \end{matrix} \] The diagram commutes by \ref{lem:inflation restriction naturality}. The first row is exact by the inductive hypothesis. Therefore the second row is also exact.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n via dimension shifting with up(M). The inductive step compares the sequences for up(M) and M through a commutative diagram.

nodes.name: Corestriction
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of finite index in $G$ and let $\{r_i\}$ be a set of representatives for the left cosets $r_i S$. For any representation $M$ of $G$ there is a linear map $N_{G/S} : M^S \to M^G$ defined by \[ N_{G/S}(m) = \sum_i r_i \bullet m. \] This map does not depend on the choice of coset representatives. Also, the map $N_{G/S}$ is a morphism of functors, i.e. for every map $f : A \to B$ in $\Rep(R,G)$ we have a commuting square in $\Mod(R)$: \[ \begin{matrix} A^S & \to & B^S \\ \downarrow && \downarrow \\ A^G & \to & B^G \end{matrix}, \] where the horizontal maps are induced by $f$ and the vertical maps are $N_{G/S}$. The corestriction maps $\cor^n : H^n(S,M) \to H^n(G,M)$ are defined recursively as follows: \begin{itemize} \item The map $\cor^0 : H^0(S,M) \to H^0(G,M)$ is defined to be $N_{G/S}$. \item Assume that we have defined $\cor^n$. For any $M$ we have a commutative diagram in which the rows are exact and the vertical arrows are $\cor^n$: \[ \begin{matrix} H^n(S,\coind_1'(M)) & \to & H^n(S,\up(M)) & \to &H^{n+1}(S,M) & \to & 0 \\ \downarrow &&\downarrow \\ H^n(G,\coind_1'(M)) & \to & H^n(G,\up(M)) & \to &H^{n+1}(G,M) & \to & 0 \end{matrix}. \] It follows that there is a unique linear map $\cor^{n+1} : H^{n+1}(S,M) \to H^{n+1}(G,M)$ such that the following square commutes: \[ \begin{matrix} H^n(S,\up(M)) & \to & H^{n+1}(S,M) \\ \downarrow &&\downarrow \\ H^n(G,\up(M)) & \to &H^{n+1}(G,M) \end{matrix}. \] \end{itemize} The map $\cor^{n} : H^n(S , -) \to H^n(G,-)$ is a morphism of functors.
nodes.statement_short: Corestriction H^n(S,M) -> H^n(G,M), defined in degree 0 by the relative norm and recursively by dimension shifting.
nodes.label: def:corestriction

nodes.name: Corestriction after restriction is multiplication by the index
nodes.statement: For all $\sigma \in H^n(G,M)$ we have \(\cor(\rest(\sigma)) = [G:S] \cdot \sigma\).
nodes.label: lem:cor comp rest

nodes.name: Proof of cor after rest
nodes.statement: We'll prove the result by induction on $n$. In the case $n = 0$, this follows from the relation for all $m \in M^G$: \[ N_{G/S} (m) = [G:S] \cdot m, \] The identity above holds because each term in the sum defining $N_{G/S}(m)$ is equal to $m$. Let's assume that the lemma is true for some $n$. We then have a diagram in which the vertical maps are the dimension shifting maps, which are all surjective: \[ \begin{matrix} H^{n}(G,\up\ M) & \stackrel{\rest}\to & H^{n}(S,\up\ M) & \stackrel{\cor}\to & H^{n}(G,\up\ M)\\ \downarrow &&\downarrow &&\downarrow \\ H^{n+1}(G, M) & \stackrel{\rest}\to & H^{n+1}(S,M) & \stackrel{\cor}\to & H^{n+1}(G,M) \end{matrix}. \] By the inductive hypothesis, the composition of the maps on the top row is multiplication by $[G:S]$. The square on the left commutes by \ref{lem:inflation restriction naturality}, and the square on the right commutes by definition of the corestriction map. Therefore the composition on the bottom row is multiplication by $[G:S]$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on n: degree 0 is the relative norm of an invariant; the inductive step uses surjective dimension-shifting maps.

nodes.name: Tate cohomology is killed by the group order
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a representation of a finite group $G$ then for all $n \in \Z$ and all $\sigma \in H^n_{\Tate}(G,M)$ we have $|G| \cdot \sigma = 0$.
assumptions: $M$ is a representation of a finite group $G$
nodes.label: cor:cohomology G-torsion

nodes.name: Proof that |G| kills Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: By dimension-shifting (\ref{cor:Tate up down isos}) it's enough to prove the result for $n > 0$, in which case by \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology} Tate cohomology is isomorphic to cohomology. Take $S$ to be the trivial subgroup $1$ of $G$. By \ref{lem:cor comp rest} it's sufficient to prove that $\cor(\rest(\sigma))= 0$. This follows because $\rest(\sigma) \in H^n(1,M) \cong 0$ by \ref{lem:Hn unit}.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension shift to n>0 and apply cor after rest through the trivial subgroup.

nodes.name: Restriction to a Sylow subgroup is injective on p-parts
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$ and let $S_p$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ for some prime number $p$. Then for any $n \in \Z$, $H^n_{\Tate}(G,M)[p^\infty]$ is isomorphic to an $R$-submodule of $H^n_{\Tate}(S_p,M)$.
assumptions: $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$
nodes.label: cor:cohomology sub Sylow

nodes.name: Proof of Sylow injectivity
nodes.statement: By dimension-shifting it's enough to prove the result for $n > 0$, in which case Tate cohomology is isomorphic to cohomology. It follows from \ref{lem:cor comp rest} that the composition $\cor \circ \rest$ is injective on $H^n(G,M)[p^\infty]$. Therefore the restriction map is an injective map from $H^n(G,M)[p^\infty]$ to $H^n(S_p,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension shift to n>0; cor after rest is multiplication by a prime-to-p index, hence injective on p-parts.

nodes.name: G is finite cyclic of order n
nodes.statement: In this section we shall assume that $G$ is a finite cyclic group of order $n$.

nodes.name: Fixed generator of the cyclic group
nodes.statement: We shall write $\gen$ for a fixed generator of $G$.

nodes.name: The map map_1 on coind_1'(M)
nodes.statement: Given any representation $M$ of $G$, there is a map $\map_1 : \coind_1'(M) \to \coind_1'(M)$ which takes a function $f : G \to M$ to the function \[ x \mapsto f(x) - f(\gen^{-1}\cdot x). \]

nodes.name: Kernel of map_1 is the constant functions
nodes.statement: The kernel of $\map_1$ consists of the constant functions $G \to M$, i.e. the image of the map $M \to \coind_1'(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: The kernel of map_1 is the image of M in coind_1'(M).

nodes.name: Image of map_1 is isomorphic to up(M)
nodes.statement: Hence by the first isomorphism theorem, the image of $\map_1$ is isomorphic to $\up(M)$.
conclusions: the image of $\map_1$ is isomorphic to $\up(M)$

nodes.name: The map map_2 on ind_1'(M)
nodes.statement: Since $G$ is finite, the representations $\coind_1'(M)$ and $\ind_1'(M)$ are isomorphic, and we define $\map_2$ to be the corresponding map $\ind_1'(M) \to \ind_1'(M)$. This is given by \[ \map_2(f) (x) = f(x) - f(\gen^{-1} \cdot x), \qquad i.e.\; \map_2(\single(x,m)) = \single(x,m) - \single(\gen \cdot x, m). \]

nodes.name: Image of map_2 is down(M)
nodes.statement: The image of $\map_2 : \ind_1'(M) \to \ind_1'(M)$ is precisely the set of functions $G \to_0 M$ which sum to zero. This is the kernel of the map $\ind_1'(M) \to M$, which we are calling $\down(M)$.
conclusions: The image of $\map_2 : \ind_1'(M) \to \ind_1'(M)$ is precisely the set of functions $G \to_0 M$ which sum to zero.
nodes.label: lem:map2 image

nodes.name: Proof of the image of map_2
nodes.statement: It's clear that the values of $\map_2(f)$ sum to $0$, so the image of $\map_2$ is contained in the kernel. Conversely suppose $h : G \to_0 M$ satisfies $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h(\gen^i) = 0$. Then we have \begin{align*} h & = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \single(\gen^i, h(\gen^i))\\ & = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\single(\gen^i, h(\gen^i)) - \single(1, h(\gen^i))). \end{align*} Furthermore each of the terms $\single(\gen^i, m) - \single(1, m)$ is in the image of $\map_2$: \begin{align*} \map_2 (\single(1,m) + \cdots + \single(\gen^{i-1},m)) &=\single(1,m) - \single(\gen^i,m). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Image lies in the sum-zero functions; conversely write a sum-zero function as a sum of differences, each in the image.

nodes.name: Isomorphism up(M) = down(M) for cyclic groups
nodes.statement: We have a commutative square with vertical isomorphisms: \[ \begin{matrix} \ind_1'(M) & \stackrel{\map_2}\to & \ind_1'(M) \\ \downarrow && \downarrow \\ \coind_1'(M) & \stackrel{\map_1}\to & \coind_1'(M) \\ \end{matrix}. \] It follows that $\image(\map_1) \cong \image(\map_2)$, i.e. \[ \up(M) \cong \down(M). \] This is an isomorphism of functors; i.e. for each map $f : M \to N$ in $\Rep(R,G)$ we have a commuting square: \[ \begin{matrix} \up(M) & \stackrel{\up(f)}\to & \up(N) \\[2mm] \downarrow && \downarrow \\ \down(M) & \stackrel{\down(f)}\to & \down(N) \end{matrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: For cyclic G, the images of map_1 and map_2 agree, giving a natural isomorphism up(M) = down(M).
nodes.label: def:up iso down

nodes.name: Periodicity of cohomology of finite cyclic groups
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group. For all $n > 0$ and all representations $M$ we have an isomorphism $H^{n}(G,M) \cong H^{n+2}(G,M)$. Similarly for all integers $n$ we have isomorphisms $H^{n}_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong H^{n+2}_{\Tate}(G,M)$.
nodes.label: cor:periodic cohomology

nodes.name: Proof of periodicity
nodes.statement: By the dimension-shifting isomorphisms we have $H^{n}(G,M) \cong H^{n+1}(G,\down(M)) \cong H^{n+1}(G,\up(M)) \cong H^{n+2}(G,M)$, and similarly for Tate cohomology.
nodes.statement_short: Compose dimension shifting through down(M) = up(M).

nodes.name: Cohomology of a finite cyclic group with Z coefficients
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group of order $n$. Then $H^1(G,\Z) \cong 0$ and $H^2(G,\Z) \cong \Z/n\Z$.
assumptions: $G$ be a finite cyclic group of order $n$
nodes.label: lem:H2 cyclic Z

nodes.name: Proof of the cohomology of a cyclic group in Z
nodes.statement: Since the module $\Z$ is trivial, we have $H^1(G,\Z)\cong \Hom(G,\Z) \cong 0$. It follows from \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology} that $H^0_{\Tate}(G,\Z) \cong \Z /n\Z$. Hence by periodicity there is an isomorphism $H^2(G,\Z) \cong \Z/ n\Z$.
nodes.statement_short: H^1 = Hom(G,Z) = 0; H^2 = H^0_Tate = Z/nZ by periodicity.

nodes.name: Local invariant of a cyclic group
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group of order $n$ generated by an element $\gen$. Then the map \begin{align*} \inv_G : H^2(G,\Z) & \to \Z/n\Z \\ \sigma & \mapsto \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \sigma(\gen^i,\gen) \end{align*} is called the \emph{local invariant} of $G$.
nodes.label: def:local inv

nodes.name: The local invariant is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group of order $n$ generated by an element $\gen$. The local invariant $\inv_G : H^2(G,\Z) \to \Z/n\Z$ is an isomorphism. The pre-image of $1 \in \Z/n\Z$ is the cohomology class of the cocycle \[ \sigma_G (\gen^i, \gen^j) = \begin{cases} 1 & i+j \ge n \\ 0 & i+j < n, \end{cases} \qquad 0 \le i,j < n. \]
nodes.statement_short: inv_G : H^2(G,Z) -> Z/nZ is an isomorphism, with an explicit carry cocycle sigma_G mapping to 1.
assumptions: $G$ be a finite cyclic group of order $n$ generated by an element $\gen$
conclusions: The local invariant $\inv_G : H^2(G,\Z) \to \Z/n\Z$ is an isomorphism.
nodes.label: lem:local inv iso

nodes.name: Proof that the local invariant is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that the formula for $\inv_\Z$ defines a homomorphism $H^2(G,\Z) \to \Z / n \Z$ (i.e. the coboundaries are in the kernel). $\sigma_G$ is a 2-cocycle since one can write $\sigma_G(\gen^i, \gen^j)$ as $\tilde i + \tilde j - (\widetilde{i + j})$ for $\tilde\cdot : \Z/n\Z \to \Z$ a section. It follows from the definitions that all the terms in the sum defining the local invariant are zero apart from the term $i=n-1$, so we have \[ \inv_G(\sigma_G) = \sigma_G(\gen^{n-1}, \gen)) = 1. \] It follows that $\inv_G : H^2(G,\Z) \to \Z/n\Z$ is surjective. By \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}, $|H^2(G,\Z)| = |\Z/n\Z|$, therefore $\inv_G$ is in fact an isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: The carry cocycle maps to 1, so inv_G is surjective; equal cardinalities give an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a finite cyclic group and $M$ a representation of $G$. Recall that there are isomorphisms $H^n_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong H^{n+2}_{\Tate}(G,M)$. We define the Herbrand quotient of $M$ to be \[ h(G,M) = \frac{|H^0_{\Tate}(G,M)|}{|H^1_{\Tate}(G,M)|}. \] If either of the two cohomology groups are infinite then $h(G,M)$ defaults to $0$.
nodes.label: def:herbrand quotient

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of Z
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a cyclic group and $\Z$ has the trivial action of $G$ then $h(G,\Z) = |G|$. This follow immediately from \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}.
nodes.label: eg:herbrand Z

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of a finite module is 1
nodes.statement: If $M$ is finite then $h(G,M)=1$.
nodes.label: lem:herbrand finite

nodes.name: Proof that finite modules have Herbrand quotient 1
nodes.statement: Let $\gen$ be a generator of $G$. Recall that $H^0_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong M^G / N_GM$. Also, we can write $M^G$ as $\ker(1-\gen : M \to M)$. Similarly $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is isomorphic to $\ker (N_G : M \to M) / \image (1-\gen : M \to M)$. The result follows because \begin{align*} |\ker(N_G : M \to M)| \cdot |\image(N_G : M \to M)| &=|M|\\ &=|\ker(1-g : M \to M)| \cdot |\image(1-g : M \to M)|. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Express H^0 and H^{-1} via kernels and images of N_G and 1-g; for finite M, |ker||im| = |M| for both.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient is multiplicative on short exact sequences
nodes.statement: Suppose we have a short exact sequence of representations of a finite cyclic group $G$: \[ 0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0. \] If two of the representations $A$, $B$, $C$ have non-zero Herbrand quotient then so does the third, and $h(G,B) = h(G,A) \cdot h(G,C)$.
assumptions: a short exact sequence of representations of a finite cyclic group $G$
two of the representations $A$, $B$, $C$ have non-zero Herbrand quotient
nodes.label: lem:herbrand ses

nodes.name: Proof of multiplicativity of the Herbrand quotient
nodes.statement: It follows from the long exact sequence that if two of the representations $A,B,C$ have finite cohomology groups then so does the third. Also, by periodicity (\ref{cor:periodic cohomology}), the long exact sequence reduces to an exact hexagon: \[ \begin{matrix} && H^0_{\Tate}(G,B) \\ &\nearrow && \searrow \\ H^0_{\Tate}(G,A) && && H^0_{\Tate}(G,C) \\ \uparrow & & & & \downarrow \\ H^1_{\Tate}(G,C) &&&& H^1_{\Tate}(G,A) \\ & \nwarrow && \swarrow\\ && H^1_{\Tate}(G,B) \end{matrix}. \] The result follows because the alternating product of the finite group orders in the hexagon is $1$.
nodes.statement_short: By periodicity the long exact sequence becomes an exact hexagon, whose alternating product of orders is 1.

nodes.name: Triviality criterion for solvable groups
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a representation of a finite solvable group $G$ (note that the solvability condition will be removed in the next theorem). Suppose we have positive natural numbers $e$ and $o$ with $e$ even and $o$ odd, such that for all subgroups $S$ of $G$ we have \[ H^e(S,M) \cong 0, \qquad H^o(S,M) \cong 0. \] Then $M$ has trivial cohomology.
assumptions: $M$ be a representation of a finite solvable group $G$
positive natural numbers $e$ and $o$ with $e$ even and $o$ odd
for all subgroups $S$ of $G$ we have \[ H^e(S,M) \cong 0, \qquad H^o(S,M) \cong 0. \]
nodes.label: thm:triviality criterion solvable

nodes.name: Proof of the solvable triviality criterion
nodes.statement: We must prove that $H^{n}(S,M) = 0$ for all $S$ and all $n > 0$. We'll prove this by induction on $S$. The result is true for the trivial subgroup of $G$. Assume that the result is true for $S$, and assume that $S' / S$ is cyclic. The inductive hypothesis implies that (for all $n$) the inflation restriction sequence is exact: \[ 0 \to H^{n} (S'/S, M^S) \to H^{n}(S' , M) \to H^{n}(S,M)= 0. \] We therefore have isomorphisms $H^{n} (S'/S, M^S) \cong H^{n}(S' , M)$. In particular we have $H^{e} (S'/S, M^S) \cong 0$ and $H^{o} (S'/S, M^S) \cong 0$. Using periodicity of the cohomology of a cyclic group, we have $H^{n}(S'/S,M^S) \cong 0$ for all $n>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on subgroups with cyclic quotients, using inflation-restriction and periodicity of cyclic cohomology.

nodes.name: Triviality criterion
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$ (no longer assumed to be solvable). Suppose we have positive natural numbers $e$ and $o$ with $e$ even and $o$ odd, such that for all subgroups $S$ of $G$ we have \[ H^e(S,M) =0, \qquad H^o(S,M) = 0. \] Then $M$ has trivial cohomology.
nodes.statement_short: If H^e and H^o vanish on all subgroups for some even e and odd o, then M has trivial cohomology.
assumptions: $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$
positive natural numbers $e$ and $o$ with $e$ even and $o$ odd
for all subgroups $S$ of $G$ we have \[ H^e(S,M) =0, \qquad H^o(S,M) = 0. \]
nodes.label: thm:triviality criterion

nodes.name: Proof of the triviality criterion
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of $G$. Fix a prime number $p$ and let $S_p$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $S$. Since $S_p$ is solvable, \ref{thm:triviality criterion solvable} implies that $H^n(S_p,M) \cong 0$ for all $n > 0$. By \ref{cor:cohomology sub Sylow}, it follows that $H^n(S,M)[p^\infty] \cong 0$. Since this holds for all primes $p$, \ref{cor:cohomology G-torsion} implies that $H^n(S,M) \cong 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to Sylow subgroups (solvable), then use Sylow injectivity and |G|-torsion.

nodes.name: up and down preserve trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a representation of a finite group $G$ and $M$ has trivial cohomology then $\up(M)$ and $\down(M)$ have trivial cohomology.
assumptions: $M$ is a representation of a finite group $G$
nodes.label: cor:up and down trivial cohomology

nodes.name: Proof that up and down preserve trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: For each subgroup $S$ of $G$ we have \[ H^1(S,\up(M)) \cong H^2(S,M) \cong 0, \qquad H^2(S,\up(M)) \cong H^3(S,M) \cong 0. \] By \ref{thm:triviality criterion} $\up(M)$ has trivial cohomology. Similarly \[ H^2(S,\down(M)) \cong H^1(S,M) \cong 0, \qquad H^3(S,\down(M)) \cong H^2(S,M) \cong 0, \] so $\down(M)$ has trivial cohomology.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension shifting gives two vanishing degrees of opposite parity; apply the triviality criterion.

nodes.name: Trivial cohomology implies trivial Tate cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$, and assume that $M$ has trivial cohomology. Then $M$ has trivial Tate cohomology.
assumptions: $M$ be a representation of a finite group $G$
nodes.label: thm:trivial cohomology implies trivial Tate

nodes.name: Proof that trivial cohomology implies trivial Tate
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $n$ and choose a natural number $m$ such that $m + n > 0$. By \ref{cor:up and down trivial cohomology}, $\down^m(M)$ has trivial cohomology. Therefore \[ H^n_{\Tate}(H,M) \cong H^{n+m}(H, \down^m(M)) \cong 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Shift degree n up to positive degrees using down^m(M), which still has trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous 2-cocycle representing sigma
nodes.statement: We shall write $\sigma'$ for an inhomogeneous 2-cocycle representing $\sigma$. This means $\sigma' : G \times G \to M$ satisfies the following 2-cocycle relation for all $x,y,z\in G$ \begin{equation} \sigma'(x,y) + \sigma'(xy,z) = \sigma'(x,yz) + x \bullet \sigma'(y,z). \end{equation}

nodes.name: 2-cocycle relation
nodes.statement: \sigma'(x,y) + \sigma'(xy,z) = \sigma'(x,yz) + x \bullet \sigma'(y,z).
nodes.label: def:2-cocycle relation

nodes.name: Splitting module
nodes.statement: The splitting module of $\sigma'$ is the $R$-module $M \times \aug(R,G)$, with the action of an element $g \in G$ given by \[ g \bullet (m,f) = \left(g \bullet m + \sum_{x \in G} f(x) \sigma'(g,x) , g \bullet f\right), \qquad m \in M, \; f \in \aug(R,G). \] We'll write $\Split(\sigma')$ for the splitting module. Although we don't need this fact, it's worth knowing that up to isomorphism, the splitting module depends only on the cohomology class of $\sigma'$.
nodes.statement_short: Split(sigma') is M x aug(R,G) with the action twisted by the cocycle sigma'.
nodes.label: def:splitting module

nodes.name: Splitting module short exact sequence
nodes.statement: 0 \to M \to \Split(\sigma') \to \aug(R,G) \to 0.
nodes.label: eq:split ses

nodes.name: The cocycle splits in the splitting module
nodes.statement: The image of $\sigma'$ in $H^2(G,\Split(\sigma))$ is zero.
conclusions: The image of $\sigma'$ in $H^2(G,\Split(\sigma))$ is zero.
nodes.label: lem:splits in splitting module

nodes.name: Proof that the cocycle splits
nodes.statement: We can check that the cocycle $\sigma'$ is the coboundary of the $1$-cochain $\tau : G \to \Split(\sigma)$ defined by \[ \tau (x) = (x \bullet σ'(1,1), [x]-[1]). \] (Here we are using the notation $[x]$ to mean the function with value $1$ at $x$ and $0$ elsewhere). By definition we have \begin{align*} d\tau (x,y) &= \tau(x) + x \bullet \tau(y) - \tau(xy) \\ &= (x \bullet σ'(1,1), [x]-[1]) + x \bullet (y \bullet σ'(1,1), [y]-[1]) -(xy \bullet σ'(1,1), [xy]-[1])\\ &= (x \bullet σ'(1,1), [x]-[1]) + (xy \bullet σ'(1,1) + \sigma'(x,y) -\sigma'(x,1), [xy]-[x]) - (xy \bullet σ'(1,1), [xy]-[1])\\ &= (x \bullet \sigma'(1,1) + \sigma'(x,y) -\sigma'(x,1) , 0). \end{align*} It remains to prove that $\sigma'(x,1) = x \bullet \sigma'(1,1)$. This follows from the $2$-cocycle relation \ref{def:2-cocycle relation} in the case $y=z=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Exhibit an explicit 1-cochain tau whose coboundary is sigma', using the cocycle relation with y=z=1.

nodes.name: Finite class formation and fundamental class
nodes.statement: In this section $G$ is a finite group and $R$ is a commutative ring. If $M$ is a representation of $G$ over $R$ then we shall call $M$ (or more precisely the triple $(R,G,M)$) a \emph{finite class formation} if: \begin{itemize} \item The ring $R$ has no additive torsion. This implies for all subgroups $S$ of $G$: \[ H^2(S,\aug(R,G)) \cong H^1(S,R) \cong \Hom(S,R) = 0. \] \item For all subgroups $S \le G$ we have $H^1(S,M) \cong 0$. \item For all subgroups $S \le G$, $H^2(S,M)$ is isomorphic as an $R$-module to $R / |S| \cdot R$. \end{itemize} If $M$ is a finite class formation then a generator $\sigma$ for $H^2(G,M)$ (by which we mean the image of 1 under some isomorphism $R/|G|R\equiv H^2(G,M)$) is called a \emph{fundamental class}.
nodes.statement_short: (R,G,M) is a finite class formation if R is torsion-free and H^1(S,M)=0, H^2(S,M)=R/|S|R for all S; a generator of H^2(G,M) is a fundamental class.
nodes.label: def:fundamental class

nodes.name: Remarks on finite class formations
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item Given $G$ and $R$, there can be several nonisomorphic $M$ which are finite class formations. For example if $M$ is a finite class formation then so is $M\oplus N$ where $N$ is any cohomologically trivial module. \item I know of no example in class field theory where $R$ is any ring other than $\Z$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Z is a finite class formation over a cyclic group
nodes.statement: If $G$ is a finite cyclic group then the trivial representation $\Z$ (or more precisely the triple $(\Z,G,\Z)$) is a finite class formation. This follows from \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}. The cocycle $\sigma_G$ defined in \ref{lem:local inv iso} (which depends on a choice of generator for $G$) is a fundamental class. Note that it is unsurprising that the cocycle depends on a choice of generator, as the reciprocity isomorphism gives an isomorphism $G\cong \Z/|G|\Z.$

nodes.name: Surjective endomorphisms of R/I are injective
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be an ideal of a commutative ring $R$ and let $f:R/I \to R/I$ be a surjective $R$-linear map. Then $f$ is injective.
assumptions: $I$ be an ideal of a commutative ring $R$
nodes.label: lem:linear injective of surjective

nodes.name: Proof that surjective endomorphisms of R/I are injective
nodes.statement: (This lemma is already in Mathlib.) Without loss of generality $I=0$, since such a map is also $R/I$-linear. Let $c\in R$ be a preimage of $1$ and let $d = f(1)$. We have $cd = cf(1) = f(c) = 1$. The map $f$ is given by $f(x) = dx$ and the map $x \mapsto cx$ is an inverse.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to I=0; f is multiplication by f(1), which is a unit.

nodes.name: Counting proof for R=Z
nodes.statement: In the case $R=\Z$ and $I\not=0$, which is the only case we shall use in applications, the lemma can just be proved by counting.

nodes.name: Restriction of a fundamental class generates
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma \in H^2(G,M)$ be a fundamental class. Then the restriction of $\sigma$ to any subgroup $S$ of $G$ is a generator for $H^2(S,M)$.
conclusions: the restriction of $\sigma$ to any subgroup $S$ of $G$ is a generator for $H^2(S,M)$
nodes.label: lem:restriction fundamental class generates

nodes.name: Proof that restrictions of fundamental classes generate
nodes.statement: The restriction and corestriction maps are $R$-linear maps \[ H^2(G,M) \stackrel{\rest}\to H^2(S,M) \stackrel{\cor}\to H^2(G,M). \] We need to prove that the restriction map is surjective. By the conditions on $M$, we can think of these maps as \[ R / |G| \to R / |S| \to R / |G|. \] Since $R$ has no additive torsion, the image of $R/|S|$ in $R/|G|$ is contained in the $S$-torsion, which is $[G:S] R / |G|$. Furthermore, since the composition is $[G:S]$, it follows that the image of $\cor$ contains $[G:S] R / |G|$. Therefore the image of $\cor$ is precisely $[G:S] R / |G|$, which is isomorphic to $R/|S|$. Hence $\cor$ may be regarded as a surjective linear map $R/|S| \to R/|S|$. By \ref{lem:linear injective of surjective}, $\cor$ is injective with image $[G:S] H^2(G,M)$. Now let $b \in H^2(S,M)$. We have $\cor(b) = [G:S]c$ for some $c \in H^2(G,M)$. This implies $\cor(b) = \cor (\rest( c))$, and since $\cor$ is injective we have $b = \rest(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Corestriction R/|S| -> R/|G| is a surjection onto [G:S]R/|G|, hence injective; then cor after rest shows restriction is surjective.

nodes.name: Simpler proof for R=Z
nodes.statement: Again when $R=\Z$ the above proof can be made much simpler.

nodes.name: Splitting module of a fundamental class has trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $\sigma'$ be a 2-cocycle representing a fundamental class in $H^2(G,M)$. Then $\Split(\sigma')$ has trivial cohomology.
assumptions: $\sigma'$ be a 2-cocycle representing a fundamental class in $H^2(G,M)$
nodes.label: thm:splitting module trivial

nodes.name: Proof that the splitting module has trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: By \ref{thm:triviality criterion}, it's enough to prove for every subgroup $S$ of $G$ that $H^1(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$ and $H^2(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$. We have a long exact sequence with the following terms: \[ 0 \to H^1(S,\Split(\sigma')) \to H^1(S,\aug(R,G)) \to H^2(S,M) \to H^2(S,\Split(\sigma')) \to 0. \] By \ref{lem:restriction fundamental class generates} and \ref{lem:splits in splitting module}, the map $H^2(S,M) \to H^2(S,\Split(\sigma'))$ is zero. Hence $H^2(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$. The $R$-modules $H^1(S,\aug(R,G))$ and $H^2(S,M)$ are both isomorphic to $R / |S|R$, and the map from one to the other is surjective. By \ref{lem:linear injective of surjective}, the map from $H^1(S,\aug(R,G))$ to $H^2(S,M)$ is also injective. Therefore $H^1(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Triviality criterion with degrees 1, 2: use the long exact sequence, the splitting of sigma' and injectivity of surjective R/|S|-endomorphisms.

nodes.name: Reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement: The theorem implies that we have isomorphisms for all $n\in \Z$ (which depend on $\sigma$): \[ H^{n}_{\Tate}(G,\aug(R,G)) \cong H^{n+1}_{\Tate}(G,M) . \] In particular in the case $n = -1$ we have the reciprocity isomorphism \[ \begin{matrix} G^{\ab} \otimes R & \cong & H^{-1}_{\Tate}(G,\aug(R,G)) &\cong& H^0_{\Tate}(G,M), \\ gG' \otimes 1 & \mapsto & [g] - [1] & \mapsto & \delta ([g] - [1]) \end{matrix}. \] Here $\delta$ is the connecting map for the short exact sequence \ref{eq:split ses}.
nodes.statement_short: Dimension shifting through the splitting module gives G^ab tensor R = H^{-1}(G,aug) = H^0_Tate(G,M).
nodes.label: def:reciprocity iso

nodes.name: Cocycle formula for the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement: The reciprocity isomorphism for a fundamental class $\sigma \in H^2(G,M)$ is given by \[ \reciprocity(gG' \otimes 1) \equiv \sum_{x \in G} \sigma'(x,g) \bmod N_G M. \] This depends only on the cohomology class $\sigma$ rather than the cocycle $\sigma'$.
conclusions: This depends only on the cohomology class $\sigma$ rather than the cocycle $\sigma'$.
nodes.label: lem:reciprocity formula

nodes.name: Proof of the reciprocity cocycle formula
nodes.statement: We have a diagram with exact rows. Note that $C^0(G,M)$ and $C^{-1}(G,M)$ are both $M$ and the vertical maps are Tate coboundary maps, which are all $N_G$. \[ \begin{matrix} 0 \to & C^{-1}(G,M) & \to & C^{-1}(G,\Split(\sigma')) & \to & C^{-1}(G,\aug(R,G)) & \to 0 \\ &\downarrow &&\downarrow &&\downarrow \\ 0 \to & C^{0}(G,M) & \to & C^{0}(G,\Split(\sigma')) & \to & C^{0}(G,\aug(R,G)) & \to 0 \end{matrix} \] Choose an element $g \in G$. By \ref{lem:Tate -1 aug}, the element $gG' \otimes 1 \in G^{\ab} \otimes R$ maps to the cocycle $[g]-[1] \in C^{-1}(G,\aug(\Z,G))$. An obvious pre-image of this element in $C^{-1}(G,\Split(\sigma))$ is the element $(0,[g]-[1])$. The image of $(0,[g]-[1])$ in $C^{0}(G,\Split(\sigma))$ is \[ N_G(0,[g]-[1]) = \left(\sum_{x \in G} (\sigma'(x,g) - \sigma'(x,1)), 0\right). \] By the cocycle relation we have $\sigma'(x,1) = x \bullet \sigma'(1,1)$ for all $x\in G$. Hence the reciprocity map is given by \[ \reciprocity(gG' \otimes 1) \cong \sum_{x \in G} \sigma'(x,g) - N_G \sigma'(1,1) \cong \sum_{x \in G} \sigma'(x,g) \in M^G / N_G M. \] If we modify $\sigma'$ by a coboundary $d\tau$: \[ \sigma''(x,y) = \sigma'(x,y) + x \bullet \tau(y) - \tau(xy) + \tau(x), \] then we will add the following term to $\reciprocity(g)$: \[ \sum_{x \in G} (x \bullet \tau(g) - \tau(xg) + \tau(x)). \] The second and third terms cancel each other out after reindexing, so we are left with $N_G(\tau(g))$, which is zero in $H^0_{\Tate}(G,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the connecting map on [g]-[1] via the lift (0,[g]-[1]) and the norm, then check independence of the cocycle.

nodes.name: Compatibility of reciprocity with subgroups
nodes.statement: Let $(R,G,M)$ be a finite class formation with a fundamental class $\sigma_G$ and let $S$ be a subgroup of $G$. Then $(R, S, M \downarrow S)$ is a finite class formation. The restriction $\sigma_S$ of $\sigma_G$ to $S$ is a fundamental class in $H^2(S,M)$. Furthermore there is a commuting square \[ \begin{matrix} S^{\ab} \otimes R & \cong & M^S / N_SM \\ \downarrow && \downarrow \\ G^{\ab} \otimes R & \cong & M^G / N_GM \end{matrix} \] The horizontal maps are the reciprocity isomorphisms defined by the fundamental classes $\sigma_G$ and $\sigma_S$; the left hand vertical map is $sS' \mapsto sG'$ and the right hand map is induced by $N_{G/S} :M^S \to M^G$.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting a class formation to S gives one, and the reciprocity maps for S and G commute with inclusion and the relative norm.
assumptions: $(R,G,M)$ be a finite class formation with a fundamental class $\sigma_G$
conclusions: Then $(R, S, M \downarrow S)$ is a finite class formation.
The restriction $\sigma_S$ of $\sigma_G$ to $S$ is a fundamental class in $H^2(S,M)$.
Furthermore there is a commuting square
nodes.label: lem:subgroup compatibility

nodes.name: Proof of compatibility with subgroups
nodes.statement: The fact that $(R, S, M \downarrow S)$ is a finite class formation is a tautology. The fact that $\sigma_S$ is a fundamental class is \ref{lem:restriction fundamental class generates}. It remains to prove that the diagram commutes. We'll write $\theta_G$ and $\theta_S$ for the horizontal maps in the diagram. For an element $s \in S$ we have by \ref{lem:reciprocity formula}: \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{x \in G} \sigma_G(x,s). \] Let $R$ be a set of representatives for the cosets $rS$ of $S$ in $G$. Then we have \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{r \in R} \sum_{x \in S} \sigma_G(rx,s). \] Using the cocycle relation we have \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{r \in R} \sum_{x \in S} \left(\sigma_G(r,xs) + r \bullet \sigma_G(x,s) - \sigma_G(r,x)\right). \] The first and last terms cancel after reindexing, and we are left with \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{r \in R} r \bullet \left(\sum_{x \in S} \sigma_S(x,s)\right). \] The right hand side is $N_{G/S} \theta_S(s)$ by \ref{lem:reciprocity formula}.
nodes.statement_short: Use the cocycle formula for reciprocity, split the sum over cosets and apply the cocycle relation.

nodes.name: Norm submodule
nodes.statement: For a finite subgroup $S$ of $G$, we shall call $N_{G/S}M^S$ the \emph{norm submodule} corresponding to $S$. This is a submodule of $M^G$ containing $N_G M$. By the commutative diagram in \ref{lem:subgroup compatibility}, the image of $SG'/G' \otimes R$ under the reciprocity map is equal to $N_{G/S}(M^S) / N_G M$.
nodes.label: def:norm submodule

nodes.name: Norm submodules detect subgroups modulo the commutator
nodes.statement: Let $(\Z,G,M)$ be a finite class formation and let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be two subgroups of $G$. Then $S_1 G' \subseteq S_2 G'$ if and only if $N_{G/S_1}(M^{S_1}) \subseteq N_{G/S_2}(M^{S_2})$.
conclusions: $S_1 G' \subseteq S_2 G'$ if and only if $N_{G/S_1}(M^{S_1}) \subseteq N_{G/S_2}(M^{S_2})$
nodes.label: cor:norm submodule mono

nodes.name: Norm Limitation Theorem
