nodes.statement: Let $(R,G,M)$ be a finite class formation. Then \[ N_G M = N_{G/G'} (M^{G'}). \]
nodes.label: cor:norm limitiation

nodes.name: Norm submodules classify subgroups of an abelian class formation
nodes.statement: Suppose $(\Z,G,M)$ is a finite class formation with $G$ abelian. Let $S_1$ and $S_2$ be subgroups of $G$. Then $S_1 \subseteq S_2$ if and only if $N_{G/S_1}(M^{S_1}) \subseteq N_{G/S_2}(M^{S_2})$
assumptions: $(\Z,G,M)$ is a finite class formation with $G$ abelian
conclusions: $S_1 \subseteq S_2$ if and only if $N_{G/S_1}(M^{S_1}) \subseteq N_{G/S_2}(M^{S_2})$
nodes.label: cor:abelian norm submodule mono

nodes.name: Finite Galois extensions of local fields
nodes.statement: In this chapter we shall consider finite Galois extensions of non-archimedean local fields $l/k$.

nodes.name: l^x as a Galois representation
nodes.statement: We shall regard the multiplicative group $l^\times$ as a representation of $\Gal(l/k)$ over the ring $\Z$, where addition in the module is the operation which is usually written as multiplication.

nodes.name: Notation H(l/k,-)
nodes.statement: We shall always write $H^\bullet(l/k,-)$ as an abbreviation of $H^\bullet(\Gal(l/k),-)$.

nodes.name: H^0(l/k,l^x) = k^x
nodes.statement: By the fundamental theorem of Galois theory we have \[ H^0(l/k,l^\times) = (l^\times)^G = k^\times. \]

nodes.name: H^0_Tate(l/k,l^x) = k^x / N(l^x)
nodes.statement: The norm map $N_{\Gal(l/k)} : l^\times \to l^\times$ defined in \ref{def:norm} takes values in $k^\times$ and coincides with the usual norm map $N : l^\times \to k^\times$. This implies by \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology} the isomorphism \[ H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,l^\times) \cong k^\times / N(l^\times). \]

nodes.name: Outline of the proof that l^x is a class formation
nodes.statement: The proof that $l^\times$ is a class formation is achieved in the following steps: \begin{enumerate} \item It is already proven in Mathlib that $H^1(l/k,l^\times) \cong 0$; this result is known as Hilbert's theorem 90. It remains to check that each $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ is cyclic of order $[l:k]$, and to choose a generator. \item In the case that $\Gal(l/k)$ is cyclic, we can show that $|H^2(l/k,l^\times)| = [l:k]$ by Herbrand quotients. By inflation-restriction, this implies $|H^2(l/k,l^\times)| \le [l:k]$ for all Galois extensions. Hence to prove that $l^\times$ is a class formation it's sufficient to find an element in $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ of order $[l:k]$; such an element is a fundamental class. \item Suppose $l/k$ is unramified. In this case we have a decomposition: \[ l ^\times \cong \cO_l^\times \oplus \Z. \] The subrepresentation $\cO_l^\times$ has trivial cohomology in this unramified case. Therefore for any intermediate field $l/m/k$ we have $H^\bullet(l/m,l^\times) \cong H^\bullet(l/m,\Z)$. Since $\Z$ is a finite class formation over a cyclic group, it follows that $l^\times$ is a finite class formation. The cocycle $\sigma_1$ defined in \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z} is a fundamental class, where we use the Frobenius element as a generator. \item Suppose $l/k$ is a Galois extension which is not necessarily unramified. To define the fundamental class in this case, we let $l'/k$ be the unramified extension with the same degree as $l/k$. We have already constructed the fundamental class $\sigma_1 \in H^2(l'/k, l'^\times)$. We let $\sigma_2$ be the inflation of $\sigma_1$ to $H^2(ll'/k, (ll')^\times)$. The extension $ll' / l$ is unramified, so we already have an explicit isomorphism $H^2(ll'/l, (ll')^\times) \cong \Z / [ll':l]$. Using this isomorphism, we can show that the restriction of $\sigma_2$ to $H^2(ll'/l, (ll')^\times)$ is zero. Hence by inflation-restriction there exists a unique $\sigma \in H^2(l/k, l^\times)$ whose inflation is $\sigma_2$. It is then easy to check that $\sigma$ is a fundamental class in $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Proof outline: Hilbert 90, Herbrand quotients for cyclic extensions and inflation-restriction bound H^2; the unramified case is explicit and the general case is reached by inflation from l l'.

nodes.name: Hilbert's Theorem 90
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of fields. Then $H^1(l/k, l^\times) \cong 0$.
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of fields
nodes.label: thm:hilbert 90

nodes.name: Proof of Hilbert's Theorem 90
nodes.statement: This is already in Mathlib.

nodes.name: Additive group of a Galois extension is induced
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of fields. Then there is an isomorphism of $\Gal(l/k)$-representations: \[ l \cong \ind_1(k). \] In particular $l$ has trivial Tate cohomology as a representation of $\Gal(l/k)$.
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of fields
conclusions: In particular $l$ has trivial Tate cohomology as a representation of $\Gal(l/k)$.
nodes.label: thm:additive field trivial

nodes.name: Proof via a normal basis
nodes.statement: Recall from Galois theory that there is a normal basis for $l$ over $k$, i.e. a basis of the form \[ \{x \bullet b_0 : x \in \Gal(l/k)\}. \] Define a map $\ind_1(k) \cong l$ by \[ \Phi (f : G \to_0 k) = \sum_{x \in \Gal(l/k)} f(x) \cdot x^{-1} \bullet b_0. \] The map $\Phi$ is clearly a linear bijection; we check that it commutes with the Galois action: \[ \Phi(g\bullet f) = \sum_x f(xg) \cdot x^{-1} \bullet b_0 = \sum_x f(x) \cdot (xg^{-1})^{-1} \bullet b_0 = g \bullet \Phi(f). \]
nodes.statement_short: A normal basis gives an explicit Galois-equivariant linear bijection ind_1(k) -> l.

nodes.name: Serre's approximation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group and let $M$ be a $G$-module. Say we have a decreasing sequence $M=M_0\supseteq M_1\supseteq M_2\supseteq \cdots$ of $G$-submodules with the property that the natural map $M\to\varprojlim(M/M_i)$ is an isomorphism. Assume for some natural $q$ that the group cohomology $H^{q+1}(G,M_i/M_{i+1})=0$ for all $i$. Then $H^{q+1}(G,M)=0.$
nodes.origin_citation: Serre, Local Class Field Theory, in Cassels-Froehlich
nodes.statement_short: If M is the inverse limit of a filtration whose graded pieces have vanishing H^{q+1}, then H^{q+1}(G,M)=0.
assumptions: $G$ be a group and let $M$ be a $G$-module
a decreasing sequence $M=M_0\supseteq M_1\supseteq M_2\supseteq \cdots$ of $G$-submodules with the property that the natural map $M\to\varprojlim(M/M_i)$ is an isomorphism
nodes.label: lem:serre_approx

nodes.name: Proof of Serre's approximation lemma
nodes.statement: Let $f_0$ be a $q+1$-cocycle with values in $M=M_0$. Since $H^{q+1}(G,M/M_1)=0$ we can find a $q$-cochain $\psi_0$ of $G$ with values in $M$ such that $f_0=\delta\psi_0+f_1$ where now $f_1$ is a $q+1$-cocycle in $M_1$. In general given the $q+1$-cocycle $f_n$ with values in $M_n$ we recursively define a $q$-chain $\psi_n$ with values in $M_n$ such that $f_n=\delta\psi_n+f_{n+1}$ with $f_{n+1}$ a $q+1$-cocycle taking values in $M_{n+1}$. Now set $\psi:=\psi_0+\psi_1+\cdots$, which converges by our hypothesis $M=\varprojlim(M/M_i)$. More precisely, $\psi$ can be thought of as an element of the projective limit of $C^q(M/M_i)$, which equals $C^q(M)$. In particular $\psi$ defines a $q$-cochain of $G$ with values in $M$; an elementary calculation now shows $f_0=\delta\psi$ and thus $f_0$ is a coboundary.
nodes.statement_short: Successive approximation: peel off coboundaries level by level and sum the convergent series of cochains.

nodes.name: Does the approximation argument work for Tate cohomology?
nodes.statement: What the proof above seems to use is: (1) group cohomology of $M$ is computed as cohomology of a complex $C^\bullet(M)$; (2) the complex is functorial in $M$; (3) $C^\bullet$ preserves epis and limits (and in particular $C^n(\varprojlim_i M/M_i)=\varprojlim_i C^n(M/M_i)$). These facts are certainly true for the standard complex computing group cohomology (where $C^n(M)=Hom(G^n,M)=\prod_{G^n}M$); is it true for the integer-indexed complex computing Tate cohomology when $G$ is finite? If so then the same proof would work for Tate cohomology. The reason I remark this is that Serre's proof in Cassels--Froehlich seems to be a statement about Tate cohomology; my instinct is that the same proof might work.
nodes.statement_short: Asks whether the same proof works for the Z-indexed Tate complex, which Serre's proof seems to need.

nodes.name: Open subgroup of local units with trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of local fields. There is a Galois-invariant open subgroup $M \subseteq \cO_l^\times$ such that $H^{q+1}(l/k,M)=0$ for all naturals $q$.
nodes.origin_citation: Serre, Local Class Field Theory, in Cassels-Froehlich
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of local fields
conclusions: There is a Galois-invariant open subgroup $M \subseteq \cO_l^\times$ such that $H^{q+1}(l/k,M)=0$ for all naturals $q$.
nodes.label: lem:serre_cor

nodes.name: Proof of existence of a cohomologically trivial open subgroup
nodes.statement: We know that $l\cong k[G]$ by the normal basis theorem so we may choose $\alpha\in L$ such that $\{g\alpha:g\in G\}$ forms a $k$-basis for $l$. If $\pi_k$ denotes a uniformiser of $k$ then by multiplying $\alpha$ by an appropriate power of $\pi_k$ we may assume $\alpha\in\cO_l$. Set $A=\oplus_{g\in G}\cO_k g\alpha\subseteq\cO_l$. This is an open additive subgroup of $l$ so there exists some natural $N$ such that $\pi_k^N\cO_l\subseteq A$. Set $B=\pi_k^{N+1}A\subseteq\pi_k\cO_l$ and set $M=1+B\subseteq \cO_l^\times$. We claim that this $M$ works. It is clearly open and $G$-stable, so what remains is $H^{q+1}(l/k,M)=0$ for all naturals $q$. First observe that $B\cdot B\subseteq \pi_kB$, as $B\cdot B\subseteq\pi_k^{2N+2}A\cdot A \subseteq \pi_k^{2N+2}\cO_l\subseteq \pi_k^{N+2}A=\pi_kB.$ Now define subgroups $M_i=1+\pi_k^iB$; we claim that lemma~\ref{lem:serre_approx} applies for all $q$. To check this, we need to show that $H^{q+1}(G,M_i/M_{i+1})=0$ for all $i$. But it is not difficult to check that the map $M_i\to B$ sending $1+\pi_k^ib$ to $b$ induces a $G$-equivariant isomorphism $M_i/M_{i+1}=B/\pi_kB$ (the case $i=0$ needs $B\cdot B\subseteq \pi_kB$), and the latter has trivial cohomology because it is isomorphic to $(\cO_k/\pi_k)[G]$ and thus induced.
nodes.statement_short: Build M = 1 + B from a normal-basis lattice; filter by M_i = 1 + pi^i B whose quotients are induced, and apply the approximation lemma.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of local units is 1
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is a cyclic extension then $h(l/k, \cO_l^\times) = 1$.
nodes.label: lem:herbrand local units

nodes.name: Proof that local units have Herbrand quotient 1
nodes.statement: Choose a subgroup $M\subseteq \cO_l^\times$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:serre_cor}. Since $\cO_l^\times / M$ is finite (because $M$ is open and $\cO_l^\times$ is compact) we have (using lemmas~\ref{lem:herbrand finite} and \ref{lem:herbrand ses}) \[ h(\cO_l^\times) = h(M). \] The right hand side is $1$ by \ref{lem:serre_cor}.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the open subgroup of finite index with trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of l^x is [l:k]
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is a cyclic extension of local fields then $h(l/k, l^\times)= [l:k]$.
assumptions: $l/k$ is a cyclic extension of local fields
nodes.label: lem:herbrand local l*

nodes.name: Proof of the Herbrand quotient of l^x
nodes.statement: We have a short exact sequence of representations \[ 0 \to \cO_l^\times \to l^\times \to \Z \to 0, \] where the second map is the valuation. We've shown in \ref{lem:herbrand local units}, \ref{eg:herbrand Z} that $h(l/k,\cO^\times)=1$ and $h(l/k,\Z) = [l:k]$. Therefore $h(l/k,l^\times) = [l:k]$.
nodes.statement_short: Valuation sequence 0 -> O^x -> l^x -> Z -> 0 and multiplicativity.

nodes.name: |H^2(l/k,l^x)| = [l:k] for cyclic local extensions
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is a cyclic extension of local fields then $|H^2(l/k,l^\times)| = [l:k]$.
assumptions: $l/k$ is a cyclic extension of local fields
nodes.label: lem:local H2 l*

nodes.name: Proof of |H^2| for cyclic local extensions
nodes.statement: The follows from \ref{lem:herbrand local l*} and \ref{thm:hilbert 90}.

nodes.name: Upper bound for H^2(l/k,l^x)
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a Galois extension of local fields. Then $|H^2(l/k,l^\times)| \le [l:k]$.
assumptions: $l/k$ be a Galois extension of local fields
nodes.label: lem:local H2 upper bound

nodes.name: Proof of the upper bound for H^2(l/k,l^x)
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be prime number dividing the degree $[l:k]$ and let $k_p$ be the fixed field of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $S_p$ of $\Gal(l/k)$. By \ref{cor:cohomology G-torsion} and \ref{cor:cohomology sub Sylow} it is sufficient to prove that $|H^2(l/k_p,l^\times)| \le [l:k_p]$, which is a special case of the theorem. In the special case, the Galois group is $S_p$, which is a solvable group. It is therefore sufficient to prove the theorem in the case that $\Gal(l/k)$ is solvable. (Note that $\Gal(l/k)$ is always solvable if $l/k$ is an extension of local fields, but we do not need to prove this.) We shall prove the theorem by induction on $k$, starting with $k=l$ and moving down in cyclic steps. The case $k=l$ follows by \ref{lem:Hn unit}. Assume the result for $l/k$ and let $k_0$ be a subfield of $k$ with $k/k_0$ cyclic. It follows from \ref{thm:hilbert 90} that we have an inflation-restriction sequence in dimension 2: \[ 0 \to H^2(k/k_0, k^\times) \to H^2( l/k_0, l^\times) \to H^2(l/k, l^\times). \] The first term has order $[k : k_0]$ by \ref{lem:local H2 l*}, and the last term has order at most $[l:k]$ by the inductive hypothesis. Therefore $H^2( l/k_0, l^\times)$ has order at most $[l:k] \times [k : k_0] = [l: k_0]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Sylow (solvable) subgroups, then induct down a chain of cyclic steps using inflation-restriction.

nodes.name: l/k is unramified
nodes.statement: In this section we assume that $l/k$ is unramified.

nodes.name: Residue fields F_l and F_k
nodes.statement: In this case $\Gal(l/k)$ may be identified with $\Gal(\F_l / \F_k)$ where $\F_l$ and $\F_k$ are the residue class fields of $l$ and $k$ respectively.

nodes.name: Frobenius element F_k
nodes.statement: This group is cyclic and is generated by the Frobenius element $F_k$.

nodes.name: Uniformizer pi_k
nodes.statement: If we choose a uniformizer $\pi_k$ in $k$ (i.e. a generator for the maximal ideal in $\cO_k$) then $\pi_k$ is also a uniformizer in $l$, so we may identify $\F_l$ with $\cO_l / \pi_k \cO_l$.

nodes.name: Residue field modules have trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: The Galois modules $\F_l$ and $\F_l^\times$ have trivial cohomology.
conclusions: The Galois modules $\F_l$ and $\F_l^\times$ have trivial cohomology.
nodes.label: lem:finite field trivial

nodes.name: Proof for residue field modules
nodes.statement: In the case of $l$, this follows from \ref{thm:additive field trivial} as $\Gal(l/k)$ may be identified with $\Gal(\F_l / \F_k)$, so we focus on the representation $l^\times$. Given any subgroup $S$ of the Galois group we must prove that $H^\bullet_{\Tate}(l/m,l^\times) \cong 0$, where $m$ is the fixed field of $S$. Note that $l/m$ is also unramified, so has cyclic Galois group. By \ref{cor:periodic cohomology}, it's sufficient to prove that $H^1(l/m,l^\times)$ and $H^2(l/m,l^\times)$ are trivial. By \ref{lem:herbrand finite} the representation $\F_l^\times$ has Herbrand quotient $1$, so it's enough to prove that $H^1$ is trivial. This follows from \ref{thm:hilbert 90}.
nodes.statement_short: Additive case by normal basis; multiplicative case by periodicity, Herbrand quotient 1 and Hilbert 90.

nodes.name: Unramified integers have a normal integral basis
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is unramified then there is a normal basis for $\cO_l$ over $\cO_k$. Hence there is an isomorphism of Galois representations $\cO_l \cong \ind_1 \cO_k$. In particular $\cO_l$ has trivial cohomology.
conclusions: there is a normal basis for $\cO_l$ over $\cO_k$
there is an isomorphism of Galois representations $\cO_l \cong \ind_1 \cO_k$
nodes.label: lem:unramified additive trivial

nodes.name: Proof of normal integral basis
nodes.statement: By \ref{thm:additive field trivial} we may choose $x_0 \in \F_l$ such that $\{g \bullet x_0 :g \in \Gal(l/k)\}$ is a normal basis. Let $y \in \cO_l$ be a lift of $x_0$. It follows from Nakayama's lemma that $\{g \bullet y\}$ is a normal basis in $\cO_l$. As in earlier proofs, this implies the isomorphism $\cO_l \cong \ind_1 \cO_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift a residue-field normal basis and apply Nakayama's lemma.

nodes.name: Unramified units have trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is unramified then $\cO_l^\times$ has trivial group cohomology.
nodes.label: lem:unramified units trivial

nodes.name: Proof that unramified units have trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: Because replacing $Gal(l/k)$ with a subgroup is the same as replacing $k$ with an extension, it suffices to prove that $H^{q+1}(l/k,\cO_l^\times)=0$ for all local fields $k$, unramified extensions $l$ and naturals $q$. Filter $\cO_l^\times$ as $\cO_l^\times\supset 1+\pi_k\cO_l\supset 1+\pi_k^2\cO_l\supset\cdots$. By lemma~\ref{lem:serre_approx} it suffices to prove that all the subquotients have trivial cohomology. However the first subquotient is $\F_l^\times$ and all the others are $\F_l$, so it suffices to prove that $H^q(G,\F_l^\times)\cong H^q(G,\F_l)\cong 0$ for all $q\geq1$. But these follow from lemma~\ref{lem:finite field trivial}.
nodes.statement_short: Filter units by 1 + pi^i O_l; graded pieces are F_l^x and F_l, which are cohomologically trivial; apply the approximation lemma.

nodes.name: Valuation isomorphism for unramified extensions
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be an unramified extension of local fields. Then there are isomorphisms \[ H^\bullet_{\Tate}(l/k,l^\times) \cong H^\bullet_{\Tate} (l/k,\Z) \] defined by the valuation map $v : l^\times \to \Z$. The inverse map is defined by $n \mapsto \pi_k^n$, and does not depend on the choice of $\pi_k$.
assumptions: $l/k$ be an unramified extension of local fields
conclusions: there are isomorphisms \[ H^\bullet_{\Tate}(l/k,l^\times) \cong H^\bullet_{\Tate} (l/k,\Z) \] defined by the valuation map $v : l^\times \to \Z$
nodes.label: cor:cohomology unramified iso cohomology Z

nodes.name: Proof of the valuation isomorphism
nodes.statement: This follows from the long exact sequence using \ref{lem:unramified units trivial}.
nodes.statement_short: Long exact sequence of the valuation sequence with trivial units.

nodes.name: Fundamental class of an unramified extension
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be an unramified cyclic extension of local fields. Then $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ is cyclic of order $[l:k]$. It is generated by the cohomology class of the following 2-cocycle \[ \sigma_{l/k} (F_k^r, F_k^s) = \begin{cases} 1 & r + s < [l:k], \\ \pi_k & r + s \ge [l:k]. \end{cases} \] Here $F_k$ is the Frobenius element generating $\Gal(l/k)$ and $r$ and $s$ are chosen to be integers in the range $0 \le r,s <[l:k]$. It follows that $l / k$ is a finite class formation and $\sigma_{l/k}$ is a fundamental class.
nodes.statement_short: H^2(l/k,l^x) is cyclic of order [l:k], generated by the explicit carry cocycle with value pi_k.
assumptions: $l/k$ be an unramified cyclic extension of local fields
conclusions: It follows that $l / k$ is a finite class formation and $\sigma_{l/k}$ is a fundamental class.
nodes.label: lem:unramified fundamental class

nodes.name: Proof of the unramified fundamental class
nodes.statement: This follows from \ref{cor:cohomology unramified iso cohomology Z} together with the description of $H^2(l/k,\Z)$ in \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer the description of H^2(l/k,Z) along the valuation isomorphism.

nodes.name: The fundamental class in the unramified case
nodes.statement: We call this choice of $\sigma$ \emph{the} fundamental class for local class field theory in the unramified case.

nodes.name: Unramified local reciprocity sends Frobenius to a uniformizer
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite unramified extension of local fields and let $F_k$ be the Frobenius element in $\Gal(l/k)$. Let $\pi_k$ be a uniformizer of $k$. Then we have \[ \reciprocity (F_k)= \pi_k, \] where the reciprocity map is defined by the fundamental class $\sigma_{l/k}$.
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite unramified extension of local fields
nodes.label: lem:local unramified reciprocity

nodes.name: Proof of unramified reciprocity
nodes.statement: This follows from \ref{lem:reciprocity formula} and \ref{lem:unramified fundamental class}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the cocycle formula to the unramified fundamental class.

nodes.name: Local invariant for unramified extensions
nodes.statement: The \emph{local invariant} $\inv_{l/k} : H^2(l/k, l^\times) \cong \frac{1}{[l:k]}\Z / \Z$ is the composition of the isomorphism $H^2(l/k, l^\times) \cong H^2(l/k, \Z)$ from \ref{lem:unramified units trivial} with the local invariant $\inv_{\Gal(l/k)} : H^2(l/k, \Z) \cong \frac{1}{[l:k]}\Z / \Z$ from \ref{def:local inv} with generator the Frobenius.
nodes.label: def:unramified local inv

nodes.name: Local invariant of the unramified fundamental class
nodes.statement: The fundamental class $\sigma_{l/k}$ has local invariant $\frac{1}{[l:k]}$.
conclusions: The fundamental class $\sigma_{l/k}$ has local invariant $\frac{1}{[l:k]}$.
nodes.label: lem:local inv fundamental class

nodes.name: Proof of the local invariant of the fundamental class
nodes.statement: Corollary of $\inv_{\Gal(l/k)}(\sigma_{\Gal(l/k)}) = 1$ from \ref{lem:local inv iso}.

nodes.name: Restriction of unramified fundamental classes in towers
nodes.statement: Let $m / l / k$ be an unramified tower of extensions of local fields Then the restriction to $m/l$ of $\sigma_{m/k}$ is $\sigma_{m/l}$.
assumptions: $m / l / k$ be an unramified tower of extensions of local fields
nodes.label: lem:local unram rest

nodes.name: Proof of restriction in unramified towers
nodes.statement: Up to cohomology, $\sigma_{l/k}$ does not depend on the choice of uniformizer, so we may assume $\pi_k=\pi_l$ in our definitions of $\sigma_{m/k}$ and $\sigma_{m/l}$. We have $F_l = F_k^f$ where $f = [l:k]$. Hence \begin{align*} \sigma_{m/k}(F_l^r, F_l^s) &= \sigma_{m/k}(F_k^{fr}, F_k^{fs})\\ &= \begin{cases} 1 & fr + rs < [m:k] \\ \pi_k & fr + fs \ge [m:k] \end{cases}\\ &= \begin{cases} 1 & r + s < [m:l] \\ \pi_k & r + s \ge [m:l] \end{cases}\\ &=\sigma_{m/l}(F_l^r,F_l^s). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Choose a common uniformizer and compare the explicit cocycles using F_l = F_k^f.

nodes.name: Local invariant commutes with inflation
nodes.statement: Let $m / l / k$ be a tower of unramified extensions of local fields and let $\infl : H^2(l/k,l^\times) \to H^2(m/k,m^\times)$ be the inflation map. Then \[ \inv_{m/k} \circ \infl = \inv_{l/k}. \] In particular $\infl(\sigma_{l/k}) = [m:l]\cdot \sigma_{m/k}$.
assumptions: $m / l / k$ be a tower of unramified extensions of local fields
$\infl : H^2(l/k,l^\times) \to H^2(m/k,m^\times)$ be the inflation map
nodes.label: lem:local unram inv infl

nodes.name: Proof that the local invariant commutes with inflation
nodes.statement: We shall write $F_{m/k}$ and $F_{l/k}$ for the Frobenius elements in $\Gal(m/k)$ and $\Gal(l/k)$ respectively. Note that $F_{l/k}$ is the restriction of $F_{m/k}$ to $l$, so is the coset of $F_{m/k}$ when we regard $\Gal(l/k)$ as a quotient of $\Gal(m/k)$. From the definition we have (for any $\sigma \in H^2(l/k,l^\times)$): \[ \inv_{m/k}(\infl(\sigma)) = \frac{1}{[m:k]}\sum_{i=0}^{[m:k]-1} v_k(\sigma(F_{l/k}^i,F_{l/k})). \] The terms in the sum are periodic since $F_{l/k}^{[l:k]}=1$. This implies (by the tower law): \[ \inv_{m/k}(\infl(\sigma)) = \frac{1}{[m:k]} [m:l]\sum_{i=0}^{[l:k]-1} v_k(\sigma(F_{l/k}^i,F_{l/k})). \] The right hand side is equal to $\inv_{l/k}(\sigma)$. The formula $\infl(\sigma_{l/k}) = [m:l]\cdot \sigma_{m/k}$ follows since both sides of the equation have local invariant equal to $\frac{1}{[l:k]}$ (by \ref{lem:local inv fundamental class}).
nodes.statement_short: Inflated cocycle sums are periodic, so the tower law turns the sum for m/k into the sum for l/k.

nodes.name: Unramified extension l' of the same degree
nodes.statement: Now let $l/k$ be a Galois extension of local fields of degree $n$ and let $l'$ be the unramified extension of the same degree.

nodes.name: Compositum m of l and l'
nodes.statement: We shall let $m$ be the field generated by $l$ and $l'$.

nodes.name: Ramification index e and inertia degree f
nodes.statement: Let $e$ and $f$ be the ramification index and inertia degree of $l/k$.

nodes.name: [m:l] = e
nodes.statement: Then we have $[m:l] = e$, $v_l(\pi_k)= e$.

nodes.name: Frobenius elements F_{m/l} and F_{l'/k}
nodes.statement: We shall write $F_{m/l}$ for the Frobenius element in $\Gal(m/l)$, which we regard as a subgroup of $\Gal(m/k)$. We also write $F_{l'/k}$ for the Frobenius element in $\Gal(l'/k)$.

nodes.name: Restriction of F_{m/l} to l'
nodes.statement: With this notation we have: \[ F_{m/l}|l' = F_{l'/k}^f. \]

nodes.name: Inflated class psi
nodes.statement: Let $\psi\in H^2(m/k,m^\times)$ be the inflation of $\sigma_{l'/k}$.

nodes.name: Computation that psi restricts to zero on m/l
nodes.statement: By \ref{thm:hilbert 90} the inflation map is injective, so $\psi$ has order exactly $[l':k] = [l:k]$. We also have an inflation restriction sequence \[ 0 \to H^2(l/k, l^\times) \to H^2(m/k , m^\times) \to H^2(m/l, m^\times) \] We'll calculate the restriction of $\psi$ to $H^2(m/l, m^\times)$. Since $m/l$ is unramified, we have an isomorphism \[ \inv_{m/l} : H^2(m/l, m^\times) \cong \frac{1}{e}\Z/ \Z. \] We have \begin{align*} \inv_{m/l}(\psi) &=\frac{1}{e} \sum_{i=0}^{e-1} v_l (\psi (F_l^i,F_l))\\ &=\frac{1}{e} \sum_{i=0}^{e-1} v_l (\sigma_{l'/k}((F_l|l')^i,F_l|l'))\\ &=\frac{1}{e} \sum_{i=0}^{e-1} v_l (\sigma_{l'/k}(F_k^{if},F_k^f))\\ &=\frac{1}{e} v_l (\pi_k) = 1 \equiv 0 \bmod \Z. \end{align*} The first line above is the definition of $\inv_{m/l}$. The second line is the definition of inflation of cocycles. The calculation above shows that the image of $\psi$ in $H^2(m/l, m^\times)$ is $0$.
nodes.statement_short: psi has order [l:k] by injectivity of inflation; its local invariant on m/l is v_l(pi_k)/e = 1, i.e. 0 mod Z, so its restriction vanishes.

nodes.name: Existence of sigma_{l/k}
nodes.statement: Therefore $\psi$ is the inflation of a unique element $\sigma_{l/k} \in H^2(l/k,l^\times)$. Since the inflation map is injective $\sigma_{l/k}$ also has order $[l:k]$.
conclusions: $\psi$ is the inflation of a unique element $\sigma_{l/k} \in H^2(l/k,l^\times)$

nodes.name: The fundamental class of a finite Galois extension of local fields
nodes.statement: We call this element $\sigma_{l/k}$ ``the fundamental class'' for the finite Galois extension $l/k$.

nodes.name: Agreement with the unramified fundamental class
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that in the case where $l/k$ is unramified, this definition coincides with the definition of ``the'' fundamental class already given (as $l=l'=m$).
conclusions: this definition coincides with the definition of ``the'' fundamental class already given

nodes.name: Local fundamental class theorem
nodes.statement: For every finite Galois extension $l/k$ of local fields, $(\Z,\Gal(l/k),l^\times)$ is a finite class formation. The element $\sigma_{l/k}$ defined above is a fundamental class. Corresponding the $\sigma_{l/k}$ there is a reciprocity isomorphism \[ \Gal(l/k) \cong k^\times / N(l^\times). \]
nodes.statement_short: For every finite Galois extension of local fields, l^x is a finite class formation with fundamental class sigma_{l/k}, giving local reciprocity.
conclusions: The element $\sigma_{l/k}$ defined above is a fundamental class.
nodes.label: thm:local fund class

nodes.name: Proof of the local fundamental class theorem
nodes.statement: From \ref{thm:hilbert 90} we know that $H^1(l/k,l^\times) \cong 0$. From \ref{lem:local H2 upper bound}, we know that $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ has no more than $[l:k]$ elements. We have constructed an element $\sigma_{l/k}\in H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ of order $[l:k]$, so $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ is cyclic of order $[l:k]$ and is generated by $\sigma_{l/k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Hilbert 90 plus the upper bound |H^2| <= [l:k] and the constructed element of order [l:k].

nodes.name: Local norm limitation theorem
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of local fields and let $l^{\ab}$ be the maximal subfield of $l$ which is an abelian extension of $k$, i.e. the fixed field of the commutator subgroup of $\Gal(l/k)$. Then $N_{l/k}(l^\times) = N_{l^\ab/k}(l^{\ab\times})$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of local fields
$l^{\ab}$ be the maximal subfield of $l$ which is an abelian extension of $k$
nodes.label: thm:local norm limitation

nodes.name: Proof of local norm limitation
nodes.statement: This follows from \ref{cor:norm limitiation} and \ref{thm:local fund class}.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Abstract norm limitation plus the local class formation.

nodes.name: Abelian extensions are classified by norm groups
nodes.statement: Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be two abelian extensions of $k$ contained in a field $m$. Then $l_1 \subseteq l_2$ if and only if $N_{l_1/k}(l_1^\times) \supseteq N_{l_2/k}(l_2^\times)$ and $l_1 = l_2$ if and only if $N_{l_1/k}(l_1^\times) = N_{l_2/k}(l_2^\times)$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
assumptions: $l_1$ and $l_2$ be two abelian extensions of $k$ contained in a field $m$
conclusions: $l_1 \subseteq l_2$ if and only if $N_{l_1/k}(l_1^\times) \supseteq N_{l_2/k}(l_2^\times)$
$l_1 = l_2$ if and only if $N_{l_1/k}(l_1^\times) = N_{l_2/k}(l_2^\times)$
nodes.label: lem:local abelian classification

nodes.name: Proof of the classification by norm groups
nodes.statement: This follows from \ref{cor:norm submodule mono}.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Norm group of a compositum
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite abelian extension and let $m_1$ and $m_2$ be two intermediate fields between $k$ and $l$ such that $l = m_1 m_2$. Then we have \[ N_{l/k}(l^\times) = N_{m_1/k} (m_1^\times) \cap N_{m_2/k} (m_2^\times). \]
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
assumptions: $m_1$ and $m_2$ be two intermediate fields between $k$ and $l$ such that $l = m_1 m_2$
nodes.label: lem:norm composite intersection

nodes.name: Proof of the norm group of a compositum
nodes.statement: Clearly if $x \in N_{l/k}(l^\times)$ then $x$ is a norm from both $m_1$ and $m_2$. Suppose conversely that $x$ is a norm from both $m_1$ and $m_2$. Let $S_i=\Gal(l/m_i)$ for $i=1,2$. By the commutative diagram in \ref{lem:subgroup compatibility}, the coset $xN(l^\times)$ is in the image of each $S_i$ under the reciprocity map. Since the reciprocity map is bijective, $xN(l^\times)$ is in the image of $S_1 \cap S_2$. The condition $l = m_1 m_2$ implies $S_1 \cap S_2 = 1$. Therefore $x \in N(l^\times)$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Via reciprocity, a common norm lies in the image of S_1 cap S_2 = 1.

nodes.name: Norm group of an unramified extension
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be an unramified extension of local fields of degree $f$. Then $N(l^\times) = \pi_k^{f\Z} \times \cO_k^\times$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
assumptions: $l/k$ be an unramified extension of local fields of degree $f$
nodes.label: lem:local unramified norms

nodes.name: Proof of the unramified norm group
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:unramified units trivial} we have $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\cO_l^\times) \cong 0$, which implies that every element of $\cO_k^\times$ is a norm. The element $\pi_k^f$ is the norm of $\pi_k$. Therefore $\pi_k^{f\Z} \times \cO_k^\times \subseteq N(l^\times)$. To prove equality, we note that these subgroups of $k^\times$ have the same index. Indeed by \ref{lem:unramified fundamental class}, $k^\times / N(l^\times)$ is isomorphic to $\Gal(l/k)^\ab$, which has order $f$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Units are norms and pi_k^f is a norm; equality by comparing indices via reciprocity.

nodes.name: Image of inertia under local reciprocity
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite abelian extension of local fields and let $I \subseteq \Gal(l/k)$ be the inertia subgroup. Then the image of $I$ in $k^\times / N(l^\times)$ is the subgroup $\cO_k^\times / N(\cO_l^\times)$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite abelian extension of local fields
conclusions: the image of $I$ in $k^\times / N(l^\times)$ is the subgroup $\cO_k^\times / N(\cO_l^\times)$
nodes.label: lem:local image inertia

nodes.name: Proof of the image of inertia
nodes.statement: Let $m$ be the fixed field of $I$. By \ref{lem:subgroup compatibility} the image of $I$ in $k^\times / N(l^\times)$ is $N_{m/k}(m^\times) / N_{l/k}(l^\times)$. Since $m/k$ is unramified, \ref{lem:local unramified norms} implies \[ N_{m/k}(m^\times) = \cO_k^\times \times \pi_k^{f\Z}, \] where $f$ is the inertial degree of $l/k$. If $\pi_l$ is a uniformizer in $l$ then $N(\pi_l)$ is a unit multiple of $\pi_k^f$. This implies \[ N_{m/k}(m^\times) = \cO_k^\times \times N(\pi_l^{\Z}). \] The result follows from this.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Use subgroup compatibility with the inertia field, which is unramified, and its norm group.

nodes.name: Exponential isomorphism on high principal units
nodes.statement: Assume $l/k$ is a finite Galois extension of characteristic zero local fields, and let $P$ be the maximal ideal of $\cO_l$. For $n \in \N$ sufficiently large, the exponential map gives an isomorphism \[ (P^n,+) \cong (1 + P^n, \times). \] This isomorphism commutes with the action of the Galois group, so is an isomorphism of representations.
assumptions: $l/k$ is a finite Galois extension of characteristic zero local fields
conclusions: exponential map gives an isomorphism \[ (P^n,+) \cong (1 + P^n, \times). \]
This isomorphism commutes with the action of the Galois group, so is an isomorphism of representations.
nodes.label: lem:local isomorphism

nodes.name: Proof of the exponential isomorphism
nodes.statement: Choose $n$ large enough so that $\exp(x)$ converges for all $x \in P^n$, and such that all the terms $x^r/r!$ are in $P^n$ for $r \ge 1$ and all the terms $x^r / r!$ with $r \ge 2$ have strictly larger valuation than that of $x$. It is already proved in Mathlib that $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$, and the fact that $\exp$ commutes with the Galois action is straightforward. We'll show that the map is a bijection from $P^n$ to $1+P^n$. Suppose $\exp(x)=1$ with $x \in P^n$. If $x \ne 0$ then $x = \pi^mu$ for some unit $u$. By assumption on $n$, $\exp(x) = 1 + \pi^m u + O(\pi^{m+1})$; this gives a contradiction. Therefore the map $\exp : P^n \to 1+P^n$ is injective. One can show that the map $P^n \to 1+P^n$ is surjective using Hensel's lemma as follows. Choose $y \in 1+P^n$. Then $x_0 = y-1$ is in $P^n$ and $\exp(x) \equiv y \bmod P^{n+1}$. Furthermore $\exp'(x_0) = \exp(x_0) \not\equiv 0 \bmod P$. Hensel's lemma shows that there exists a solution to $\exp(x)=y$ with $x \equiv x_0 \bmod P^{n+1}$. In particular $x \in P^n$.
nodes.statement_short: For large n, exp is a Galois-equivariant homomorphism; injective by leading-term valuation and surjective by Hensel's lemma.

nodes.name: Norm group of a cyclotomic extension of Q_p
nodes.statement: Let $l = \Q_p(\zeta)$ where $\zeta$ is a primitive $p^n$-th root of unity for some $n > 0$. Then $N(l^\times) = p^\Z \times (1+p^n \Z_p)$.
assumptions: $l = \Q_p(\zeta)$ where $\zeta$ is a primitive $p^n$-th root of unity for some $n > 0$
nodes.label: lem:local cyclotomic norms

nodes.name: Proof of the cyclotomic norm group
nodes.statement: By Eisenstein's criterion, the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{p^n}(X) = \frac{X^{p^n}-1}{X^{p^{n-1}}-1}$ is irreducible over $\Q_p$. Hence the degree of the extension is $\phi(p^n)=p^n - p^{n-1}$. This coincides with the index: \begin{align*} [\Q_p^\times : p^\Z \times (1+p^n \Z_p)] &= [\Z_p^\times : (1+p^n \Z_p)] \\ &= | (\Z / p^n \Z)^\times |. \end{align*} It it therefore sufficient to prove that every element of $p^\Z \times (1+p^n \Z_p)$ is a norm. We have $p = N(1-\zeta)$. It is therefore sufficient to show that every $x \in 1 + p^n \Z_p$ is the norm of an element of $\Z_p[\zeta]$. We split this into cases. \begin{itemize} \item Suppose $p$ is an odd prime, so that $\exp(pz)$ converges for all $z\in \Z_p$. If $a \in 1 +p^n\Z_p^\times$ then by \ref{lem:local isomorphism} (with $l=k=\Q_p$) there is an expression of $a$ of the form \[ a = \exp(p^n y), \qquad y \in \Z_p. \] It follows that \[ a= \exp(p\frac{y}{p-1}) ^{[\Q_p(\zeta):\Q_p]} = N_{\Q_p(\zeta)/\Q_p}(\exp(py/(p-1))). \] In particular, $x\in N(\Q_p(\zeta)^\times)$. \item In the case $p^n = 2$ we have $l = \Q_2$, so every element of $\Q_2$ is a norm. \item In the case $p=2$, $n \ge 2$, there is an intermediate field $l / \Q_2(i) / \Q_2$, and we have \[ N_{\Q_p(i) / \Q_p} (x+i y) = x^2 + y^2. \] It's easy to show (for example using Hensel's lemma) that if $a \equiv 1 \bmod 4$ then $a$ is the norm of an element of $\Q_p(i)$. If $a \in 1 + 2^n \Z_2$ then we have for some $b \in \Z_2$: \[ a = \exp(2^n b) = \exp(4b)^{[l:\Q_2(i)]}. \] The the exponential above converges to an element of $1+4\Z_2$. In particular there is an element $b \in \Q_2(i)$ such that \[ a = N_{\Q_2(i)/\Q_2} (b) ^ [l:\Q_2(i)] = N_{l/\Q_2} (b) \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Degree equals index, so it suffices that each element is a norm: p = N(1-zeta), and principal units are norms via the exponential, with cases for p odd and p=2.

nodes.name: Local Kronecker-Weber theorem
nodes.statement: Let $l/\Q_p$ be a finite abelian extension. Then $l$ is isomorphic to a subfield of a cyclotomic extension.
conclusions: Then $l$ is isomorphic to a subfield of a cyclotomic extension.
nodes.label: thm:local Kronecker Weber

nodes.name: Proof of local Kronecker-Weber
nodes.statement: The subgroup $N_{l/\Q_p}(l^\times)$ is open in $\Q_p^\times$, so it must contain a subgroup of the form $1+p^n\Z_p$ for some $n$. Let $f$ be the order of $p$ in $\Q_p^\times / N(l^\times)$. \[ N(l^\times) \supset p^{f\Z} \times (1 + p^n\Z_p). \] The subgroup $p^{f\Z} \times \Z_p^\times$ is the norm subgroups for the unramified extension of degree $f$, which is $\Q_p(\zeta_{p^f-1})$. The group $p^\Z \times (1_p^n \Z_p)$ is the norm subgroup of $\Q_p(\zeta_{p^n})$. Hence $l$ is contained in $\Q_p(\zeta_{p^f-1}, \zeta_{p^n})$.
nodes.statement_short: The open norm group contains p^{fZ} x (1+p^n Z_p), the norm group of a cyclotomic field, so l embeds in it.

nodes.name: Kronecker-Weber theorem
nodes.statement: Let $l/\Q$ be a finite abelian extension. Then there exists a natural number $n$ such that $l$ is isomorphic to a subfield of $\Q(\zeta_n)$.
conclusions: there exists a natural number $n$ such that $l$ is isomorphic to a subfield of $\Q(\zeta_n)$
nodes.label: thm:Kronecker Weber

nodes.name: Proof of the Kronecker-Weber theorem
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a the set of primes which ramify in $l$. For each $p \in S$ we let $\hat p$ be a prime of $l$ above $p$. We therefore have an abelian extension $l_{\hat p} / \Q_p$. Choose $r_p$ such that $1+p^{r_p} \Z_p \subseteq N(l_{\hat p}^\times)$. Let $n = \prod_{p \in S} p^{r_p}$. Let $m = l(\zeta_n)$. We shall prove that $m = \Q(\zeta_n)$, which implies $l$ is isomorphic to a subfield of $\Q(\zeta_n)$. For a prime $p \in S$, let $D_p$ and $I_p$ be the decomposition subgroup and inertia subgroup of $\Gal(m/\Q)$ at $p$. We may identify $D_p$ with $\Gal(m_p / \Q_p)$, and we have a reciprocity isomorphism \[ D_p \cong \Q_p^\times / N(m_p^\times). \] By \ref{lem:local image inertia} The image of $I_p$ under the reciprocity map is \[ I_p \cong \Z_p^\times / N(m_p^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times. \] We have \[ N_{m_p/\Q_p} (m_p^\times) = N_{l_p/\Q_p} (l_p^\times) \cap N_{\Q_p(\zeta_n) / \Q_p} (\Q_p(\zeta_n)^\times). \] Note that by \ref{lem:local cyclotomic norms}, \ref{lem:subgroup compatibility} and \ref{lem:local image inertia}, \[ N_{\Q_p(\zeta_n) / \Q_p} (\Q_p(\zeta_n)^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times = N_{\Q_p(\zeta_{p^{r_p}}) / \Q_p} (\Q_p(\zeta_{p^{r_p}})^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times = 1+p^r \Z_p \supseteq N_{l_p/\Q_p} (l_p^\times). \] This implies $N_{m_p/\Q_p} (m_p^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times = 1+p^r \Z_p$. It follows that $I_p \cong \Z_p^\times / (1+p^{r_p} \Z_p) \cong (\Z / p^{r_p})^\times$. In particular $|I_p| = \phi(p^{r_p})$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function. Let $I$ be the subgroup generated by the $I_p$ for $p \in S$. The fixed field of $I$ is an unramified extension of $\Q$, and is therefore equal to $\Q$. Therefore $I = \Gal(m/\Q)$ and we have \[ [m : \Q] = |I| \le \prod |I_p| = \phi(n) = [\Q(\zeta_n) : \Q]. \] Hence $m = \Q(\zeta_n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute inertia groups of l(zeta_n) via local reciprocity and cyclotomic norm groups. Since Q has no unramified extensions, inertia generates and a degree count gives m = Q(zeta_n).

nodes.name: Finite Galois extension of number fields
nodes.statement: In this chapter we let $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of algebraic number fields.

nodes.name: Idele class group
nodes.statement: We shall consider the idele class group $\Cl_l = \A_l^\times / l^\times$ as a module for the Galois group $\Gal(l/k)$ and we shall describe the construction of fundamental classes in $H^2(l/k, \Cl_l)$.

nodes.name: Invariants of the idele class group
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of number fields (or even global fields). The map $\Cl_k \to \Cl_l ^ {\Gal(l/k)}$ is an isomorphism.
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of number fields (or even global fields)
nodes.label: lem:idele class invariants

nodes.name: Proof of invariants of the idele class group
nodes.statement: We have a short exact sequence \[ 0 \to l^\times \to \A_l^\times \to \Cl_l \to 0. \] Taking $\Gal(l/k)$-invariants gives a long exact sequence beginning with \[ 0 \to k^\times \to \A_k^\times \to \Cl_l^{\Gal(l/k)} \to H^1(l/k, l^\times). \] The last term is zero by \ref{thm:hilbert 90}. This implies the result.
nodes.statement_short: Take invariants of 0 -> l^x -> A_l^x -> Cl_l -> 0 and use Hilbert 90.

nodes.name: H^0_Tate of the idele class group
nodes.statement: By the lemma, we may regard $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ as the quotient $\Cl_k / N_{l/k} \Cl_l$.
conclusions: we may regard $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ as the quotient $\Cl_k / N_{l/k} \Cl_l$

nodes.name: Set S of places
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite set of places of $k$, containing all of the infinite primes and all of the primes which ramify in $l$.

nodes.name: S-ideles
nodes.statement: We shall use the notation \[ \A_{l,S} = \prod_{v \in S} \prod_{w | v} l_w \times \prod_{v \notin S} \prod_{w | v} \cO_v. \]

nodes.name: Ring of S-integers
nodes.statement: We also write $\cO_{l,S}$ for the ring $S$-integers in $l$: \[ \cO_{l,S} = \{x \in l, \forall v \not\in S, \forall w | v, |x|_v \le 1\} = l \cap \A_{l,S}. \]

nodes.name: S-ideles modulo units are fractional ideals
nodes.statement: The quotient $\A_l^\times / \A_{l,S}^\times$ is naturally isomorphic to the group of non-zero fractional ideals of $\cO_{l,S}$.
conclusions: The quotient $\A_l^\times / \A_{l,S}^\times$ is naturally isomorphic to the group of non-zero fractional ideals of $\cO_{l,S}$.

nodes.name: S-integers form principal ideal domains
nodes.statement: By adding more primes to $S$ if necessary, we may assume that $\cO_{k,S}$ and $\cO_{l,S}$ are both principal ideal domains (this can be achieved by adding to $S$ primes $P$ whose ideal classes generate the class groups of $k$ and $l$).

nodes.name: Idele class group via S-ideles and S-units
nodes.statement: With such a choice of $S$ we have: \[ \A_{l}^\times = \A_{l,S}^\times l^\times, \qquad \A_k^\times = \A_{k,S}^\times k^\times, \] and therefore \[ \Cl_{l} = \A_{l,S}^\times / \cO_{l,S}^\times, \qquad \Cl_{k} = \A_{k,S}^\times / \cO_{k,S}^\times. \]

nodes.name: Place v-hat above v
nodes.statement: Let $v$ be a place of $k$ and $\hat v$ a place of $l$ above $v$.

nodes.name: Decomposition group D_{v-hat}
nodes.statement: We'll write $D_{\hat v}$ the decomposition group at $\hat v$.

nodes.name: Semi-local units and ideles as coinduced modules
nodes.statement: Then there are isomorphisms \[ \prod_{w | v} l_w^\times \cong \coind_{D_{\hat v}}^{\Gal(l/k)} l_{\hat v}^\times, \qquad \prod_{w | v} \cO_w^\times \cong \coind_{D_{\hat v}}^{\Gal(l/k)} \cO_{\hat v}^\times. \]
nodes.label: lem:semi-local iso coind

nodes.name: Proof of the semi-local coinduction isomorphism
nodes.statement: We'll write $x$ for an element of $\prod_{w | v} l_w^\times$ and $x_w$ for it's component in $l_w$. Define a map $\Phi : \prod_{w | v} l_w^\times \to (\Gal(l/k) \to l_{\hat v}^\times)$ by \[ \Phi (x) = (g \mapsto g \bullet x_{g^{-1} \hat v}). \] Note that for $h \in D_{\hat v}$ we have \[ \Phi (x) (hg) = h \bullet (g \bullet x_{g^{-1} \hat v}) = h \bullet \Phi(x) (g). \] Therefore $\Phi(x)$ is in the subspace $\coind_{D_v} l_{\hat v}$, and it's easy to check that $\Phi$ gives a group isomorphism $\prod_{w | v} l_w^\times \cong \coind_{D_v} l_{\hat v}^\times$. We'll check that this map intertwines the actions of $G$. For $g \in G$, then element $g \bullet x$ has $w$-component $g \bullet x_{g^{-1}\bullet w}$. This implies \[ \Phi( g \bullet x)(h) = h\bullet (g \bullet x)_{h^{-1} \bullet \hat v} = h g \bullet x_{(hg)^{-1} \bullet \hat v} = \Phi (x) (hg). \] The proof of the isomorphism for $\prod_{w | v} \cO_w^\times$ is similar.
nodes.statement_short: Define Phi(x) = (g -> g.x_{g^{-1} v}) and check it lands in the coinduced module and is equivariant.

nodes.name: Cohomology of S-ideles decomposes into local cohomology
nodes.statement: There are isomorphisms for all $n > 0$ \[ H^n(l/k, \A_{S,l}^\times) \cong \prod_{v \in S} H^n(l_{\hat v} / k_v, l_{\hat v}^\times). \]
conclusions: H^n(l/k, \A_{S,l}^\times) \cong \prod_{v \in S} H^n(l_{\hat v} / k_v, l_{\hat v}^\times).
nodes.label: lem:cohomology S-ideles decomp

nodes.name: Proof of the decomposition of S-idele cohomology
nodes.statement:
We note that by ef{lem:semi-local iso coind} we have \[ \A_{S,l}^	imes \cong \prod_{v \in S} \coind_{D_{\hat v}} l_{\hat v}^	imes 	imes \prod_{v 
ot\in S} \coind_{D_{\hat v}} \cO_{\hat v}^	imes \] By Shapiro's lemma (ef{lem:Shapiro}) we have \[ H^n(l/k,\A_{S,l}^	imes) \cong \prod_{v \in S} H^n(l_{\hat v}/k_v , l_{\hat v}^	imes) 	imes \prod_{v 
ot\in S} H^n(l_{\hat v}/k_v , \cO_{\hat v}^	imes) \] For $v 
ot\in S$, the extension $l_{\hat{v}}/l_v$ is unramified, so by ef{lem:unramified units trivial} $\cO_{\hat v}^	imes$ has trivial cohomology.
nodes.statement_short: Coinduction and Shapiro's lemma, with unramified unit factors trivial.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of the S-ideles
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is a cyclic extension then we have \[ h(l/k, \A_{S,l} ^\times ) = \prod_{v \in S} |D_{\hat v}|. \]
nodes.label: lem:herbrand S-ideles

nodes.name: Proof of the Herbrand quotient of S-ideles
nodes.statement: This follows from \ref{lem:cohomology S-ideles decomp} and \ref{lem:herbrand local l*}.
nodes.statement_short: Local decomposition and local Herbrand quotients.

nodes.name: Logarithmic space V_S
nodes.statement: Define the \emph{logarithmic space} $V_S$ to be the following finite dimensional vector space over the real numbers: \[ V_S = \prod_{v \in S} \prod_{w | v} \R. \]

nodes.name: V_S as an induced Galois representation
nodes.statement: We consider $V_S$ as a representation of $\Gal(l/k)$, where the Galois action permutes the places $w$ lying above each $v \in S$. As a Galois representation we have \[ V_S \cong \prod_{v \in S} \ind_{D_{\hat v}}^{\Gal(l/k)} \R. \]

nodes.name: Lattice L_S
nodes.statement: Contained in $V_S$ we have a lattice $L_S$ consisting of vectors whose components are all in $\Z$.

nodes.name: Lattice
nodes.statement: Here we are using the word ``lattice'' to mean the $\Z$-space of a basis for $V_S$.

nodes.name: L_S as an induced Galois representation
nodes.statement: We have an isomorphism \[ L_S \cong \prod_{v \in S} \ind_{D_{\hat v}}^{\Gal(l/k)} \Z. \]

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of the lattice L_S
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is a cyclic extension then $h(l/k,L_S) = \prod_{v \in S} |D_{\hat v}|$.
nodes.label: lem:herbrand L_S

nodes.name: Proof of the Herbrand quotient of L_S
nodes.statement: This follows from Shapiro's lemma (\ref{lem:Shapiro}) together with the calculation of the cohomology of a cyclic group with values in $\Z$ (\ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}).
nodes.statement_short: Shapiro's lemma and cohomology of cyclic groups in Z.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of any invariant lattice
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be cyclic and let $M$ be any Galois-invariant lattice in $V_S$. Then $h(l/k,M) = \prod_{v \in S} |D_{\hat v}|$
nodes.label: lem:herbrand log lattice

nodes.name: Proof for invariant lattices
nodes.statement: The representations $M \otimes \Q$ and $L_S \otimes \Q$ have the same character (this is just the character of the representation $V_S$). Therefore the representations $M \otimes \Q$ and $L_S \otimes \Q$ are isomorphic. Hence $M$ is isomorphic to subrepresentation of finite index in $L_S$, so by \ref{lem:herbrand ses} and \ref{lem:herbrand finite} they have the same Herbrand quotient. The result then follows from \ref{lem:herbrand L_S}.
nodes.statement_short: Rationally isomorphic lattices are commensurable, so have the same Herbrand quotient as L_S.

nodes.name: Diagonal vector spans a trivial subrepresentation
nodes.statement: The vector $(1,1,\ldots,1) \in V_S$ is fixed by all elements of $\Gal(l/k)$, so it spans a subrepresentation isomorphic to the trivial representation $\Z$.
conclusions: The vector $(1,1,\ldots,1) \in V_S$ is fixed by all elements of $\Gal(l/k)$
it spans a subrepresentation isomorphic to the trivial representation $\Z$

nodes.name: Logarithmic map log_S
nodes.statement: Recall the we have a logarithmic map \[ \log_S : \cO_S^\times \to V_S, \] where the $w$-component of $\log_S(x)$ is $\log |x|_w$.

nodes.name: Kernel of log_S is the roots of unity
nodes.statement: The kernel of $\log_S$ is the finite group of roots of unity in $k$.
conclusions: The kernel of $\log_S$ is the finite group of roots of unity in $k$.

nodes.name: Dirichlet's unit theorem
nodes.statement: $\log_S(\cO_S^\times)$ has zero intersection with $\Span (1,1,\ldots,1)$. The direct sum of these subrepresentations is a lattice in $V_S$.
conclusions: The direct sum of these subrepresentations is a lattice in $V_S$.
nodes.label: thm:Dirichlet unit theorem

nodes.name: Proof of Dirichlet's unit theorem
nodes.statement: An equivalent statement is already in Mathlib as \texttt{NumberField.Units.dirichletUnitTheorem.unitLattice\_span\_eq\_top}.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of the S-units
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a cyclic extension. Then \[ h(l/k,\cO_{l,S}^\times) = \frac{\prod_{v\in S} |D_{\hat v}|}{[l:k]}. \]
nodes.label: lem:herbrand S-units

nodes.name: Proof of the Herbrand quotient of S-units
nodes.statement: Since $\log_S$ has finite kernel, the Herbrand quotient of $\cO_{l,S}^\times$ is equal to that of $\log_S(\cO_S^\times)$. By Dirichlet's unit theorem, $\log_S(\cO_S^\times) \oplus \Z$ is a lattice in $V_S$. We know the Herbrand quotient of $\log_S(\cO_S^\times) \oplus \Z$ from \ref{lem:herbrand log lattice}, and the Herbrand quotient of $\Z$ from \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the log lattice; Dirichlet's unit theorem plus the trivial line Z.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient of the idele class group
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is cyclic then $h(l/k,\Cl_l) = [l:k]$.
nodes.label: lem:herbrand idele class group

nodes.name: Proof of the Herbrand quotient of Cl_l
nodes.statement: Our choice of $S$ implies $\Cl_l \cong \A_{l,S}^\times / \cO_{l,S}^\times$. We have calculated the Herbrand quotients of $\A_{l,S}^\times$ and $\cO_{l,S}^\times$ in \ref{lem:herbrand S-ideles} and \ref{lem:herbrand S-units}.
nodes.statement_short: Cl_l = A_S^x / O_S^x and the two computed quotients.

nodes.name: Dirichlet density
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a set of primes of $\cO_k$. We'll say that $M$ has a \emph{Dirichlet density} $c \in \R$ if \[ \sum_{P \in M} N(P)^{-s} \stackrel{s \to 1+}\sim c \cdot \log\left(\frac{1}{s-1}\right). \] where $s$ tends to $1$ through the real numbers $s>1$. The symbol $\sim$ denotes asymptotic equivalence, which means that the ratio of the left hand side to the right hand side converges to $1$ as $s$ tends to $1$ from above. Implied constants may depend of the set $M$ and the field $k$.
nodes.label: def:Dirichlet density

nodes.name: Additivity of Dirichlet density
nodes.statement: Suppose $M_1$ and $M_2$ are disjoint sets of primes of $\cO_l$. If two of the sets $M_1, M_2, M_1 \cup M_2$ have a Dirichlet density, then so does the third and we have \[ \density(M_1 \cup M_2) = \density(M_1) + \density(M_2). \]
assumptions: $M_1$ and $M_2$ are disjoint sets of primes of $\cO_l$
two of the sets $M_1, M_2, M_1 \cup M_2$ have a Dirichlet density
nodes.label: lem:Dirichlet density union

nodes.name: Proof of additivity of density
nodes.statement: This is trivial.

nodes.name: All primes have Dirichlet density 1
nodes.statement: The set of all primes of $\cO_k$ has Dirichlet density $1$.
conclusions: The set of all primes of $\cO_k$ has Dirichlet density $1$.
nodes.label: lem:Dirichlet density top

nodes.name: Proof that all primes have density 1
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a prime. For $s > 1$ we have \[ \left|N(P)^{-s} - \log\left( \frac{1}{1-N(P)^{-s}}\right)\right| \ll N(P)^{-2s} \] Since $\sum N(P)^{-2s}$ is bounded in the region $s > 1$ (this follows from the convergence of the Dedekind zeta function), we have \[ \sum_P N(P)^{-s} \sim \sum_P \log\left( \frac{1}{1-N(P)^{-s}} \right) = \log \zeta_l(s), \] where $\zeta_l$ is the Dedekind zeta function (\texttt{NumberField.dedekindZeta}). By the analytic class number formula (\verb!NumberField.tendsto_sub_one_mul_dedekindZeta_nhdsGT!) there is a positive real number $r$ such that \[ \zeta_l(s) = \frac{r}{s-1} + O(1) \qquad (s > 1). \] This implies \[ \log(\zeta_l(s)) \sim \log\left( \frac{1}{s-1}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Compare the prime sum with log zeta and use the simple pole of the Dedekind zeta function at s=1.

nodes.name: Degree-one primes have Dirichlet density 1
nodes.statement: The set of primes of $\cO_l$ of degree one has Dirichlet density $1$.
conclusions: The set of primes of $\cO_l$ of degree one has Dirichlet density $1$.
nodes.label: lem:Dirichlet density degree one

nodes.name: Proof that degree-one primes have density 1
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be the set of primes of degree larger than one. It's sufficient to prove that $M$ has Dirichlet density $0$. We have \[ \sum_{P \in M} N(P)^{-s} = \sum_{n \in \N} A(n) n^{-s}, \] Where $A$ is the number of primes of degree $>1$ with norm $n$. Note that $A(n) \le [l:\Q]$. Also $A(n)=0$ unless $n=m^r$ for positive integer $m$ and $1 \le r \le [l:Q]$. This implies \[ \sum_{P \in M} N(P)^{-s} \le [l:\Q] \sum_{r=2}^{[l:\Q]} \sum_{m =1} ^\infty m^{-rs} \le [l:\Q] (\zeta_\Q(2) + \cdots + \zeta_\Q([l:\Q]) ). \] Since the sum above is bounded on the region $s > 1$, the set $M$ has Dirichlet density $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Primes of higher degree contribute a bounded sum of zeta values at s>=2.

nodes.name: Density of completely split primes
nodes.statement: Let $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of number fields. Then the set of degree $1$ primes of $k$ which split completely in $l$ has density $\frac{1}{[l:k]}$.
assumptions: $l/k$ be a finite Galois extension of number fields
conclusions: the set of degree $1$ primes of $k$ which split completely in $l$ has density $\frac{1}{[l:k]}$
nodes.label: lem:Dirichlet density split

nodes.name: Proof of the density of split primes
nodes.statement: Let $M_k$ be the set of degree $1$ primes of $k$ and $M_l$ the set of degree $1$ primes of $l$. Every prime $Q$ in $M_l$ lies above some prime $P \in M_k$. If there is a prime $Q$ above $P$, then there are precisely $[l:k]$ of them; this happens when $P$ splits completely in $l$. Let $M$ be the set of $P \in M_k$ which split completely in $l$. Then we have \[ \sum_{P \in M} N(P)^{-s} = \frac{1}{[l:k]} \sum_{Q \in M_l} N(Q)^{-s} \sim \frac{1}{[l:k]} \log\left( \frac{1}{s-1}\right). \] Here we have used \ref{lem:Dirichlet density degree one}.
nodes.statement_short: Degree-one primes of l lie [l:k]-to-1 over split degree-one primes of k.

nodes.name: Finiteness of H^0 of the idele class group
nodes.statement: $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ is finite.
nodes.label: lem:H0 idele class group finite

nodes.name: Proof of finiteness of H^0(Cl_l)
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} \Cl_{k} / N(\Cl_l) & \cong \A_{k,S}^\times / \cO_{k,S}^\times N(\A_{l,S}^\times) \\ & \cong \left(\prod_{v \in S} k_v^\times / N(l_{\hat v}^\times)\right) / \cO_{k,S}^\times, \end{align*} where $\hat v$ is a place of $l$ lying above $v$. The result follows because each of the groups $k_v^\times / N(l_w)$ is finite (in fact by the local reciprocity isomorphism this is isomorphic to the abelianization of the decomposition group at $\hat v$).
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a quotient of a finite product of finite local norm quotients.

nodes.name: Idele pi_P
nodes.statement: Given any maximal ideal $P$ of $\cO_{k,S}$, we let $\pi_P$ be an idele whose $P$-component is a uniformizer in $k_P$, and whose other components are all $1$.

nodes.name: Class of pi_P is independent of the uniformizer
nodes.statement: The coset of $\pi_P$ in $H^0(l/k,\Cl_l)$ does not depend on the choice of uniformizer since all the local units at $P$ are local norms from $l_{Q}$ for any $Q|P$ (because $P$ is unramified in $l$).
conclusions: The coset of $\pi_P$ in $H^0(l/k,\Cl_l)$ does not depend on the choice of uniformizer

nodes.name: Class of pi_P via a generator
nodes.statement: Equivalently, if we choose a generator $P=(\pi)$ with $\pi \in \cO_{k,S}$ then the coset of $\pi_P$ is the inverse of the image of $\pi$ in $\prod_{v \in S} k_v^\times / N(l_{\hat v}^\times)$.
conclusions: the coset of $\pi_P$ is the inverse of the image of $\pi$ in $\prod_{v \in S} k_v^\times / N(l_{\hat v}^\times)$

nodes.name: Map iota from fractional ideals to H^0_Tate
nodes.statement: This clearly extends to a homomorphism \[ \iota : \textrm{non-zero fractional ideals of $\cO_{k,S}$} \to H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l), \] whose kernel is the subgroup of ideals with a generator which is a local norm at $v$ for all $v \in S$.

nodes.name: L-function of a character
nodes.statement: Let $\chi : H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l) \to \C^\times$ be a character. For a non-zero ideal $I$ of $\cO_{k,S}$, we shall write $\chi(I)$ in place of $\chi(\iota(I))$. We define the $L$-function of $\chi$ by \[ L(s,\chi) = \sum_{I} \chi(I) \cdot N(I)^{-s} = \prod_{P} \frac{1}{1-\chi(P) \cdot N(P)^{-s}}. \] Here $s$ is a complex number with real part greater than $1$; both the product and the series converge absolutely in that region. In the sum, $I$ ranges over the non-zero ideals of $\cO_{k,S}$, and in the product $P$ ranges over the maximal ideals of $\cO_{k,S}$. If $\chi$ is the trivial character, then $L(s,\chi)$ is (up to finitely many Euler factors for primes in $S$) equal to the Dedekind zeta function of $k$.
nodes.label: def:L-function

nodes.name: Meromorphic continuation of L(s,chi)
nodes.statement: It's known that $L(s,\chi)$ has a meromorphic continuation to $\C$ and is entire if $\chi$ is non-trivial (see for example Tate's thesis, which is chapter XV of \cite{cassells frohlich}).

nodes.name: Weak lemma
nodes.statement: If $\chi$ is a non-trivial character then $L(s,\chi)$ is bounded on the interval $(1,2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Non-trivial character L-functions are bounded on (1,2).
nodes.label: lem:L-function bound

nodes.name: Density bound for primes with trivial image
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a set of primes of $\cO_S$ whose image in $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ is zero. There exists a real number $c$ depending only on the fields $k$ and $l$, such that for all $s > 1$ we have: \[ \sum_{p \in M} N(P)^{-s} \le \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \log\left(\frac{1}{s-1}\right) + c. \]
nodes.statement_short: Primes trivial in H^0_Tate(Cl_l) have prime sum at most log(1/(s-1))/|H^0| + c.
assumptions: $M$ be a set of primes of $\cO_S$ whose image in $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ is zero
conclusions: There exists a real number $c$ depending only on the fields $k$ and $l$, such that for all $s > 1$ we have:
nodes.label: lem:density bound

nodes.name: Proof of the density bound
nodes.statement: Let $s > 1$. All the series in the following calculation converge absolutely in this region. The implied constants in the $O(1)$ terms do not depend on $s$. \begin{align*} \sum_{P \in M} |N(P)|^{-s} &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_P \sum_\chi \chi(P) N(P)^{-s}\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_P \sum_\chi -\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}) + O(1)\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_P \sum_\chi -\log |1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}| + O(1)\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_\chi \sum_P -\log |1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}| + O(1)\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \log \left(\prod_\chi |L(s,\chi)| \right) + O(1)\\ &\le \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \log \left(\frac{1}{s-1}\right) + O(1). \end{align*} Interchanging the order of summation is justified because the series converge absolutely. We need to be slightly careful about which branch of the logarithm we are using here. In the expression $\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ we shall mean the branch which is continuous on the ball of radius $1$, centred about $1$. The imaginary parts of $\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ and $\log(1-\bar \chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ cancel out; this justifies replacing $\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ by $\log |1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}|$.
nodes.statement_short: Character orthogonality expresses the prime sum through log of the product of L-functions; the trivial character gives the pole, others are bounded.

nodes.name: Exact density of primes with trivial image
nodes.statement: In fact the density of the set $M$ in this lemma is precisely $\frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|}$. This can be proved by showing that each $L(s,\chi)$ has a continuation to a neighbourhood of $s=1$, and is non-zero at $s=1$. However, proving this is more difficult than the weak lemma above, and we only need the inequality of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: The density is exactly 1/|H^0|, but proving it requires non-vanishing of L(1,chi).

nodes.name: First inequality
nodes.statement: For any finite Galois extension $l/k$ be have \[ |H^0_{\Tate}(l/k, \Cl_{l}) | \le [l : k]. \]
nodes.label: thm:first inequality

nodes.name: Proof of the first inequality
nodes.statement: Let $M_1$ be the set of degree $1$ primes of $\cO_{k,S}$ which split in $l$ and let $M_2$ be the set of primes of $\cO_{k,S}$ whose image in $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ is zero. Given $P \in M_1$, the norm map $l_{\hat v}^\times \to k_v^\times$ is the identity map, and is in particular surjective. Hence the image of $P$ in $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ is zero. This shows that $M_1 \subseteq M_2$. This implies for $s> 1$: \[ \sum_{P \in M_1} N(P)^{-s} \le \sum_{P \in M_2} N(P)^{-s} . \] By \ref{lem:density bound} we have \[ \sum_{P \in M_1} N(P)^{-s} \le \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \log \left(\frac{1}{1-s}\right) + O(1). \] By \ref{lem:Dirichlet density split} the left hand side is asymptotic to $\frac{1}{[l:k]}\log \left(\frac{1}{1-s}\right)$. Therefore $\frac{1}{[l:k]} \le \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|}$.
nodes.statement_short: Split degree-one primes are trivial in H^0; compare their density 1/[l:k] with the density bound.

nodes.name: Cohomology of the idele class group for cyclic extensions
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is cyclic then $|H^2(l/k, \Cl_{l})| = [l:k]$ and $H^1(l/k, \Cl_{l}) = 0$.
nodes.label: cor:H1 H2 cyclic idele class

nodes.name: Proof for cyclic idele class cohomology
nodes.statement: This follows immediately from (a) the first inequality, (b) the periodicity of the cohomology for a cyclic group, and (c) the calculation of the Herbrand quotient of $\Cl_{l}$.
nodes.statement_short: First inequality, periodicity and the Herbrand quotient.

nodes.name: Global cohomology bound
nodes.statement: If $l/k$ is any finite Galois extension then $H^1(l/k, \Cl_{l}) \cong 0$ and $|H^2(l/k, \Cl_{l})| \le [l:k]$.
nodes.label: thm:global cohomology bound

nodes.name: Proof of the global cohomology bound
nodes.statement: For each prime number $p$ dividing $[l:k]$ we let $k_p$ be the fixed field of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $S_p$ of $\Gal(l/k)$. By \ref{cor:cohomology sub Sylow}, it's suffient to prove \[ H^1(l/k_p, \Cl_{l}) = 0, \qquad |H^2(l/k_p, \Cl_{l})| \le [l:k_p]. \] Since $S_p$ is solvable, this reduces us to the case that $\Gal(l/k)$ is solvable. We'll prove the result by induction on $k$ starting with $k=l$ and working downwards in cyclic quotients. Clearly the result holds for $k=l$. Assume the result for a subfield $m$ of $l$ and let $m/k$ be cyclic. We have an inflation restriction sequence: \[ 0 \to H^1(m/k, \Cl_{m}) \to H^1(l/k, \Cl_{l}) \to H^1(l/m,\Cl_{l}). \] The first term is zero by \ref{cor:H1 H2 cyclic idele class} and the last term is zero by the inductive hypothesis. Therefore $H^1(l/k,\Cl_l) \cong 0$. Since $H^1(l/m,\Cl_l)$ is assumed to be zero, we also have an inflation-restriction sequence in dimension 2: \[ 0 \to H^2(m/k, \Cl_m) \to H^2(l/k, \Cl_l) \to H^2(l/m,\Cl_l). \] By the inductive hypothesis we have $|H^2(l/m,\Cl_l)| \le [l:m]$ and by \ref{cor:H1 H2 cyclic idele class} we have $|H^2(m/k, \Cl_m)| = [m : k]$. It follows that $|H^2(l/k,\Cl_l)| \le [l : k]$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Sylow (solvable) fixed fields, then induct down cyclic steps with inflation-restriction in degrees 1 and 2.

nodes.name: Plan for constructing global fundamental classes
nodes.statement: To complete the construction of fundamental classes and the reciprocity isomorphism, we need only show that there is an element in $H^2(l/k,\Cl_l)$ of order $[l:k]$. Such an element is constructed first for a cyclic cyclotomic extension $l'/k$ with the same degree as $l/k$. It's then shown that the inflation of such a class to $ll'/k$ must split on $ll'/l$, and must therefore be the inflation of an element of order $[l:k]$ in $H^2(l/k,\Cl_l)$.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining step: build a class of order [l:k] for a cyclic cyclotomic l'/k and pull it back from l l' to l, as in the local case.

nodes.name: Identify cochains with M and coboundaries with alternating sums
nodes.statement: Each of the modules $C^n(G,M)$ may be identified with $M$, and the coboundary maps reduce to alternating sums of the form $d^n(m) = \sum_{i=0}^{n+1} (-1)^i m$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify cochains with M and coboundaries with alternating sums

nodes.name: Coboundaries alternate identity/zero, so image equals kernel
nodes.statement: Hence $d^n$ is the identity map for odd $n$, and is the zero map for even $m$. It follows that the image of $d^n$ is equal to the kernel of $d^{n+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Coboundaries alternate identity/zero, so image equals kernel

nodes.name: Reduce to the two squares involving connecting maps
nodes.statement: Most of the commuting squares have already been proved if inflation and restriction are defined as morphisms of functors. The remaining two squares are: \[ \begin{matrix} H^n(G,C)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G,A)\\ \rest\downarrow&&\downarrow\rest \\ H^n(S,C)& \stackrel{\delta} \to& H^{n+1}(S,A) \end{matrix} \qquad\textrm{ and }\qquad \begin{matrix} H^n(G/S,C^S)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G/S,A^S)\\ \infl\downarrow&&\downarrow\infl\\ H^n(G,C)& \stackrel{\delta}\to& H^{n+1}(G,A) \end{matrix} . \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the two squares involving connecting maps

nodes.name: Apply Mathlib's delta_naturality
nodes.statement: Both of these can be deduced from the following statement in Mathlib: \begin{quote} \texttt{HomologicalComplex.HomologySequence.$\delta$\_naturality} \end{quote}

nodes.name: Every 1-chain is a cycle
nodes.statement: Since $M$ is trivial, the map $d_0 : C_1(G,M) \to C_0(G,M)$ is zero, so every $1$-chain is a 1-cycle. The map $d_1 : C_1(G,M) \to C_0(G,M)$ is given by \[ d_1 \single((x,y),m) = \single(y,x^{-1} \bullet m) - \single(xy,m) + \single(x,m). \]

nodes.name: Present H_1 by relations
nodes.statement: Therefore $H_1(G,M)$ is the quotient of $G \to_0 M$ by the relations \[ \single(xy,m) = \single(x,m) + \single(y,m), \qquad x,y \in G. \]

nodes.name: Homomorphism in x descends to G^ab
nodes.statement: If we fix an $m \in M$, then these relations imply that the map $G \to H_1(G,M)$ defined by $x \mapsto \single(x,m)$ is a group homomorphism. In particular this map descends to a homomorphism $G^{\ab} \to H_1(G,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Homomorphism in x descends to G^ab

nodes.name: Bilinearity
nodes.statement: If we fix $x \in G$ and allow $m$ to vary, then $\single(x,m)$ is $\Z$-linear in $m$. It is therefore a $\Z$-bilinear map $G^\ab \times M \to H_1(G,M)$.

nodes.name: Construct Phi on the tensor product
nodes.statement: Such a map lifts to a linear map $\Phi : G^{\ab} \otimes_{\Z} M \to H_1(G,M)$ given by \[ xG' \otimes m \mapsto \single(x,m) \]
nodes.statement_short: Construct Phi on the tensor product

nodes.name: Construct inverse Psi and conclude
nodes.statement: To construct an inverse of $\Phi$, we note that all of the relations are in the kernel of the linear map $(G\to_0 M) \to (G^\ab \otimes_\Z M)$ defined by $\single(x,m) \mapsto xG' \otimes m$. Therefore this map descends to a linear map $\Psi : H_1(G,M) \to (G^\ab \otimes_\Z M)$. It is trivial to check that $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are inverses.

nodes.name: Only degrees 0 and -1 need discussion
nodes.statement: This result is clear from the definition for $n > 0$ and $n < -1$. We'll discuss the two remaining cases.

nodes.name: Degree 0: cocycles are M^G, coboundaries the image of N_G
nodes.statement: The $0$-cocycle submodule is the kernel of the map $d^0 : C^0(G,M) \to C^1(G,M)$. This is the same as $H^0(G,M)$, which is isomorphic to $M^G$. On the other hand $B^0_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is by definition the image of $N_G : M \to M$. Similarly, $H_0(G,M)$ is the quotient of $M$ by $I_GM$, and $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is by definition the quotient of $\ker(N_G : M \to M)$ by the same submodule.
nodes.statement_short: Degree 0: cocycles are M^G, coboundaries the image of N_G

nodes.name: Restriction to S is coinduced from C -> M
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of $G$ and let $C$ be a set of representatives for the cosets $cS$ of $S$ in $G$. There is an isomorphism of $S$-representations \[ \coind_1(G,M) \downarrow S \cong \coind_1(S,C \to M). \] This isomorphism takes a function $f : G \to M$ to function $S \to (C \to M)$ defined by $s \mapsto (c \mapsto f(cs))$.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction to S is coinduced from C -> M

nodes.name: Apply Shapiro and vanishing for the trivial group
nodes.statement: The isomorphism, together with \ref{lem:Shapiro} and \ref{lem:Hn unit} implies for $n >0$: \[ H^n(S,\coind_1(G,M)) \cong H^n(S,\coind_1(S,C \to M)) \cong H^n(1,C \to M) \cong 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Apply Shapiro and vanishing for the trivial group

nodes.name: Restriction to S is induced
nodes.statement: The restriction of $\ind_1(G,A)$ to a subgroup $S$ is isomorphic to $\ind_1(S, C \to_0 A)$, where $C$ is a set of coset representatives for the cosets $cS$ of $S$ in $G$.

nodes.name: Apply Shapiro's lemma
nodes.statement: Hence by \ref{lem:Shapiro} we have \[ H_n(S,\ind_1(G,A)) \cong H_n(S,\ind_1(S,C\to_0 A)\cong H_n(1,C \to_0 A). \]

nodes.name: Homology of the trivial group vanishes
nodes.statement: The result now follows from \ref{eg:homology unit}.
nodes.statement_short: Homology of the trivial group vanishes

nodes.name: Reduce to ind_1
nodes.statement: These representations are isomorphic, so it's sufficient to prove that $\ind_1(G,A)$ has trivial Tate cohomology (this is the more convenient case to prove). We already know that $\ind_1(G,A)$ has trivial homology. Also, since it is isomorphic to $\coind_1(G,A)$, it must have trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Remaining: degrees 0 and -1
nodes.statement: It only remains to prove that $H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(M))$ and $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(M))$ are zero for all subgroups $S$ of $G$.

nodes.name: Recall the action by right translation
nodes.statement: Recall that $\ind_1(G,M)$ is the space of functions $G \to_0 M$, and the action of $G$ is by right-translation: \[ g \bullet \single(x,m) = \single(xg^{-1},m). \]
nodes.statement_short: Recall the action by right translation

nodes.name: Degree 0 via M^S / N_S M
nodes.statement: To prove that $H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A))=0$, we use the isomorphism \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology}: \[ H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A)) \cong \ind_1(G,A)^S / N_S \ind_1(G,A). \]

nodes.name: Invariant functions are norms, so H^0 vanishes
nodes.statement: A function $f : G \to_0 M$ is $S$-invariant if $f$ is constant on cosets $gS$ of $S$. If we let $\{g_i\}$ be a set of coset representatives, then we have $f = N_S (\sum_i \single(g_i, f(g_i)))$. Therefore $H^0_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A))=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Invariant functions are norms, so H^0 vanishes

nodes.name: Degree -1 via ker N_S / I_S
nodes.statement: For the $n=-1$ case we use the isomorphism \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology}: \[ H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\ind_1(G,A)) \cong \ker(N_S : \ind_1(G,A) \to \ind_1(G,A)) / I_S \ind_1(M), \] where $I_G \ind_1(M)$ is generated by elements of the form $s \bullet f - f$ for $s \in S$ and $f : G \to M$.

nodes.name: Norm-zero means coset sums vanish
nodes.statement: Suppose $f:G \to_0 M$ is in the kernel of $N_S$. This implies that the sum of the values of $f$ over each coset of $S$ is zero.

nodes.name: Write f as a sum of s.g - g terms
nodes.statement: We can then write $f$ in the form \begin{align*} f & = \sum_i \sum_{s \in S} (\single(g_i s^{-1}, f(g_is^{-1})) - \single(g_i,f(g_is^{-1})))\\ & = \sum_i \sum_{s \in S} (s \bullet \single(g_i, f(g_is^{-1})) - \single(g_i,f(g_is^{-1}))). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write f as a sum of s.g - g terms

nodes.name: Conclude H^{-1} vanishes
nodes.statement: Therefore $f \in I_S \ind_1(M)$. This shows that $H^{-1}(S,\ind_1(M)) = 0$.

nodes.name: Recall coind_1' = coind_1
nodes.statement: We've seen in Lemma \ref{lem:coind₁' iso coind₁} that $\coind_1'(M)$ is isomorphic to $\coind_1(M)$.

nodes.name: Take S-invariants of the isomorphism
nodes.statement: Applying the functor $\Invar$, we obtain an isomorphism between $\coind_1'(M)^S$ and $\coind_1(M)^S$.

nodes.name: Apply the coinduced invariants lemma
nodes.statement: The result then follows from Lemma \ref{lem:coind₁ invariants}.

nodes.name: Middle term has trivial cohomology, so connecting maps are isomorphisms
nodes.statement: We have already shown in Corollary \ref{cor:coind₁' trivial cohomology} that $\coind_1'(M)$ has trivial cohomology, so $H^{r}(S,\coind_1'(M))=0$ for all $r>0$. This implies that the connecting maps are isomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: Middle term has trivial cohomology, so connecting maps are isomorphisms

nodes.name: Naturality from delta_naturality
nodes.statement: The commuting square follows from \texttt{HomologicalComplex.HomologySequence.$\delta$\_naturality} because the short exact sequence $0 \to M \to \coind_1'(M) \to \up(M) \to 0$ is functorial in $M$.

nodes.name: Recall S^ab tensor R = H^{-2}_Tate(S,R)
nodes.statement: Recall that by \ref{lem:homology 1 trivial}, \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology} we already have an isomorphism $S^\ab \otimes R \cong H_1(S,R) \cong H^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R)$ which takes $s \otimes 1$ to (the coset of) $\single(s,1)$.

nodes.name: Dimension shift to H^{-1}(S, aug)
nodes.statement: Furthermore by \ref{cor:Tate up down isos} there is an isomorphism $H^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R) \cong H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(G,R))$.

nodes.name: Remains to identify the image of s tensor 1
nodes.statement: It remains to check that the image of $s \otimes 1$ in $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(G,R))$ is $[s]-[1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains to identify the image of s tensor 1

nodes.name: Diagram of short exact sequences of Tate complexes
nodes.statement: In the following diagram the rows are short exact sequences and the vertical maps are the differentials in the Tate complex. \[ \begin{matrix} 0 \to C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G)) & \to & C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,RG) & \to &C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R) \to 0\\ \downarrow & &\downarrow & &\downarrow \\ 0 \to C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G)) & \to & C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,RG) & \to &C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,R) \to 0 \end{matrix} \]
nodes.statement_short: Diagram of short exact sequences of Tate complexes

nodes.name: s tensor 1 is represented by single(s,1)
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:homology 1 trivial}, the image of $s \otimes 1$ in $H^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R)$ is represented by the element $\single(s,1)$ in $C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,R)$.
nodes.statement_short: s tensor 1 is represented by single(s,1)

nodes.name: Recipe for the connecting map
nodes.statement: To calculate the image in $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G))$, we take a pre-image of $\single(s,1)$ in $C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,RG)$; map that preimage into $C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,RG)$, and then take its preimage in $C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G))$.

nodes.name: Lift to single(s,[1]) and map to [s]-[1]
nodes.statement: An obvious pre-image of $\single(s,1)$ in $C^{-2}_{\Tate}(S,RG)$ is $\single(s,[1])$. The image of this in $C^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,RG) \cong RG$ is $[s]-[1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift to single(s,[1]) and map to [s]-[1]

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore the image of $s \otimes 1$ in $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(S,\aug(R,G))$ is $[s]-[1]$.

nodes.name: Base case n=1 from Mathlib
nodes.statement: This is already in Mathlib for $n=1$.

nodes.name: Inductive step by dimension shifting
nodes.statement: Assume the result is true for some $n\ge 1$; we will prove it for $n+1$ by dimension-shifting.

nodes.name: Vanishing hypothesis passes to up(M)
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a representation such that $H^i(S,M)\cong 0$ for all $0 < i < n+1$. This implies $H^i(S,\up(M)) \cong 0$ for all $0 < i < n$.

nodes.name: Exact sequence for up(M)
nodes.statement: Hence by the inductive hypothesis the following sequence is exact: \[ 0 \to H^n( G/S, \up(M)^S) \to H^n(G, \up(M)) \to H^n(S,\up(M)). \]

nodes.name: Recall the up sequence
nodes.statement: Recall that we have a short exact sequence of representations of $G$: \[ 0 \to M \to \coind_1'(M) \to \up(M) \to 0. \]

nodes.name: S-invariants stay exact since H^1(S,M)=0
nodes.statement: Since $0 < 1 < n+1$, our condition on $M$ implies $H^1(S,M) \cong 0$, so by taking $S$-invariants we obtain a short exact sequence of $G/S$-modules: \[ 0 \to M^S \to \coind_1'(M)^S \to \up(M)^S \to 0. \]

nodes.name: Dimension shift on G/S
nodes.statement: By \ref{cor:coind₁' invariants trivial cohomology}, $\coind_1'(M)^S$ has trivial cohomology, so we have an isomorphism \[ H^n(G/S, \up(M)^S) \to H^{n+1}(G/S, M^S). \]

nodes.name: Comparison diagram
