nodes.statement: We now have a diagram where the horizontal maps are inflation and restriction maps and the vertical maps are dimension-shifting isomorphisms. \[ \begin{matrix} 0 &\to& H^{n}(G/S, \up(M)^S) &\to &H^{n}(G,\up(M)) & \to & H^n(S,\up(M)) \\ & & \downarrow & & \downarrow & & \downarrow \\ 0 &\to& H^{n+1}(G/S, M^S) &\to &H^{n+1}(G,M) & \to & H^{n+1}(S,M). \end{matrix} \]

nodes.name: Diagram commutes by naturality
nodes.statement: The diagram commutes by \ref{lem:inflation restriction naturality}.

nodes.name: Top row exact by induction
nodes.statement: The first row is exact by the inductive hypothesis.

nodes.name: Bottom row exact
nodes.statement: Therefore the second row is also exact.

nodes.name: Induction on n
nodes.statement: We'll prove the result by induction on $n$.

nodes.name: Base case: relative norm of an invariant
nodes.statement: In the case $n = 0$, this follows from the relation for all $m \in M^G$: \[ N_{G/S} (m) = [G:S] \cdot m, \] The identity above holds because each term in the sum defining $N_{G/S}(m)$ is equal to $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: relative norm of an invariant

nodes.name: Inductive step: diagram with surjective dimension shifts
nodes.statement: Let's assume that the lemma is true for some $n$. We then have a diagram in which the vertical maps are the dimension shifting maps, which are all surjective: \[ \begin{matrix} H^{n}(G,\up\ M) & \stackrel{\rest}\to & H^{n}(S,\up\ M) & \stackrel{\cor}\to & H^{n}(G,\up\ M)\\ \downarrow &&\downarrow &&\downarrow \\ H^{n+1}(G, M) & \stackrel{\rest}\to & H^{n+1}(S,M) & \stackrel{\cor}\to & H^{n+1}(G,M) \end{matrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: diagram with surjective dimension shifts

nodes.name: Top row is multiplication by the index
nodes.statement: By the inductive hypothesis, the composition of the maps on the top row is multiplication by $[G:S]$.
nodes.statement_short: Top row is multiplication by the index

nodes.name: Both squares commute
nodes.statement: The square on the left commutes by \ref{lem:inflation restriction naturality}, and the square on the right commutes by definition of the corestriction map.

nodes.name: Bottom row is multiplication by the index
nodes.statement: Therefore the composition on the bottom row is multiplication by $[G:S]$.
nodes.statement_short: Bottom row is multiplication by the index

nodes.name: Reduce to n>0
nodes.statement: By dimension-shifting (\ref{cor:Tate up down isos}) it's enough to prove the result for $n > 0$, in which case by \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology} Tate cohomology is isomorphic to cohomology.

nodes.name: Take S trivial and use cor after rest
nodes.statement: Take $S$ to be the trivial subgroup $1$ of $G$. By \ref{lem:cor comp rest} it's sufficient to prove that $\cor(\rest(\sigma))= 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take S trivial and use cor after rest

nodes.name: Restriction to the trivial group vanishes
nodes.statement: This follows because $\rest(\sigma) \in H^n(1,M) \cong 0$ by \ref{lem:Hn unit}.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction to the trivial group vanishes

nodes.name: Reduce to n>0
nodes.statement: By dimension-shifting it's enough to prove the result for $n > 0$, in which case Tate cohomology is isomorphic to cohomology.

nodes.name: cor after rest is injective on the p-part
nodes.statement: It follows from \ref{lem:cor comp rest} that the composition $\cor \circ \rest$ is injective on $H^n(G,M)[p^\infty]$.
nodes.statement_short: cor after rest is injective on the p-part

nodes.name: Restriction is injective
nodes.statement: Therefore the restriction map is an injective map from $H^n(G,M)[p^\infty]$ to $H^n(S_p,M)$.

nodes.name: Image is in the kernel; conversely decompose a sum-zero h
nodes.statement: It's clear that the values of $\map_2(f)$ sum to $0$, so the image of $\map_2$ is contained in the kernel. Conversely suppose $h : G \to_0 M$ satisfies $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} h(\gen^i) = 0$. Then we have \begin{align*} h & = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \single(\gen^i, h(\gen^i))\\ & = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} (\single(\gen^i, h(\gen^i)) - \single(1, h(\gen^i))). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Image is in the kernel; conversely decompose a sum-zero h

nodes.name: Each difference is in the image of map_2
nodes.statement: Furthermore each of the terms $\single(\gen^i, m) - \single(1, m)$ is in the image of $\map_2$: \begin{align*} \map_2 (\single(1,m) + \cdots + \single(\gen^{i-1},m)) &=\single(1,m) - \single(\gen^i,m). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Each difference is in the image of map_2

nodes.name: H^1 is Hom(G,Z)=0
nodes.statement: Since the module $\Z$ is trivial, we have $H^1(G,\Z)\cong \Hom(G,\Z) \cong 0$. It follows from \ref{lem:Tate cohomology is cohomology or homology} that $H^0_{\Tate}(G,\Z) \cong \Z /n\Z$.

nodes.name: Periodicity gives H^2
nodes.statement: Hence by periodicity there is an isomorphism $H^2(G,\Z) \cong \Z/ n\Z$.

nodes.name: inv is a homomorphism and sigma_G is a cocycle
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that the formula for $\inv_\Z$ defines a homomorphism $H^2(G,\Z) \to \Z / n \Z$ (i.e. the coboundaries are in the kernel). $\sigma_G$ is a 2-cocycle since one can write $\sigma_G(\gen^i, \gen^j)$ as $\tilde i + \tilde j - (\widetilde{i + j})$ for $\tilde\cdot : \Z/n\Z \to \Z$ a section.
nodes.statement_short: inv is a homomorphism and sigma_G is a cocycle

nodes.name: Compute inv(sigma_G)=1
nodes.statement: It follows from the definitions that all the terms in the sum defining the local invariant are zero apart from the term $i=n-1$, so we have \[ \inv_G(\sigma_G) = \sigma_G(\gen^{n-1}, \gen)) = 1. \]

nodes.name: Surjectivity
nodes.statement: It follows that $\inv_G : H^2(G,\Z) \to \Z/n\Z$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Counting gives an isomorphism
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}, $|H^2(G,\Z)| = |\Z/n\Z|$, therefore $\inv_G$ is in fact an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Recall H^0_Tate = M^G / N_G M
nodes.statement: Let $\gen$ be a generator of $G$. Recall that $H^0_{\Tate}(G,M) \cong M^G / N_GM$.

nodes.name: M^G = ker(1-g)
nodes.statement: Also, we can write $M^G$ as $\ker(1-\gen : M \to M)$. Similarly $H^{-1}_{\Tate}(G,M)$ is isomorphic to $\ker (N_G : M \to M) / \image (1-\gen : M \to M)$.

nodes.name: Counting kernels and images
nodes.statement: The result follows because \begin{align*} |\ker(N_G : M \to M)| \cdot |\image(N_G : M \to M)| &=|M|\\ &=|\ker(1-g : M \to M)| \cdot |\image(1-g : M \to M)|. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Finiteness passes to the third term
nodes.statement: It follows from the long exact sequence that if two of the representations $A,B,C$ have finite cohomology groups then so does the third.
nodes.statement_short: Finiteness passes to the third term

nodes.name: Long exact sequence becomes an exact hexagon
nodes.statement: Also, by periodicity (\ref{cor:periodic cohomology}), the long exact sequence reduces to an exact hexagon: \[ \begin{matrix} && H^0_{\Tate}(G,B) \\ &\nearrow && \searrow \\ H^0_{\Tate}(G,A) && && H^0_{\Tate}(G,C) \\ \uparrow & & & & \downarrow \\ H^1_{\Tate}(G,C) &&&& H^1_{\Tate}(G,A) \\ & \nwarrow && \swarrow\\ && H^1_{\Tate}(G,B) \end{matrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Long exact sequence becomes an exact hexagon

nodes.name: Alternating product of orders is 1
nodes.statement: The result follows because the alternating product of the finite group orders in the hexagon is $1$.

nodes.name: Induction on S
nodes.statement: We must prove that $H^{n}(S,M) = 0$ for all $S$ and all $n > 0$. We'll prove this by induction on $S$. The result is true for the trivial subgroup of $G$.

nodes.name: Inductive step: S'/S cyclic
nodes.statement: Assume that the result is true for $S$, and assume that $S' / S$ is cyclic.

nodes.name: Inflation-restriction is exact
nodes.statement: The inductive hypothesis implies that (for all $n$) the inflation restriction sequence is exact: \[ 0 \to H^{n} (S'/S, M^S) \to H^{n}(S' , M) \to H^{n}(S,M)= 0. \]

nodes.name: H^e and H^o of S'/S vanish
nodes.statement: We therefore have isomorphisms $H^{n} (S'/S, M^S) \cong H^{n}(S' , M)$. In particular we have $H^{e} (S'/S, M^S) \cong 0$ and $H^{o} (S'/S, M^S) \cong 0$.
nodes.statement_short: H^e and H^o of S'/S vanish

nodes.name: Periodicity gives vanishing in all degrees
nodes.statement: Using periodicity of the cohomology of a cyclic group, we have $H^{n}(S'/S,M^S) \cong 0$ for all $n>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Periodicity gives vanishing in all degrees

nodes.name: Fix S, a prime p and a Sylow S_p
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a subgroup of $G$. Fix a prime number $p$ and let $S_p$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix S, a prime p and a Sylow S_p

nodes.name: Solvable criterion for S_p
nodes.statement: Since $S_p$ is solvable, \ref{thm:triviality criterion solvable} implies that $H^n(S_p,M) \cong 0$ for all $n > 0$.

nodes.name: p-primary part of H^n(S,M) vanishes
nodes.statement: By \ref{cor:cohomology sub Sylow}, it follows that $H^n(S,M)[p^\infty] \cong 0$.

nodes.name: All p-parts vanish and H^n is torsion
nodes.statement: Since this holds for all primes $p$, \ref{cor:cohomology G-torsion} implies that $H^n(S,M) \cong 0$.
nodes.statement_short: All p-parts vanish and H^n is torsion

nodes.name: Dimension shift H^1, H^2 of up(M)
nodes.statement: For each subgroup $S$ of $G$ we have \[ H^1(S,\up(M)) \cong H^2(S,M) \cong 0, \qquad H^2(S,\up(M)) \cong H^3(S,M) \cong 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Dimension shift H^1, H^2 of up(M)

nodes.name: Criterion for up(M)
nodes.statement: By \ref{thm:triviality criterion} $\up(M)$ has trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Same for down(M)
nodes.statement: Similarly \[ H^2(S,\down(M)) \cong H^1(S,M) \cong 0, \qquad H^3(S,\down(M)) \cong H^2(S,M) \cong 0, \] so $\down(M)$ has trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Choose m with m+n>0; down^m(M) has trivial cohomology
nodes.statement: Fix an integer $n$ and choose a natural number $m$ such that $m + n > 0$. By \ref{cor:up and down trivial cohomology}, $\down^m(M)$ has trivial cohomology.
nodes.statement_short: Choose m with m+n>0; down^m(M) has trivial cohomology

nodes.name: Dimension shift to conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore \[ H^n_{\Tate}(H,M) \cong H^{n+m}(H, \down^m(M)) \cong 0. \]

nodes.name: Define the cochain tau
nodes.statement: We can check that the cocycle $\sigma'$ is the coboundary of the $1$-cochain $\tau : G \to \Split(\sigma)$ defined by \[ \tau (x) = (x \bullet σ'(1,1), [x]-[1]). \] (Here we are using the notation $[x]$ to mean the function with value $1$ at $x$ and $0$ elsewhere).

nodes.name: Compute d tau
nodes.statement: By definition we have \begin{align*} d\tau (x,y) &= \tau(x) + x \bullet \tau(y) - \tau(xy) \\ &= (x \bullet σ'(1,1), [x]-[1]) + x \bullet (y \bullet σ'(1,1), [y]-[1]) -(xy \bullet σ'(1,1), [xy]-[1])\\ &= (x \bullet σ'(1,1), [x]-[1]) + (xy \bullet σ'(1,1) + \sigma'(x,y) -\sigma'(x,1), [xy]-[x]) - (xy \bullet σ'(1,1), [xy]-[1])\\ &= (x \bullet \sigma'(1,1) + \sigma'(x,y) -\sigma'(x,1) , 0). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Remains sigma'(x,1) = x.sigma'(1,1)
nodes.statement: It remains to prove that $\sigma'(x,1) = x \bullet \sigma'(1,1)$.

nodes.name: Cocycle relation with y=z=1
nodes.statement: This follows from the $2$-cocycle relation \ref{def:2-cocycle relation} in the case $y=z=1$.

nodes.name: WLOG I=0
nodes.statement: (This lemma is already in Mathlib.) Without loss of generality $I=0$, since such a map is also $R/I$-linear.

nodes.name: f(1) is a unit
nodes.statement: Let $c\in R$ be a preimage of $1$ and let $d = f(1)$. We have $cd = cf(1) = f(c) = 1$.

nodes.name: Multiplication by c is the inverse
nodes.statement: The map $f$ is given by $f(x) = dx$ and the map $x \mapsto cx$ is an inverse.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication by c is the inverse

nodes.name: Restriction and corestriction maps
nodes.statement: The restriction and corestriction maps are $R$-linear maps \[ H^2(G,M) \stackrel{\rest}\to H^2(S,M) \stackrel{\cor}\to H^2(G,M). \]

nodes.name: Goal: restriction surjective
nodes.statement: We need to prove that the restriction map is surjective.

nodes.name: Identify the groups with R/|G| and R/|S|
nodes.statement: By the conditions on $M$, we can think of these maps as \[ R / |G| \to R / |S| \to R / |G|. \]
nodes.statement_short: Identify the groups with R/|G| and R/|S|

nodes.name: Image of cor lies in the S-torsion
nodes.statement: Since $R$ has no additive torsion, the image of $R/|S|$ in $R/|G|$ is contained in the $S$-torsion, which is $[G:S] R / |G|$.
nodes.statement_short: Image of cor lies in the S-torsion

nodes.name: Image of cor contains [G:S]R/|G|
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since the composition is $[G:S]$, it follows that the image of $\cor$ contains $[G:S] R / |G|$.

nodes.name: cor is a surjection R/|S| -> R/|S|
nodes.statement: Therefore the image of $\cor$ is precisely $[G:S] R / |G|$, which is isomorphic to $R/|S|$. Hence $\cor$ may be regarded as a surjective linear map $R/|S| \to R/|S|$.
nodes.statement_short: cor is a surjection R/|S| -> R/|S|

nodes.name: cor is injective
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:linear injective of surjective}, $\cor$ is injective with image $[G:S] H^2(G,M)$.

nodes.name: Write cor(b) = [G:S]c
nodes.statement: Now let $b \in H^2(S,M)$. We have $\cor(b) = [G:S]c$ for some $c \in H^2(G,M)$.

nodes.name: Injectivity gives b = rest(c)
nodes.statement: This implies $\cor(b) = \cor (\rest( c))$, and since $\cor$ is injective we have $b = \rest(c)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to H^1 and H^2 on subgroups
nodes.statement: By \ref{thm:triviality criterion}, it's enough to prove for every subgroup $S$ of $G$ that $H^1(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$ and $H^2(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to H^1 and H^2 on subgroups

nodes.name: Long exact sequence
nodes.statement: We have a long exact sequence with the following terms: \[ 0 \to H^1(S,\Split(\sigma')) \to H^1(S,\aug(R,G)) \to H^2(S,M) \to H^2(S,\Split(\sigma')) \to 0. \]

nodes.name: Map H^2(S,M) -> H^2(S,Split) is zero
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:restriction fundamental class generates} and \ref{lem:splits in splitting module}, the map $H^2(S,M) \to H^2(S,\Split(\sigma'))$ is zero.

nodes.name: H^2 vanishes
nodes.statement: Hence $H^2(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$.

nodes.name: Map H^1(S,aug) -> H^2(S,M) is surjective between R/|S|R
nodes.statement: The $R$-modules $H^1(S,\aug(R,G))$ and $H^2(S,M)$ are both isomorphic to $R / |S|R$, and the map from one to the other is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: Map H^1(S,aug) -> H^2(S,M) is surjective between R/|S|R

nodes.name: and hence injective
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:linear injective of surjective}, the map from $H^1(S,\aug(R,G))$ to $H^2(S,M)$ is also injective.

nodes.name: H^1 vanishes
nodes.statement: Therefore $H^1(S,\Split(\sigma')) \cong 0$.

nodes.name: Diagram of Tate complexes with norm maps
nodes.statement: We have a diagram with exact rows. Note that $C^0(G,M)$ and $C^{-1}(G,M)$ are both $M$ and the vertical maps are Tate coboundary maps, which are all $N_G$. \[ \begin{matrix} 0 \to & C^{-1}(G,M) & \to & C^{-1}(G,\Split(\sigma')) & \to & C^{-1}(G,\aug(R,G)) & \to 0 \\ &\downarrow &&\downarrow &&\downarrow \\ 0 \to & C^{0}(G,M) & \to & C^{0}(G,\Split(\sigma')) & \to & C^{0}(G,\aug(R,G)) & \to 0 \end{matrix} \]
nodes.statement_short: Diagram of Tate complexes with norm maps

nodes.name: g tensor 1 maps to [g]-[1]
nodes.statement: Choose an element $g \in G$. By \ref{lem:Tate -1 aug}, the element $gG' \otimes 1 \in G^{\ab} \otimes R$ maps to the cocycle $[g]-[1] \in C^{-1}(G,\aug(\Z,G))$. An obvious pre-image of this element in $C^{-1}(G,\Split(\sigma))$ is the element $(0,[g]-[1])$.

nodes.name: Apply the norm
nodes.statement: The image of $(0,[g]-[1])$ in $C^{0}(G,\Split(\sigma))$ is \[ N_G(0,[g]-[1]) = \left(\sum_{x \in G} (\sigma'(x,g) - \sigma'(x,1)), 0\right). \]

nodes.name: sigma'(x,1) = x.sigma'(1,1)
nodes.statement: By the cocycle relation we have $\sigma'(x,1) = x \bullet \sigma'(1,1)$ for all $x\in G$.

nodes.name: Formula for the reciprocity map
nodes.statement: Hence the reciprocity map is given by \[ \reciprocity(gG' \otimes 1) \cong \sum_{x \in G} \sigma'(x,g) - N_G \sigma'(1,1) \cong \sum_{x \in G} \sigma'(x,g) \in M^G / N_G M. \]

nodes.name: Change the cocycle by a coboundary
nodes.statement: If we modify $\sigma'$ by a coboundary $d\tau$: \[ \sigma''(x,y) = \sigma'(x,y) + x \bullet \tau(y) - \tau(xy) + \tau(x), \] then we will add the following term to $\reciprocity(g)$: \[ \sum_{x \in G} (x \bullet \tau(g) - \tau(xg) + \tau(x)). \]
nodes.statement_short: Change the cocycle by a coboundary

nodes.name: Change is a norm, zero in H^0_Tate
nodes.statement: The second and third terms cancel each other out after reindexing, so we are left with $N_G(\tau(g))$, which is zero in $H^0_{\Tate}(G,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Change is a norm, zero in H^0_Tate

nodes.name: Class formation property is immediate
nodes.statement: The fact that $(R, S, M \downarrow S)$ is a finite class formation is a tautology.

nodes.name: Restriction is a fundamental class
nodes.statement: The fact that $\sigma_S$ is a fundamental class is \ref{lem:restriction fundamental class generates}.

nodes.name: Remains: commutativity
nodes.statement: It remains to prove that the diagram commutes.

nodes.name: Cocycle formula for theta_G
nodes.statement: We'll write $\theta_G$ and $\theta_S$ for the horizontal maps in the diagram. For an element $s \in S$ we have by \ref{lem:reciprocity formula}: \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{x \in G} \sigma_G(x,s). \]

nodes.name: Split the sum over cosets
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a set of representatives for the cosets $rS$ of $S$ in $G$. Then we have \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{r \in R} \sum_{x \in S} \sigma_G(rx,s). \]

nodes.name: Apply the cocycle relation
nodes.statement: Using the cocycle relation we have \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{r \in R} \sum_{x \in S} \left(\sigma_G(r,xs) + r \bullet \sigma_G(x,s) - \sigma_G(r,x)\right). \]

nodes.name: Cancel after reindexing
nodes.statement: The first and last terms cancel after reindexing, and we are left with \[ \theta_G(sG') = \sum_{r \in R} r \bullet \left(\sum_{x \in S} \sigma_S(x,s)\right). \]

nodes.name: Identify with N_{G/S} theta_S
nodes.statement: The right hand side is $N_{G/S} \theta_S(s)$ by \ref{lem:reciprocity formula}.

nodes.name: Outline of the steps
nodes.statement: The proof that $l^\times$ is a class formation is achieved in the following steps:

nodes.name: Hilbert 90 gives H^1 = 0
nodes.statement: It is already proven in Mathlib that $H^1(l/k,l^\times) \cong 0$; this result is known as Hilbert's theorem 90. It remains to check that each $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ is cyclic of order $[l:k]$, and to choose a generator.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotients and inflation-restriction bound |H^2|
nodes.statement: In the case that $\Gal(l/k)$ is cyclic, we can show that $|H^2(l/k,l^\times)| = [l:k]$ by Herbrand quotients. By inflation-restriction, this implies $|H^2(l/k,l^\times)| \le [l:k]$ for all Galois extensions. Hence to prove that $l^\times$ is a class formation it's sufficient to find an element in $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ of order $[l:k]$; such an element is a fundamental class.

nodes.name: Unramified case: explicit fundamental class
nodes.statement: Suppose $l/k$ is unramified. In this case we have a decomposition: \[ l ^\times \cong \cO_l^\times \oplus \Z. \] The subrepresentation $\cO_l^\times$ has trivial cohomology in this unramified case. Therefore for any intermediate field $l/m/k$ we have $H^\bullet(l/m,l^\times) \cong H^\bullet(l/m,\Z)$. Since $\Z$ is a finite class formation over a cyclic group, it follows that $l^\times$ is a finite class formation. The cocycle $\sigma_1$ defined in \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z} is a fundamental class, where we use the Frobenius element as a generator.

nodes.name: General case: inflate from l l'
nodes.statement: Suppose $l/k$ is a Galois extension which is not necessarily unramified. To define the fundamental class in this case, we let $l'/k$ be the unramified extension with the same degree as $l/k$. We have already constructed the fundamental class $\sigma_1 \in H^2(l'/k, l'^\times)$. We let $\sigma_2$ be the inflation of $\sigma_1$ to $H^2(ll'/k, (ll')^\times)$. The extension $ll' / l$ is unramified, so we already have an explicit isomorphism $H^2(ll'/l, (ll')^\times) \cong \Z / [ll':l]$. Using this isomorphism, we can show that the restriction of $\sigma_2$ to $H^2(ll'/l, (ll')^\times)$ is zero. Hence by inflation-restriction there exists a unique $\sigma \in H^2(l/k, l^\times)$ whose inflation is $\sigma_2$. It is then easy to check that $\sigma$ is a fundamental class in $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$.
nodes.statement_short: General case: inflate from l l'

nodes.name: Normal basis theorem
nodes.statement: Recall from Galois theory that there is a normal basis for $l$ over $k$, i.e. a basis of the form \[ \{x \bullet b_0 : x \in \Gal(l/k)\}. \]

nodes.name: Define Phi
nodes.statement: Define a map $\ind_1(k) \cong l$ by \[ \Phi (f : G \to_0 k) = \sum_{x \in \Gal(l/k)} f(x) \cdot x^{-1} \bullet b_0. \]

nodes.name: Phi is a Galois-equivariant bijection
nodes.statement: The map $\Phi$ is clearly a linear bijection; we check that it commutes with the Galois action: \[ \Phi(g\bullet f) = \sum_x f(xg) \cdot x^{-1} \bullet b_0 = \sum_x f(x) \cdot (xg^{-1})^{-1} \bullet b_0 = g \bullet \Phi(f). \]

nodes.name: First approximation step
nodes.statement: Let $f_0$ be a $q+1$-cocycle with values in $M=M_0$. Since $H^{q+1}(G,M/M_1)=0$ we can find a $q$-cochain $\psi_0$ of $G$ with values in $M$ such that $f_0=\delta\psi_0+f_1$ where now $f_1$ is a $q+1$-cocycle in $M_1$.

nodes.name: Recursive construction of psi_n
nodes.statement: In general given the $q+1$-cocycle $f_n$ with values in $M_n$ we recursively define a $q$-chain $\psi_n$ with values in $M_n$ such that $f_n=\delta\psi_n+f_{n+1}$ with $f_{n+1}$ a $q+1$-cocycle taking values in $M_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Sum converges in the inverse limit
nodes.statement: Now set $\psi:=\psi_0+\psi_1+\cdots$, which converges by our hypothesis $M=\varprojlim(M/M_i)$. More precisely, $\psi$ can be thought of as an element of the projective limit of $C^q(M/M_i)$, which equals $C^q(M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum converges in the inverse limit

nodes.name: f_0 is the coboundary of psi
nodes.statement: In particular $\psi$ defines a $q$-cochain of $G$ with values in $M$; an elementary calculation now shows $f_0=\delta\psi$ and thus $f_0$ is a coboundary.
nodes.statement_short: f_0 is the coboundary of psi

nodes.name: Choose a normal basis element in O_l
nodes.statement: We know that $l\cong k[G]$ by the normal basis theorem so we may choose $\alpha\in L$ such that $\{g\alpha:g\in G\}$ forms a $k$-basis for $l$. If $\pi_k$ denotes a uniformiser of $k$ then by multiplying $\alpha$ by an appropriate power of $\pi_k$ we may assume $\alpha\in\cO_l$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a normal basis element in O_l

nodes.name: Lattice A and N with pi^N O_l in A
nodes.statement: Set $A=\oplus_{g\in G}\cO_k g\alpha\subseteq\cO_l$. This is an open additive subgroup of $l$ so there exists some natural $N$ such that $\pi_k^N\cO_l\subseteq A$.
nodes.statement_short: Lattice A and N with pi^N O_l in A

nodes.name: Define B and M = 1+B
nodes.statement: Set $B=\pi_k^{N+1}A\subseteq\pi_k\cO_l$ and set $M=1+B\subseteq \cO_l^\times$. We claim that this $M$ works. It is clearly open and $G$-stable, so what remains is $H^{q+1}(l/k,M)=0$ for all naturals $q$.

nodes.name: B.B in pi B
nodes.statement: First observe that $B\cdot B\subseteq \pi_kB$, as $B\cdot B\subseteq\pi_k^{2N+2}A\cdot A \subseteq \pi_k^{2N+2}\cO_l\subseteq \pi_k^{N+2}A=\pi_kB.$

nodes.name: Filtration M_i; apply approximation lemma
nodes.statement: Now define subgroups $M_i=1+\pi_k^iB$; we claim that lemma~\ref{lem:serre_approx} applies for all $q$.

nodes.name: Need graded pieces cohomologically trivial
nodes.statement: To check this, we need to show that $H^{q+1}(G,M_i/M_{i+1})=0$ for all $i$.

nodes.name: Graded pieces are induced
nodes.statement: But it is not difficult to check that the map $M_i\to B$ sending $1+\pi_k^ib$ to $b$ induces a $G$-equivariant isomorphism $M_i/M_{i+1}=B/\pi_kB$ (the case $i=0$ needs $B\cdot B\subseteq \pi_kB$), and the latter has trivial cohomology because it is isomorphic to $(\cO_k/\pi_k)[G]$ and thus induced.

nodes.name: Finite index open subgroup has the same Herbrand quotient
nodes.statement: Choose a subgroup $M\subseteq \cO_l^\times$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:serre_cor}. Since $\cO_l^\times / M$ is finite (because $M$ is open and $\cO_l^\times$ is compact) we have (using lemmas~\ref{lem:herbrand finite} and \ref{lem:herbrand ses}) \[ h(\cO_l^\times) = h(M). \]
nodes.statement_short: Finite index open subgroup has the same Herbrand quotient

nodes.name: Its Herbrand quotient is 1
nodes.statement: The right hand side is $1$ by \ref{lem:serre_cor}.

nodes.name: Valuation short exact sequence
nodes.statement: We have a short exact sequence of representations \[ 0 \to \cO_l^\times \to l^\times \to \Z \to 0, \] where the second map is the valuation.

nodes.name: Known Herbrand quotients of units and Z
nodes.statement: We've shown in \ref{lem:herbrand local units}, \ref{eg:herbrand Z} that $h(l/k,\cO^\times)=1$ and $h(l/k,\Z) = [l:k]$.
nodes.statement_short: Known Herbrand quotients of units and Z

nodes.name: Multiply
nodes.statement: Therefore $h(l/k,l^\times) = [l:k]$.

nodes.name: Reduce to the Sylow fixed field
nodes.statement: Let $p$ be prime number dividing the degree $[l:k]$ and let $k_p$ be the fixed field of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $S_p$ of $\Gal(l/k)$. By \ref{cor:cohomology G-torsion} and \ref{cor:cohomology sub Sylow} it is sufficient to prove that $|H^2(l/k_p,l^\times)| \le [l:k_p]$, which is a special case of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the Sylow fixed field

nodes.name: Reduce to solvable Galois group
nodes.statement: In the special case, the Galois group is $S_p$, which is a solvable group. It is therefore sufficient to prove the theorem in the case that $\Gal(l/k)$ is solvable. (Note that $\Gal(l/k)$ is always solvable if $l/k$ is an extension of local fields, but we do not need to prove this.)

nodes.name: Induction down cyclic steps
nodes.statement: We shall prove the theorem by induction on $k$, starting with $k=l$ and moving down in cyclic steps.

nodes.name: Base case k=l
nodes.statement: The case $k=l$ follows by \ref{lem:Hn unit}.

nodes.name: Inductive step with k/k_0 cyclic
nodes.statement: Assume the result for $l/k$ and let $k_0$ be a subfield of $k$ with $k/k_0$ cyclic.

nodes.name: Inflation-restriction in degree 2
nodes.statement: It follows from \ref{thm:hilbert 90} that we have an inflation-restriction sequence in dimension 2: \[ 0 \to H^2(k/k_0, k^\times) \to H^2( l/k_0, l^\times) \to H^2(l/k, l^\times). \]

nodes.name: Bound the outer terms
nodes.statement: The first term has order $[k : k_0]$ by \ref{lem:local H2 l*}, and the last term has order at most $[l:k]$ by the inductive hypothesis.

nodes.name: Multiply the bounds
nodes.statement: Therefore $H^2( l/k_0, l^\times)$ has order at most $[l:k] \times [k : k_0] = [l: k_0]$.

nodes.name: Additive case via normal basis
nodes.statement: In the case of $l$, this follows from \ref{thm:additive field trivial} as $\Gal(l/k)$ may be identified with $\Gal(\F_l / \F_k)$, so we focus on the representation $l^\times$.

nodes.name: Reduce to fixed fields m
nodes.statement: Given any subgroup $S$ of the Galois group we must prove that $H^\bullet_{\Tate}(l/m,l^\times) \cong 0$, where $m$ is the fixed field of $S$.

nodes.name: l/m is cyclic
nodes.statement: Note that $l/m$ is also unramified, so has cyclic Galois group.

nodes.name: Periodicity: only H^1, H^2
nodes.statement: By \ref{cor:periodic cohomology}, it's sufficient to prove that $H^1(l/m,l^\times)$ and $H^2(l/m,l^\times)$ are trivial.

nodes.name: Herbrand quotient 1 reduces to H^1
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:herbrand finite} the representation $\F_l^\times$ has Herbrand quotient $1$, so it's enough to prove that $H^1$ is trivial.

nodes.name: Hilbert 90
nodes.statement: This follows from \ref{thm:hilbert 90}.

nodes.name: Normal basis of the residue field
nodes.statement: By \ref{thm:additive field trivial} we may choose $x_0 \in \F_l$ such that $\{g \bullet x_0 :g \in \Gal(l/k)\}$ is a normal basis.
nodes.statement_short: Normal basis of the residue field

nodes.name: Lift and apply Nakayama
nodes.statement: Let $y \in \cO_l$ be a lift of $x_0$. It follows from Nakayama's lemma that $\{g \bullet y\}$ is a normal basis in $\cO_l$.

nodes.name: Conclude O_l is induced
nodes.statement: As in earlier proofs, this implies the isomorphism $\cO_l \cong \ind_1 \cO_k$.

nodes.name: Reduce to the whole Galois group
nodes.statement: Because replacing $Gal(l/k)$ with a subgroup is the same as replacing $k$ with an extension, it suffices to prove that $H^{q+1}(l/k,\cO_l^\times)=0$ for all local fields $k$, unramified extensions $l$ and naturals $q$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the whole Galois group

nodes.name: Filtration by higher unit groups
nodes.statement: Filter $\cO_l^\times$ as $\cO_l^\times\supset 1+\pi_k\cO_l\supset 1+\pi_k^2\cO_l\supset\cdots$.

nodes.name: Approximation lemma reduces to subquotients
nodes.statement: By lemma~\ref{lem:serre_approx} it suffices to prove that all the subquotients have trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Subquotients are F_l^x and F_l
nodes.statement: However the first subquotient is $\F_l^\times$ and all the others are $\F_l$, so it suffices to prove that $H^q(G,\F_l^\times)\cong H^q(G,\F_l)\cong 0$ for all $q\geq1$.

nodes.name: Residue modules are trivial
nodes.statement: But these follow from lemma~\ref{lem:finite field trivial}.

nodes.name: Choose pi_k = pi_l
nodes.statement: Up to cohomology, $\sigma_{l/k}$ does not depend on the choice of uniformizer, so we may assume $\pi_k=\pi_l$ in our definitions of $\sigma_{m/k}$ and $\sigma_{m/l}$.

nodes.name: F_l = F_k^f
nodes.statement: We have $F_l = F_k^f$ where $f = [l:k]$.

nodes.name: Compare cocycles
nodes.statement: Hence \begin{align*} \sigma_{m/k}(F_l^r, F_l^s) &= \sigma_{m/k}(F_k^{fr}, F_k^{fs})\\ &= \begin{cases} 1 & fr + rs < [m:k] \\ \pi_k & fr + fs \ge [m:k] \end{cases}\\ &= \begin{cases} 1 & r + s < [m:l] \\ \pi_k & r + s \ge [m:l] \end{cases}\\ &=\sigma_{m/l}(F_l^r,F_l^s). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Frobenius elements in the tower
nodes.statement: We shall write $F_{m/k}$ and $F_{l/k}$ for the Frobenius elements in $\Gal(m/k)$ and $\Gal(l/k)$ respectively. Note that $F_{l/k}$ is the restriction of $F_{m/k}$ to $l$, so is the coset of $F_{m/k}$ when we regard $\Gal(l/k)$ as a quotient of $\Gal(m/k)$.

nodes.name: Formula for inv of an inflated class
nodes.statement: From the definition we have (for any $\sigma \in H^2(l/k,l^\times)$): \[ \inv_{m/k}(\infl(\sigma)) = \frac{1}{[m:k]}\sum_{i=0}^{[m:k]-1} v_k(\sigma(F_{l/k}^i,F_{l/k})). \]
nodes.statement_short: Formula for inv of an inflated class

nodes.name: Periodicity and tower law
nodes.statement: The terms in the sum are periodic since $F_{l/k}^{[l:k]}=1$. This implies (by the tower law): \[ \inv_{m/k}(\infl(\sigma)) = \frac{1}{[m:k]} [m:l]\sum_{i=0}^{[l:k]-1} v_k(\sigma(F_{l/k}^i,F_{l/k})). \]

nodes.name: Equals inv_{l/k}
nodes.statement: The right hand side is equal to $\inv_{l/k}(\sigma)$.

nodes.name: Compare local invariants of fundamental classes
nodes.statement: The formula $\infl(\sigma_{l/k}) = [m:l]\cdot \sigma_{m/k}$ follows since both sides of the equation have local invariant equal to $\frac{1}{[l:k]}$ (by \ref{lem:local inv fundamental class}).
nodes.statement_short: Compare local invariants of fundamental classes

nodes.name: psi has order [l:k]
nodes.statement: By \ref{thm:hilbert 90} the inflation map is injective, so $\psi$ has order exactly $[l':k] = [l:k]$.

nodes.name: Inflation-restriction sequence
nodes.statement: We also have an inflation restriction sequence \[ 0 \to H^2(l/k, l^\times) \to H^2(m/k , m^\times) \to H^2(m/l, m^\times) \]

nodes.name: Compute the restriction via inv_{m/l}
nodes.statement: We'll calculate the restriction of $\psi$ to $H^2(m/l, m^\times)$. Since $m/l$ is unramified, we have an isomorphism \[ \inv_{m/l} : H^2(m/l, m^\times) \cong \frac{1}{e}\Z/ \Z. \]

nodes.name: Compute inv_{m/l}(psi) = 1 = 0 mod Z
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align*} \inv_{m/l}(\psi) &=\frac{1}{e} \sum_{i=0}^{e-1} v_l (\psi (F_l^i,F_l))\\ &=\frac{1}{e} \sum_{i=0}^{e-1} v_l (\sigma_{l'/k}((F_l|l')^i,F_l|l'))\\ &=\frac{1}{e} \sum_{i=0}^{e-1} v_l (\sigma_{l'/k}(F_k^{if},F_k^f))\\ &=\frac{1}{e} v_l (\pi_k) = 1 \equiv 0 \bmod \Z. \end{align*} The first line above is the definition of $\inv_{m/l}$. The second line is the definition of inflation of cocycles.

nodes.name: Restriction of psi is 0
nodes.statement: The calculation above shows that the image of $\psi$ in $H^2(m/l, m^\times)$ is $0$.

nodes.name: H^1 vanishes
nodes.statement: From \ref{thm:hilbert 90} we know that $H^1(l/k,l^\times) \cong 0$.

nodes.name: |H^2| <= [l:k]
nodes.statement: From \ref{lem:local H2 upper bound}, we know that $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ has no more than $[l:k]$ elements.

nodes.name: Element of order [l:k] generates
nodes.statement: We have constructed an element $\sigma_{l/k}\in H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ of order $[l:k]$, so $H^2(l/k,l^\times)$ is cyclic of order $[l:k]$ and is generated by $\sigma_{l/k}$.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion; assume x is a norm from both
nodes.statement: Clearly if $x \in N_{l/k}(l^\times)$ then $x$ is a norm from both $m_1$ and $m_2$. Suppose conversely that $x$ is a norm from both $m_1$ and $m_2$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Easy inclusion; assume x is a norm from both

nodes.name: x lies in the image of each S_i
nodes.statement: Let $S_i=\Gal(l/m_i)$ for $i=1,2$. By the commutative diagram in \ref{lem:subgroup compatibility}, the coset $xN(l^\times)$ is in the image of each $S_i$ under the reciprocity map.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: x lies in the image of each S_i

nodes.name: x lies in the image of S_1 cap S_2
nodes.statement: Since the reciprocity map is bijective, $xN(l^\times)$ is in the image of $S_1 \cap S_2$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: x lies in the image of S_1 cap S_2

nodes.name: S_1 cap S_2 = 1
nodes.statement: The condition $l = m_1 m_2$ implies $S_1 \cap S_2 = 1$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Therefore $x \in N(l^\times)$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Every unit is a norm
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:unramified units trivial} we have $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\cO_l^\times) \cong 0$, which implies that every element of $\cO_k^\times$ is a norm.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: pi_k^f is a norm
nodes.statement: The element $\pi_k^f$ is the norm of $\pi_k$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Inclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore $\pi_k^{f\Z} \times \cO_k^\times \subseteq N(l^\times)$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Equal indices via reciprocity
nodes.statement: To prove equality, we note that these subgroups of $k^\times$ have the same index. Indeed by \ref{lem:unramified fundamental class}, $k^\times / N(l^\times)$ is isomorphic to $\Gal(l/k)^\ab$, which has order $f$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Image of I is a quotient of norm groups
nodes.statement: Let $m$ be the fixed field of $I$. By \ref{lem:subgroup compatibility} the image of $I$ in $k^\times / N(l^\times)$ is $N_{m/k}(m^\times) / N_{l/k}(l^\times)$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Image of I is a quotient of norm groups

nodes.name: Norm group of the unramified part
nodes.statement: Since $m/k$ is unramified, \ref{lem:local unramified norms} implies \[ N_{m/k}(m^\times) = \cO_k^\times \times \pi_k^{f\Z}, \] where $f$ is the inertial degree of $l/k$.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism
nodes.statement_short: Norm group of the unramified part

nodes.name: Rewrite with N(pi_l)
nodes.statement: If $\pi_l$ is a uniformizer in $l$ then $N(\pi_l)$ is a unit multiple of $\pi_k^f$. This implies \[ N_{m/k}(m^\times) = \cO_k^\times \times N(\pi_l^{\Z}). \]
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The result follows from this.
nodes.section: 3.6 Some consequences of the reciprocity isomorphism

nodes.name: Choose n large
nodes.statement: Choose $n$ large enough so that $\exp(x)$ converges for all $x \in P^n$, and such that all the terms $x^r/r!$ are in $P^n$ for $r \ge 1$ and all the terms $x^r / r!$ with $r \ge 2$ have strictly larger valuation than that of $x$. It is already proved in Mathlib that $\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y)$, and the fact that $\exp$ commutes with the Galois action is straightforward.

nodes.name: Remains: bijectivity
nodes.statement: We'll show that the map is a bijection from $P^n$ to $1+P^n$.

nodes.name: Injectivity: assume exp(x)=1
nodes.statement: Suppose $\exp(x)=1$ with $x \in P^n$. If $x \ne 0$ then $x = \pi^mu$ for some unit $u$.

nodes.name: Leading term contradiction
nodes.statement: By assumption on $n$, $\exp(x) = 1 + \pi^m u + O(\pi^{m+1})$; this gives a contradiction. Therefore the map $\exp : P^n \to 1+P^n$ is injective.

nodes.name: Surjectivity via Hensel
nodes.statement: One can show that the map $P^n \to 1+P^n$ is surjective using Hensel's lemma as follows.

nodes.name: Approximate solution x_0 = y-1
nodes.statement: Choose $y \in 1+P^n$. Then $x_0 = y-1$ is in $P^n$ and $\exp(x) \equiv y \bmod P^{n+1}$. Furthermore $\exp'(x_0) = \exp(x_0) \not\equiv 0 \bmod P$.

nodes.name: Hensel gives a solution in P^n
nodes.statement: Hensel's lemma shows that there exists a solution to $\exp(x)=y$ with $x \equiv x_0 \bmod P^{n+1}$. In particular $x \in P^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Hensel gives a solution in P^n

nodes.name: Degree is phi(p^n)
nodes.statement: By Eisenstein's criterion, the cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{p^n}(X) = \frac{X^{p^n}-1}{X^{p^{n-1}}-1}$ is irreducible over $\Q_p$. Hence the degree of the extension is $\phi(p^n)=p^n - p^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Index of the candidate norm group
nodes.statement: This coincides with the index: \begin{align*} [\Q_p^\times : p^\Z \times (1+p^n \Z_p)] &= [\Z_p^\times : (1+p^n \Z_p)] \\ &= | (\Z / p^n \Z)^\times |. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Index of the candidate norm group

nodes.name: Reduce to showing elements are norms
nodes.statement: It it therefore sufficient to prove that every element of $p^\Z \times (1+p^n \Z_p)$ is a norm.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to showing elements are norms

nodes.name: p is a norm
nodes.statement: We have $p = N(1-\zeta)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to principal units; split into cases
nodes.statement: It is therefore sufficient to show that every $x \in 1 + p^n \Z_p$ is the norm of an element of $\Z_p[\zeta]$. We split this into cases.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to principal units; split into cases

nodes.name: p odd: use the exponential
nodes.statement: Suppose $p$ is an odd prime, so that $\exp(pz)$ converges for all $z\in \Z_p$. If $a \in 1 +p^n\Z_p^\times$ then by \ref{lem:local isomorphism} (with $l=k=\Q_p$) there is an expression of $a$ of the form \[ a = \exp(p^n y), \qquad y \in \Z_p. \] It follows that \[ a= \exp(p\frac{y}{p-1}) ^{[\Q_p(\zeta):\Q_p]} = N_{\Q_p(\zeta)/\Q_p}(\exp(py/(p-1))). \] In particular, $x\in N(\Q_p(\zeta)^\times)$.

nodes.name: p^n = 2: trivial
nodes.statement: In the case $p^n = 2$ we have $l = \Q_2$, so every element of $\Q_2$ is a norm.

nodes.name: p=2, n>=2: via Q_2(i)
nodes.statement: In the case $p=2$, $n \ge 2$, there is an intermediate field $l / \Q_2(i) / \Q_2$, and we have \[ N_{\Q_p(i) / \Q_p} (x+i y) = x^2 + y^2. \] It's easy to show (for example using Hensel's lemma) that if $a \equiv 1 \bmod 4$ then $a$ is the norm of an element of $\Q_p(i)$. If $a \in 1 + 2^n \Z_2$ then we have for some $b \in \Z_2$: \[ a = \exp(2^n b) = \exp(4b)^{[l:\Q_2(i)]}. \] The the exponential above converges to an element of $1+4\Z_2$. In particular there is an element $b \in \Q_2(i)$ such that \[ a = N_{\Q_2(i)/\Q_2} (b) ^ [l:\Q_2(i)] = N_{l/\Q_2} (b) \]

nodes.name: Norm group contains 1+p^n Z_p
nodes.statement: The subgroup $N_{l/\Q_p}(l^\times)$ is open in $\Q_p^\times$, so it must contain a subgroup of the form $1+p^n\Z_p$ for some $n$.

nodes.name: Norm group contains p^{fZ} x (1+p^n Z_p)
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be the order of $p$ in $\Q_p^\times / N(l^\times)$. \[ N(l^\times) \supset p^{f\Z} \times (1 + p^n\Z_p). \]
nodes.statement_short: Norm group contains p^{fZ} x (1+p^n Z_p)

nodes.name: Unramified norm group
nodes.statement: The subgroup $p^{f\Z} \times \Z_p^\times$ is the norm subgroups for the unramified extension of degree $f$, which is $\Q_p(\zeta_{p^f-1})$.

nodes.name: Cyclotomic norm group
nodes.statement: The group $p^\Z \times (1_p^n \Z_p)$ is the norm subgroup of $\Q_p(\zeta_{p^n})$.

nodes.name: Classification gives containment
nodes.statement: Hence $l$ is contained in $\Q_p(\zeta_{p^f-1}, \zeta_{p^n})$.

nodes.name: Ramified primes and completions
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a the set of primes which ramify in $l$. For each $p \in S$ we let $\hat p$ be a prime of $l$ above $p$. We therefore have an abelian extension $l_{\hat p} / \Q_p$.

nodes.name: Choose conductor exponents, n and m = l(zeta_n)
nodes.statement: Choose $r_p$ such that $1+p^{r_p} \Z_p \subseteq N(l_{\hat p}^\times)$. Let $n = \prod_{p \in S} p^{r_p}$. Let $m = l(\zeta_n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose conductor exponents, n and m = l(zeta_n)

nodes.name: Goal m = Q(zeta_n)
nodes.statement: We shall prove that $m = \Q(\zeta_n)$, which implies $l$ is isomorphic to a subfield of $\Q(\zeta_n)$.

nodes.name: Decomposition group via local reciprocity
nodes.statement: For a prime $p \in S$, let $D_p$ and $I_p$ be the decomposition subgroup and inertia subgroup of $\Gal(m/\Q)$ at $p$. We may identify $D_p$ with $\Gal(m_p / \Q_p)$, and we have a reciprocity isomorphism \[ D_p \cong \Q_p^\times / N(m_p^\times). \]

nodes.name: Image of inertia
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:local image inertia} The image of $I_p$ under the reciprocity map is \[ I_p \cong \Z_p^\times / N(m_p^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times. \]

nodes.name: Norm group of the compositum
nodes.statement: We have \[ N_{m_p/\Q_p} (m_p^\times) = N_{l_p/\Q_p} (l_p^\times) \cap N_{\Q_p(\zeta_n) / \Q_p} (\Q_p(\zeta_n)^\times). \]

nodes.name: Cyclotomic norm groups on units
nodes.statement: Note that by \ref{lem:local cyclotomic norms}, \ref{lem:subgroup compatibility} and \ref{lem:local image inertia}, \[ N_{\Q_p(\zeta_n) / \Q_p} (\Q_p(\zeta_n)^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times = N_{\Q_p(\zeta_{p^{r_p}}) / \Q_p} (\Q_p(\zeta_{p^{r_p}})^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times = 1+p^r \Z_p \supseteq N_{l_p/\Q_p} (l_p^\times). \]

nodes.name: Units in the norm group
nodes.statement: This implies $N_{m_p/\Q_p} (m_p^\times) \cap \Z_p^\times = 1+p^r \Z_p$.

nodes.name: Order of I_p
nodes.statement: It follows that $I_p \cong \Z_p^\times / (1+p^{r_p} \Z_p) \cong (\Z / p^{r_p})^\times$. In particular $|I_p| = \phi(p^{r_p})$, where $\phi$ is the Euler totient function.

nodes.name: Inertia generates since Q has no unramified extension
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be the subgroup generated by the $I_p$ for $p \in S$. The fixed field of $I$ is an unramified extension of $\Q$, and is therefore equal to $\Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Inertia generates since Q has no unramified extension

nodes.name: Degree bound
nodes.statement: Therefore $I = \Gal(m/\Q)$ and we have \[ [m : \Q] = |I| \le \prod |I_p| = \phi(n) = [\Q(\zeta_n) : \Q]. \]

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence $m = \Q(\zeta_n)$.

nodes.name: Idele short exact sequence
nodes.statement: We have a short exact sequence \[ 0 \to l^\times \to \A_l^\times \to \Cl_l \to 0. \]

nodes.name: Long exact sequence of invariants
nodes.statement: Taking $\Gal(l/k)$-invariants gives a long exact sequence beginning with \[ 0 \to k^\times \to \A_k^\times \to \Cl_l^{\Gal(l/k)} \to H^1(l/k, l^\times). \]

nodes.name: Hilbert 90
nodes.statement: The last term is zero by \ref{thm:hilbert 90}. This implies the result.

nodes.name: Define Phi
nodes.statement: We'll write $x$ for an element of $\prod_{w | v} l_w^\times$ and $x_w$ for it's component in $l_w$. Define a map $\Phi : \prod_{w | v} l_w^\times \to (\Gal(l/k) \to l_{\hat v}^\times)$ by \[ \Phi (x) = (g \mapsto g \bullet x_{g^{-1} \hat v}). \]

nodes.name: Phi(x) is D-equivariant
nodes.statement: Note that for $h \in D_{\hat v}$ we have \[ \Phi (x) (hg) = h \bullet (g \bullet x_{g^{-1} \hat v}) = h \bullet \Phi(x) (g). \] Therefore $\Phi(x)$ is in the subspace $\coind_{D_v} l_{\hat v}$, and it's easy to check that $\Phi$ gives a group isomorphism $\prod_{w | v} l_w^\times \cong \coind_{D_v} l_{\hat v}^\times$.

nodes.name: Check G-equivariance
nodes.statement: We'll check that this map intertwines the actions of $G$. For $g \in G$, then element $g \bullet x$ has $w$-component $g \bullet x_{g^{-1}\bullet w}$.

nodes.name: Equivariance computed
nodes.statement: This implies \[ \Phi( g \bullet x)(h) = h\bullet (g \bullet x)_{h^{-1} \bullet \hat v} = h g \bullet x_{(hg)^{-1} \bullet \hat v} = \Phi (x) (hg). \] The proof of the isomorphism for $\prod_{w | v} \cO_w^\times$ is similar.

nodes.name: S-ideles as products of coinduced modules
nodes.statement: We note that by \ref{lem:semi-local iso coind} we have \[ \A_{S,l}^\times \cong \prod_{v \in S} \coind_{D_{\hat v}} l_{\hat v}^\times \times \prod_{v \not\in S} \coind_{D_{\hat v}} \cO_{\hat v}^\times \]
nodes.statement_short: S-ideles as products of coinduced modules

nodes.name: Shapiro's lemma
nodes.statement: By Shapiro's lemma (\ref{lem:Shapiro}) we have \[ H^n(l/k,\A_{S,l}^\times) \cong \prod_{v \in S} H^n(l_{\hat v}/k_v , l_{\hat v}^\times) \times \prod_{v \not\in S} H^n(l_{\hat v}/k_v , \cO_{\hat v}^\times) \]

nodes.name: Unramified units are trivial
nodes.statement: For $v \not\in S$, the extension $l_{\hat{v}}/l_v$ is unramified, so by \ref{lem:unramified units trivial} $\cO_{\hat v}^\times$ has trivial cohomology.

nodes.name: Same character, so rationally isomorphic
nodes.statement: The representations $M \otimes \Q$ and $L_S \otimes \Q$ have the same character (this is just the character of the representation $V_S$). Therefore the representations $M \otimes \Q$ and $L_S \otimes \Q$ are isomorphic.

nodes.name: Finite index sublattice has same Herbrand quotient
nodes.statement: Hence $M$ is isomorphic to subrepresentation of finite index in $L_S$, so by \ref{lem:herbrand ses} and \ref{lem:herbrand finite} they have the same Herbrand quotient.
nodes.statement_short: Finite index sublattice has same Herbrand quotient

nodes.name: Apply the L_S computation
nodes.statement: The result then follows from \ref{lem:herbrand L_S}.

nodes.name: Finite kernel does not change h
nodes.statement: Since $\log_S$ has finite kernel, the Herbrand quotient of $\cO_{l,S}^\times$ is equal to that of $\log_S(\cO_S^\times)$.
nodes.statement_short: Finite kernel does not change h

nodes.name: Log units plus Z form a lattice
nodes.statement: By Dirichlet's unit theorem, $\log_S(\cO_S^\times) \oplus \Z$ is a lattice in $V_S$.
nodes.statement_short: Log units plus Z form a lattice

nodes.name: Divide the known quotients
nodes.statement: We know the Herbrand quotient of $\log_S(\cO_S^\times) \oplus \Z$ from \ref{lem:herbrand log lattice}, and the Herbrand quotient of $\Z$ from \ref{lem:H2 cyclic Z}.

nodes.name: Compare N(P)^{-s} with the log Euler factor
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a prime. For $s > 1$ we have \[ \left|N(P)^{-s} - \log\left( \frac{1}{1-N(P)^{-s}}\right)\right| \ll N(P)^{-2s} \]
nodes.statement_short: Compare N(P)^{-s} with the log Euler factor

nodes.name: Prime sum is asymptotic to log zeta
nodes.statement: Since $\sum N(P)^{-2s}$ is bounded in the region $s > 1$ (this follows from the convergence of the Dedekind zeta function), we have \[ \sum_P N(P)^{-s} \sim \sum_P \log\left( \frac{1}{1-N(P)^{-s}} \right) = \log \zeta_l(s), \] where $\zeta_l$ is the Dedekind zeta function (\texttt{NumberField.dedekindZeta}).
nodes.statement_short: Prime sum is asymptotic to log zeta

nodes.name: Simple pole of zeta
nodes.statement: By the analytic class number formula (\verb!NumberField.tendsto_sub_one_mul_dedekindZeta_nhdsGT!) there is a positive real number $r$ such that \[ \zeta_l(s) = \frac{r}{s-1} + O(1) \qquad (s > 1). \]

nodes.name: log zeta ~ log 1/(s-1)
nodes.statement: This implies \[ \log(\zeta_l(s)) \sim \log\left( \frac{1}{s-1}\right). \]

nodes.name: Show higher-degree primes have density 0
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be the set of primes of degree larger than one. It's sufficient to prove that $M$ has Dirichlet density $0$.

nodes.name: Rewrite as a Dirichlet series
nodes.statement: We have \[ \sum_{P \in M} N(P)^{-s} = \sum_{n \in \N} A(n) n^{-s}, \] Where $A$ is the number of primes of degree $>1$ with norm $n$.

nodes.name: Bounds on A(n)
nodes.statement: Note that $A(n) \le [l:\Q]$. Also $A(n)=0$ unless $n=m^r$ for positive integer $m$ and $1 \le r \le [l:Q]$.

nodes.name: Bound by zeta values
nodes.statement: This implies \[ \sum_{P \in M} N(P)^{-s} \le [l:\Q] \sum_{r=2}^{[l:\Q]} \sum_{m =1} ^\infty m^{-rs} \le [l:\Q] (\zeta_\Q(2) + \cdots + \zeta_\Q([l:\Q]) ). \]

nodes.name: Density 0
nodes.statement: Since the sum above is bounded on the region $s > 1$, the set $M$ has Dirichlet density $0$.

nodes.name: Degree-one primes of k and l
nodes.statement: Let $M_k$ be the set of degree $1$ primes of $k$ and $M_l$ the set of degree $1$ primes of $l$. Every prime $Q$ in $M_l$ lies above some prime $P \in M_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Degree-one primes of k and l

nodes.name: Exactly [l:k] above split primes
nodes.statement: If there is a prime $Q$ above $P$, then there are precisely $[l:k]$ of them; this happens when $P$ splits completely in $l$.

nodes.name: Compare Dirichlet series
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be the set of $P \in M_k$ which split completely in $l$. Then we have \[ \sum_{P \in M} N(P)^{-s} = \frac{1}{[l:k]} \sum_{Q \in M_l} N(Q)^{-s} \sim \frac{1}{[l:k]} \log\left( \frac{1}{s-1}\right). \] Here we have used \ref{lem:Dirichlet density degree one}.

nodes.name: Orthogonality and L-function computation
nodes.statement: Let $s > 1$. All the series in the following calculation converge absolutely in this region. The implied constants in the $O(1)$ terms do not depend on $s$. \begin{align*} \sum_{P \in M} |N(P)|^{-s} &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_P \sum_\chi \chi(P) N(P)^{-s}\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_P \sum_\chi -\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}) + O(1)\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_P \sum_\chi -\log |1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}| + O(1)\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \sum_\chi \sum_P -\log |1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}| + O(1)\\ &= \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \log \left(\prod_\chi |L(s,\chi)| \right) + O(1)\\ &\le \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \log \left(\frac{1}{s-1}\right) + O(1). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Justify interchange
nodes.statement: Interchanging the order of summation is justified because the series converge absolutely.

nodes.name: Choice of logarithm branch
nodes.statement: We need to be slightly careful about which branch of the logarithm we are using here. In the expression $\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ we shall mean the branch which is continuous on the ball of radius $1$, centred about $1$.

nodes.name: Imaginary parts cancel
nodes.statement: The imaginary parts of $\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ and $\log(1-\bar \chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ cancel out; this justifies replacing $\log(1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s})$ by $\log |1-\chi(P) N(P)^{-s}|$.

nodes.name: Sets of split primes and of trivial primes
nodes.statement: Let $M_1$ be the set of degree $1$ primes of $\cO_{k,S}$ which split in $l$ and let $M_2$ be the set of primes of $\cO_{k,S}$ whose image in $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ is zero. Given $P \in M_1$, the norm map $l_{\hat v}^\times \to k_v^\times$ is the identity map, and is in particular surjective. Hence the image of $P$ in $H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)$ is zero. This shows that $M_1 \subseteq M_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Sets of split primes and of trivial primes

nodes.name: Compare prime sums
nodes.statement: This implies for $s> 1$: \[ \sum_{P \in M_1} N(P)^{-s} \le \sum_{P \in M_2} N(P)^{-s} . \]

nodes.name: Density bound
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:density bound} we have \[ \sum_{P \in M_1} N(P)^{-s} \le \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|} \log \left(\frac{1}{1-s}\right) + O(1). \]

nodes.name: Density of split primes
nodes.statement: By \ref{lem:Dirichlet density split} the left hand side is asymptotic to $\frac{1}{[l:k]}\log \left(\frac{1}{1-s}\right)$.

nodes.name: Compare densities
nodes.statement: Therefore $\frac{1}{[l:k]} \le \frac{1}{|H^0_{\Tate}(l/k,\Cl_l)|}$.

nodes.name: Reduce to Sylow fixed fields
nodes.statement: For each prime number $p$ dividing $[l:k]$ we let $k_p$ be the fixed field of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $S_p$ of $\Gal(l/k)$. By \ref{cor:cohomology sub Sylow}, it's suffient to prove \[ H^1(l/k_p, \Cl_{l}) = 0, \qquad |H^2(l/k_p, \Cl_{l})| \le [l:k_p]. \]

nodes.name: Reduce to solvable groups
nodes.statement: Since $S_p$ is solvable, this reduces us to the case that $\Gal(l/k)$ is solvable.

nodes.name: Induction down cyclic quotients
nodes.statement: We'll prove the result by induction on $k$ starting with $k=l$ and working downwards in cyclic quotients. Clearly the result holds for $k=l$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Assume the result for a subfield $m$ of $l$ and let $m/k$ be cyclic.

nodes.name: Degree-1 inflation-restriction
nodes.statement: We have an inflation restriction sequence: \[ 0 \to H^1(m/k, \Cl_{m}) \to H^1(l/k, \Cl_{l}) \to H^1(l/m,\Cl_{l}). \]

nodes.name: H^1 vanishes
nodes.statement: The first term is zero by \ref{cor:H1 H2 cyclic idele class} and the last term is zero by the inductive hypothesis. Therefore $H^1(l/k,\Cl_l) \cong 0$.

nodes.name: Degree-2 inflation-restriction
nodes.statement: Since $H^1(l/m,\Cl_l)$ is assumed to be zero, we also have an inflation-restriction sequence in dimension 2: \[ 0 \to H^2(m/k, \Cl_m) \to H^2(l/k, \Cl_l) \to H^2(l/m,\Cl_l). \]

nodes.name: Bound |H^2|
nodes.statement: By the inductive hypothesis we have $|H^2(l/m,\Cl_l)| \le [l:m]$ and by \ref{cor:H1 H2 cyclic idele class} we have $|H^2(m/k, \Cl_m)| = [m : k]$. It follows that $|H^2(l/k,\Cl_l)| \le [l : k]$.
